Rust · data-oriented design · build an ECS

rust-dod

Build an archetype entity component system from nothing, in fifteen chapters you read, compile and step through: from an entity as a number to a game running on it.

Start with 1.1, an entity is a number

Data-oriented design in Rust, in two courses and a dojo:

  1. Build an ECS. Start here. Fifteen chapters that build an archetype entity component system from nothing, in the order of its name: entities, then components, then systems. It ends with a game running on it. Each chapter is a program that compiles on its own, the output it must print, and a guide that builds it step by step.
  2. Advanced: layout and SIMD. Seven lessons, for after. They cover what a loop fetches from memory, aliasing and what a &mut slice promises, what the compiler vectorizes and how to check it in the assembly, and which layout suits which access pattern.
  3. The dojo. The five building blocks an ECS is made of, taken out on their own: a playground to watch each one work and break, and a kata to write it yourself, timed, against a harness, until your hands know it.

There is no renderer, no window and no crate to install: only data, and the loops that stream it. Every program is one file, and builds with plain rustc.

This is the Rust twin of rin-dod, the same courses in rin. The programs print the same output, line for line, and each guide has a table of what changed between the two.

git diff --no-index ecs/src/2.components/2.5.typed_access/typed_access.rs ecs/src/2.components/2.6.add_remove/add_remove.rs

The ECS is called kayan, after the C sketch it grew out of.

The Rust in it

The style is rin-dod's: plain structs, plain loops, data in arrays, no framework. What Rust adds is checked:

  • Components are plain data, checked. A column holds bytes, and turning bytes back into a component is only sound if any bytes are a valid value. The pod! macro checks at compile time that every field is plain data and the struct has no padding.
  • **unsafe is fenced in.** Every program starts with #![deny(unsafe_code)]. The whole ECS has five one-line unsafe blocks, each with a // SAFETY: reason: four views of a column's bytes, and one of a value's. Every program that has one runs clean under Miri, Rust's checker for undefined behaviour.
  • Several of rin-dod's quiet bugs don't compile. A table reference kept across the creation of another (2.4), a component reference kept across a spawn (2.5), despawning while iterating a table (3.3). Each is a lesson in rin-dod and a compiler error here, and the guides show the error. What the borrow checker can't see is a stale number, a row or an entity index, and generations, handles and commands are how both languages handle those.
  • Vec, used like an arena. The world's data lives in Vecs that only grow while the game runs, and the frame's commands in Vecs that are cleared every frame and keep their memory. That is an arena's allocation pattern, with nothing freed one at a time.
  • No dependencies. The standard library has everything: Vec, HashMap, slices, get_disjoint_mut for two tables at once.

Build and run

Needs Rust 1.86 or later (rustup, or your system's package). Every chapter and lesson is its own program, named after its file:

cargo run --bin archetypes

Or build one by hand, as one file with no crate around it:

rustc --edition 2024 ecs/src/2.components/2.4.archetypes/archetypes.rs -o archetypes
./archetypes

python tools/check.py builds every program with rustc and warnings as errors, runs it, and compares what it prints with its .expected file. --release builds them optimised, --clippy runs clippy over everything, --miri runs the programs with unsafe under Miri (it needs a nightly toolchain with the miri component), --bless rewrites the expected files after a deliberate change, and a word filters the programs. tools/check_snippets.py checks that every sample in the guides is in its program, and every output sample in its expected file:

python tools/check.py ecs
python tools/check.py --release --clippy
python tools/check.py --miri
python tools/check_snippets.py

Reading it in a browser

Open website/index.html. It has every chapter's and lesson's guide, its source with line numbers, and the output it must print, with an index on the left. It is generated from the files in this repository, so after changing a program or a guide run python tools/site.py to bring it up to date.

Build an ECS · part 1, entities · 1.1

An entity is a number

ecs/src/1.entities/1.1.ids/ids.rs

An ECS has three parts: Entities, Components and Systems. This chapter builds all three in the simplest way that works, about a hundred lines, so you can see the whole shape before any of it gets clever. The chapters after this one keep the shape and fix its costs, one at a time.

The idea

A game is full of things: a turret, drones, bullets. An ECS splits each thing into three parts:

  • An entity names the thing. It is just a number. It has no data and no behaviour of its own.
  • Components are the thing's data: a position, a velocity, health. Each component is plain data, a small struct or a number.
  • Systems are the behaviour: loops that run over every entity that has the components they need. Movement runs over everything with a position and a velocity.

A turret is entity 0 with a position and health. A drone is entity 1 with a position, a velocity and health. Nothing says "turret" or "drone" anywhere; what a thing is comes from which components it has.

Step 1: the entity

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Entity {
    index: u32,
}

An entity is a number, so why the struct? Because a bare u32 can be mixed up with any other u32. A function that takes an Entity cannot be handed a count or a row index by mistake, and the struct costs nothing at run time: it compiles to the same 4 bytes. It also gives the number room to grow, and in 1.3 it does.

Step 2: the world

Where do components live? The simplest answer: one array per component, with one slot for every possible entity, indexed by the entity's number. Beside each array, a flag per entity saying whether it has that component.

#[derive(Default)]
struct World {
    count: u32,
    positions: [Vec2; 8],
    has_position: [bool; 8],
    velocities: [Vec2; 8],
    has_velocity: [bool; 8],
    healths: [f32; 8],
    has_health: [bool; 8],
}

Look at the shape. This is lesson 1's struct of arrays: every position together, every velocity together. An entity's data is spread across the arrays, all at the same index. Entity 1's position is positions[1] and its health is healths[1].

Step 3: spawning

A new entity is the next number:

    fn spawn(&mut self) -> Entity {
        assert!(self.count < 8, "the world is full");
        let e = Entity { index: self.count };
        self.count += 1;
        e
    }

It has no components yet: every flag for its number is still false.

Step 4: giving it components

Giving an entity a component is writing the value at its number and raising the flag:

    fn set_position(&mut self, e: Entity, p: Vec2) {
        self.positions[e.index as usize] = p;
        self.has_position[e.index as usize] = true;
    }

set_velocity and set_health are the same, one per component. Writing one method per component type is tedious, and Part 2 replaces all of them with a single generic set. For now, plain is better: you can see exactly which bytes get written.

Building a drone is spawning a number and attaching data to it:

    let drone_a = w.spawn();
    w.set_position(drone_a, Vec2 { x: 10.0, y: 0.0 });
    w.set_velocity(drone_a, Vec2 { x: -1.0, y: 0.5 });
    w.set_health(drone_a, 100.0);

Step 5: a system

A system is a loop. Movement runs over everything with a position and a velocity:

fn movement_system(w: &mut World, dt: f32) -> u32 {
    let mut moved = 0;
    for i in 0..w.count as usize {
        if w.has_position[i] && w.has_velocity[i] {
            w.positions[i].x += w.velocities[i].x * dt;
            w.positions[i].y += w.velocities[i].y * dt;
            moved += 1;
        }
    }
    moved
}

It doesn't know about turrets, drones or bullets. It knows about positions and velocities, and anything that has both moves, including bullets that didn't exist when the system was written. That's the ECS idea in one function: behaviour attaches to data, not to types of thing.

A system is a free function, not a method of World. That's a choice worth noticing: the world owns the data, and the systems are separate code that runs over it.

Run it

spawned turret 0, drones 1 and 2, bullet 3
    entity 0  position ( 0.00,  0.00)  velocity -                health 500
    entity 1  position (10.00,  0.00)  velocity (-1.00,  0.50)  health 100
    entity 2  position ( 0.00, 10.00)  velocity ( 0.50, -1.00)  health 100
    entity 3  position ( 0.00,  0.00)  velocity ( 4.00,  4.00)  health -
step 1: the movement system looked at 4 entities and moved 3
step 2: the movement system looked at 4 entities and moved 3
...
every component array has room for 8; 4 entities exist
    positions hold 4 values, velocities 3, healths 3

The turret has no velocity, so movement skips it. The bullet has no health, and nothing cares.

What this costs

It works, and every later chapter keeps this shape: entities are numbers, components are arrays of plain data, systems are loops. But look at the last two lines of the output and at the loop:

  1. Every array is as long as the most entities the world can hold. Velocity has room for 8 and holds 3. A game with 10,000 entities and 50 component types would have 50 arrays of 10,000, mostly empty.
  2. Every system visits every entity and checks flags to skip the ones that don't apply. Movement looked at 4 and moved 3. With 10,000 entities of which 50 move, it would look at 10,000 to move 50.
  3. Nothing can be destroyed. There's no despawn, and numbers only go up.

The next chapter fixes 3. Chapter 1.4 packs the data so systems stop skipping, and Part 2 fixes 1 and 2 for good with tables.

Rust notes

The Rust this chapter uses for the first time, next to rin:

rinRust
kayan_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world)a method: fn spawn(&mut self) in impl World, called w.spawn()
w*.countself.count; a reference is followed for you when you name a field
w: kayan_world = {};#[derive(Default)] on the struct, then World::default(): every field zeroed
indexing with a u32e.index as usize: Rust indexes with usize and converts only when asked
for (i: u32 = 0; i < n; i += 1)for i in 0..n, a range that stops before n
printfmt(...); exit(1);assert!(cond, "message"): stops the program with the message if cond is false
printf("%5.2f", x)print!("{:5.2}", x), or {i} to name a variable in the string
return moved;moved as the last line, without a ;: the last expression is the value

#[derive(Clone, Copy)] on Entity lets it be copied like a number. Without it, passing an Entity to a function would move it, and the caller could not use it again.

Try

  1. Give the turret a velocity and run it. Nothing else changes: the turret moves because it now has the data movement wants.
  2. Add a lifetime: [f32; 8] component with its flags, and an aging_system that counts it down. How many places did you have to touch?
  3. Spawn a ninth entity. Read the panic message, then think about what a game would need instead of a fixed 8.

Build an ECS · part 1, entities · 1.2

Despawning, and reusing numbers

ecs/src/1.entities/1.2.despawn/despawn.rs

In the dojo: 1. free list and generations, on its own, to watch and to practise.

Games destroy things constantly: a bullet hits, a drone dies, an effect fades. 1.1 could only add. This chapter adds despawn, and with it the first real problem in ECS design: what happens to an entity's number when the entity is gone?

Step 1: a free list

If despawned numbers were never reused, a game firing one bullet a frame would use up 8 numbers in 8 frames and 4 billion in a couple of years of play. More to the point, every array would keep growing. So despawned numbers go on a free list, and spawning takes from it first:

#[derive(Default)]
struct World {
    count: u32,
    alive: [bool; 8],
    free: [u32; 8],
    free_count: u32,

count is now how many numbers have ever been handed out, not how many entities exist; the numbers on the free list are the gaps. alive says which numbers are in use.

Step 2: spawning reuses

    fn spawn(&mut self) -> Entity {
        let index = if self.free_count > 0 {
            self.free_count -= 1;
            self.free[self.free_count as usize]
        } else {
            assert!(self.count < 8, "the world is full");
            self.count += 1;
            self.count - 1
        };
        self.alive[index as usize] = true;
        Entity { index }
    }

The free list is a stack: the last number freed is the first reused.

Step 3: despawning

    fn despawn(&mut self, e: Entity) {
        let i = e.index as usize;
        self.alive[i] = false;
        self.has_position[i] = false;
        self.has_velocity[i] = false;
        self.has_health[i] = false;
        self.free[self.free_count as usize] = e.index;
        self.free_count += 1;
    }

Despawning lowers every flag, so the entity's old components can't leak into whatever reuses the number. The values stay in the arrays, but with the flags down nobody reads them. Systems need no change: a despawned entity has no flags, so movement skips it without knowing anything about despawning.

Step 4: the bug

Now the problem. Things in a game refer to other things: a turret aims at a drone, a missile chases a target, a health bar follows a unit. With entities as numbers, a reference is a number:

    let target = drone_a;

The program then destroys the drone, and the turret fires. The bullet is a new entity, and it takes the first free number, the drone's:

the turret targets entity 1, a drone
...
entity 1 is destroyed and despawned
    entity 1  (free)
the turret fires: the bullet is entity 1
...
the turret aims at entity 1, at (2.00, 2.00), moving (4.00, 4.00)
    that is the turret's own bullet, not the drone: the number was reused

Nothing told the turret its target died, and nothing could: references can be anywhere, in any number of places. The number in target is still a valid number, it just names a different entity now. No crash, no error, just a turret shooting at its own bullet. In a real game this is the bug where a homing missile turns around mid-flight, or a health bar jumps to another unit.

Rust doesn't catch this. The borrow checker tracks references: a &Vec2 pointing at the drone's position could not outlive the drone. But target is a number, copied out of an Entity, and the borrow checker has nothing to say about numbers. A stale number is a logic bug, and logic bugs compile. Keep that in mind: this course will meet it again, and Rust's guarantees stop at the same place each time.

Run it

the turret targets entity 1, a drone
    entity 0  position ( 0.00,  0.00)  velocity -                health 500
    entity 1  position (10.00,  0.00)  velocity (-1.00,  0.50)  health 100
    entity 2  position ( 0.00, 10.00)  velocity ( 0.50, -1.00)  health 100

the turret fires: the bullet is entity 1
...

Why not just...

  • ...never reuse numbers? The arrays would grow forever, and every system would walk an ever-longer list of dead numbers.
  • ...find and clear every reference on despawn? You'd need to know where every reference lives. That's exactly what an ECS is trying to avoid: things refer to each other loosely, by number.
  • **...check alive[target.index]?** It says true: the number is alive. It's alive as a different entity, and nothing can tell the two apart.

The next chapter tells them apart with one extra number per entity.

an out-of-range index, unchecked in a Release buildevery array index is checked, in Release too; past the end, the program stops

Try

  1. Despawn the bullet too, then spawn two more entities. Which numbers do they get, and in what order? Why?
  2. Comment out the lines that lower the flags in despawn and run it. What does the new bullet have that it shouldn't?
  3. Despawn drone_a twice. What does the free list look like after? Spawn twice more and see why that is a problem.

Build an ECS · part 1, entities · 1.3

Generations

ecs/src/1.entities/1.3.generations/generations.rs

In the dojo: 1. free list and generations, on its own, to watch and to practise.

1.2 ended with a turret aiming at its own bullet. The number it remembered was reused, and nothing could tell the old entity from the new one. The fix is small and used by nearly every ECS: count each number's lives.

The idea

Give each number a generation. Entity 1 in its first life is 1:1. When it's despawned, number 1's generation goes up to 2, so the next entity to reuse it is 1:2. A reference carries both numbers:

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Entity {
    index: u32,
    generation: NonZeroU32,
}

A reference with a generation is called a handle. The turret's target is the handle 1:1. After the drone dies and the bullet becomes 1:2, the target still says 1:1, and 1:1 != 1:2. One comparison catches the bug.

Why NonZeroU32? Generations start at 1, so 0 is never a real generation. NonZeroU32 makes that a rule of the type, and Rust puts the forbidden 0 to use: an Option<Entity> stores its None there. So "no entity" is None, and it costs nothing. The program checks: an Option<Entity> is 8 bytes, the same as an Entity.

Step 1: the world keeps generations

#[derive(Default)]
struct World {
    count: u32,
    generations: [Option<NonZeroU32>; 8],
    free: [u32; 8],
    free_count: u32,

generations[i] is the life number i is in now, or the life it'll be in next if i is free; None means the number was never handed out. 1.2's alive array is gone, because the generations already say it:

    fn alive(&self, e: Entity) -> bool {
        e.index < self.count && self.generations[e.index as usize] == Some(e.generation)
    }

A handle is alive when its generation is the one its number is in now.

Step 2: despawn bumps the generation

    fn despawn(&mut self, e: Entity) -> Result<(), Error> {
        if !self.alive(e) {
            return Err(Error::Dead);
        }
        let i = e.index as usize;
        self.has_position[i] = false;
        self.has_velocity[i] = false;
        self.has_health[i] = false;
        self.generations[i] = e.generation.checked_add(1);
        self.free[self.free_count as usize] = e.index;
        self.free_count += 1;
        Ok(())
    }

The generation goes up at despawn, not at the next spawn. So a free number already holds a generation that no handle has been given yet, and no handle can match it. That's why there's no separate alive flag: "free" and "every existing handle is stale" are the same fact.

Despawning a dead handle now returns Err(Error::Dead) and changes nothing. In 1.2, despawning twice put the same number on the free list twice, and two later entities would have shared it.

Step 3: a result you can't ignore

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
enum Error {
    Dead,
}

despawn returns Result<(), Error>: Ok(()), or why nothing happened. A Result is must-use: dropping one unread is a warning, and this course builds with warnings as errors. Where the program knows a handle is alive, it says so:

    w.despawn(drone_a).expect("the drone is alive");

expect unwraps an Ok and stops the program with the message on an Err. That's stronger than ignoring the result: if the belief is ever wrong, you find out on that line.

Step 4: generations start at 1

            assert!(self.count < 8, "the world is full");
            self.generations[self.count as usize] = Some(ONE);
            self.count += 1;
            self.count - 1

A brand-new number starts at generation 1, NonZeroU32::MIN. So no handle can ever have generation 0, and "no entity" is None rather than a special handle.

Step 5: every access checks

    fn get_position(&self, e: Entity) -> Option<&Vec2> {
        if !self.alive(e) || !self.has_position[e.index as usize] {
            return None;
        }
        Some(&self.positions[e.index as usize])
    }

Reading through a handle checks it first. A dead handle gives None instead of whatever data now sits at the number. The turret checks its target every time it aims, and picks a new one when the old one is gone:

    let p = match w.get_position(*target) {
        Some(p) => p,
        None => {
            println!("the turret's target {target} is dead; it picks {fallback} instead");
            *target = fallback;
            w.get_position(*target).expect("the fallback is alive and has a position")
        }
    };

drone 1:1 is destroyed and despawned
the turret fires: the bullet is 1:2, the same number in its next life

    entity 1:2  position ( 2.00,  2.00)  velocity ( 4.00,  4.00)  health -
    entity 2:1  position ( 0.25,  9.50)  velocity ( 0.50, -1.00)  health 100

no entity is None, and an Option<Entity> is 8 bytes, the same as an Entity's 8

The same moment that ended 1.2, and this time the handle knows.

Notes

  • Cost: a handle is 8 bytes instead of 4, and checking one is one load and one compare. Cheap enough to do on every access.
  • Running out: checked_add(1) gives None after a number's 4 billionth life, and reusing it then stops the program at the expect in spawn, rather than silently wrapping around to a generation an old handle might hold. Some ECSs use fewer bits for the generation, packing index and generation into one u32 or u64. The idea is the same.
  • What it doesn't fix: the arrays are still as long as the most entities, and systems still skip holes. That's next.

Build an ECS · part 1, entities · 1.4

The entity index

ecs/src/1.entities/1.4.entity_index/entity_index.rs

In the dojo: 2. swap-remove and the back-reference, 3. the slot map, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

Handles fixed identity. Two costs from 1.1 remain: every array is as long as the most entities, and every system walks all of it, skipping holes. This chapter packs the data: live entities in rows 0 to len - 1, no holes, so a system is a straight loop over the rows. That's the stream lesson 1 measured as the fast case.

Packing has a consequence that the rest of the course is built around: an entity's data no longer sits at its number, and it moves.

To keep this chapter about the index, every entity is the same kind of thing: a particle with a position and a velocity. Part 2 brings back different kinds, each packed in a table of its own.

Step 1: two halves

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Slot {
    generation: NonZeroU32,
    row: u32,
}
#[derive(Default)]
struct World {
    slots: Vec<Slot>,
    free: Vec<u32>,

    entities: Vec<Entity>,
    positions: Vec<Vec2>,
    velocities: Vec<Vec2>,
}

The world now has two halves:

  • The slots, indexed by the entity's number. A number never moves, so this is where a handle looks first. A slot holds the generation from 1.3, and now also the row the entity's data is in.
  • The rows, packed. Each row's components side by side in the Vecs, and entities[row] saying which entity owns the row. All three Vecs always have the same length: the number of live entities.

The two point at each other: slot to row, row to entity. That two-way link is called the entity index.

The fixed [_; 8] arrays are gone too. Part 1 used them to keep the first chapters about one thing at a time; from here on everything is a Vec, and the 8-entity limit goes with them.

Step 2: spawning appends a row

        let slot = &mut self.slots[index as usize];
        slot.row = self.entities.len() as u32;
        let e = Entity { index, generation: slot.generation };
        self.entities.push(e);
        self.positions.push(p);
        self.velocities.push(v);
        e

The number comes from the free list or the end, exactly as in 1.3; the free list is now a Vec used as a stack, so pop takes the last number freed. The data goes in the next row, which is always the end of the packed rows. The slot records where.

Step 3: despawning swap-removes

To keep the rows packed, a hole can't be left behind. The last row moves into it, called swap-remove, and Vec has it built in:

    fn despawn(&mut self, e: Entity) -> Result<(), Error> {
        if !self.alive(e) {
            return Err(Error::Dead);
        }
        let slot = &mut self.slots[e.index as usize];
        let row = slot.row as usize;
        slot.generation = slot.generation.checked_add(1).expect("a number has lived 4 billion lives");
        self.entities.swap_remove(row);
        self.positions.swap_remove(row);
        self.velocities.swap_remove(row);
        if let Some(moved) = self.entities.get(row) {
            self.slots[moved.index as usize].row = row as u32;
        }
        self.free.push(e.index);
        Ok(())
    }

swap_remove(row) moves the last element into row and shortens the Vec by one. What no Vec can do for you is the part that matters:

        if let Some(moved) = self.entities.get(row) {
            self.slots[moved.index as usize].row = row as u32;
        }

The entity that owned the last row now lives somewhere else, and its slot must say so. entities[row] is how we know whose slot to fix: without that column, a moved row would be anonymous. If the despawned row was the last one, nothing moved and get(row) is None. Forget these lines and the moved entity's handle still finds a row, just the wrong one, and nothing crashes.

Swap-remove costs one row copy, however many rows there are. Vec::remove shifts everything after the hole down to keep the order, at the cost of a copy of every later row. ECSs don't promise order, so they take the cheap one.

Step 4: reading through the index

    fn get_position(&self, e: Entity) -> Option<&Vec2> {
        if !self.alive(e) {
            return None;
        }
        Some(&self.positions[self.slots[e.index as usize].row as usize])
    }

Handle to slot to row. That's one extra lookup compared with 1.3, and it's the price of packing. Systems don't pay it, because they don't go through handles. In fact, the system no longer needs the world at all:

fn movement_system(positions: &mut [Vec2], velocities: &[Vec2], dt: f32) {
    for (p, v) in positions.iter_mut().zip(velocities) {
        p.x += v.x * dt;
        p.y += v.y * dt;
    }
}

No flags, no holes, no handles: every row is a live particle, so the system takes the two columns as slices and streams them. zip walks them together and stops at the shorter one, so the loop has no index to check. This is the loop the rest of the course works to keep. Calling it hands it two fields of the world at once:

    movement_system(&mut w.positions, &w.velocities, 0.5);

Step 5: checking the invariant

Rows move all the time, and one missed slot update corrupts the world silently. So the world can check itself:

    fn verify(&self) -> u32 {
        let mut problems = 0;
        for (row, &e) in self.entities.iter().enumerate() {
            if !self.alive(e) {
                println!("verify: row {row} holds dead entity {e}");
                problems += 1;
            } else if self.slots[e.index as usize].row as usize != row {
                println!("verify: {e} is in row {row}, its slot says row {}", self.slots[e.index as usize].row);
                problems += 1;
            }
        }
        let live = self.slots.len() - self.free.len();
        if live != self.entities.len() {
            println!("verify: {} rows, {live} live entities", self.entities.len());
            problems += 1;
        }
        problems
    }

The invariant: every row belongs to a live entity whose slot points back at that row, and there are as many rows as live entities. Every structural change in this course has to keep it true. When something goes wrong later, run verify first.

Run it

spawned 5 particles
    row 0  0:1  position ( 0.00,  0.00)
    row 1  1:1  position ( 1.00,  0.00)
    ...
    row 4  4:1  position ( 4.00,  0.00)
    slots:  0 -> row 0  1 -> row 1  2 -> row 2  3 -> row 3  4 -> row 4
despawn 1:1, in row 1: the last row moves into the hole
    row 0  0:1  position ( 0.00,  0.00)
    row 1  4:1  position ( 4.00,  0.00)
    row 2  2:1  position ( 2.00,  0.00)
    row 3  3:1  position ( 3.00,  0.00)
    slots:  0 -> row 0  1 free  2 -> row 2  3 -> row 3  4 -> row 1

...
verify: 0 problems

Follow 4:1: it starts in row 4, moves to row 1 when 1:1 is removed, and its handle still finds it there because its slot was updated.

Part 1 in one picture

handle 4:1 ──> slots[4] { generation 1, row 1 } ──> rows[1] { owner 4:1, position, velocity }
  • Handles never change: they're what the rest of the game keeps.
  • Slots never move: one per number, holding the generation and the row.
  • Rows move all the time, and stay packed so systems can stream them.

Part 2 keeps exactly this, and generalizes the one kind of row into tables, one per combination of components.

Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.1

Components and signatures

ecs/src/2.components/2.1.components/components.rs

Part 1 hard-coded its components: a positions Vec, a velocities Vec, a flag for each. Adding a component meant editing the world, spawn, despawn and every printer. Part 2 builds a world that works for components it has never heard of. This chapter lays the ground with four ideas:

  1. A component is a plain struct.
  2. Each component type has an id, a small number fixed at compile time.
  3. The world keeps a registry: per id, the component's size, alignment and name, which is all it needs to store bytes it doesn't understand.
  4. A set of components is a signature: one bit per id in a u64.

There are no entities in this chapter. 2.3 puts the two halves together.

Step 1: components are plain structs

component!(Position { at: Vec2 });
component!(Velocity { per_second: Vec2 });
component!(Health { points: f32, max: f32 });
component!(Damage { amount: f32 });
component!(Lifetime { seconds: f32 });
component!(Burning { per_second: f32 });
component!(Turret { cooldown: f32, timer: f32 });

Each line declares a struct with those fields, plus what the world needs to know about it (Step 4 opens the macro up). No methods, no references to other entities, no idea that a world exists. That's deliberate. Behaviour belongs to systems, and data that knows nothing can be copied, moved and stored as raw bytes, which the world is about to do.

Why Position { at: Vec2 } rather than using Vec2 directly? Because a component's type is how the world tells components apart. Position and velocity are both two floats, but they're different things, and making them different types is what lets you ask for one and not the other.

Step 2: an id per component type

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
enum ComponentId {
    Position,
    Velocity,
    Health,
    Damage,
    Lifetime,
    Burning,
    Turret,
}

The enum gives each component a number: its position in the list. Every component implements a trait that carries its id, and its reflect record:

trait Component: Copy + 'static {
    const ID: u32;
    const INFO: &'static Info;
}

Position::ID is a constant, 0, known at compile time. Nothing is looked up at run time; in generated code, the id is just a number.

Copy + 'static says what a component may be: something you can copy byte for byte, holding no borrowed references. That rules out a String or a Vec inside a component (they own memory elsewhere, so copying their bytes would copy a pointer, not the data). Components are their bytes and nothing else.

Step 3: the world speaks ids, never types

The world can't be generic over component types. Which combinations exist is only known while the game runs. So the world works in ids and bits, and a small typed layer translates:

fn bit(id: u32) -> u64 {
    1 << id
}

// The typed layer: from a type to the bit the world works in.
fn mask_of<T: Component>() -> u64 {
    bit(T::ID)
}

Game code says mask_of::<Velocity>(), and the world only ever sees 2, a bit.

Step 4: the reflect record, written by the compiler

To store a component as bytes, the world needs three facts about it: how many bytes, what alignment, and a name for printing. The compiler knows all three, and the component! macro asks it to write them down:

macro_rules! component {
    ($name:ident { $($field:ident: $ty:ty),* $(,)? }) => {
        #[derive(Clone, Copy, Default, Debug)]
        struct $name {
            $($field: $ty),*
        }

        impl Component for $name {
            const ID: u32 = ComponentId::$name as u32;
            const INFO: &'static Info = &Info { name: stringify!($name), layout: Layout::new::<$name>() };
        }
    };
}

macro_rules! matches the text you write (Position { at: Vec2 }) and expands it into code. Here it writes the struct, then the trait impl:

  • the id is the enum variant with the same name as the struct;
  • stringify!($name) turns the name into the string "Position";
  • Layout::new::<Position>() is the compiler's own size and alignment.

The record is a constant, built at compile time and stored in the program, the same thing rin's position<> is.

struct Info {
    name: &'static str,
    layout: Layout,
}

Step 5: the registry

The registry is an array of records, indexed by id:

struct World {
    infos: [Option<&'static Info>; 64],
    component_count: u32,
}
    fn register<T: Component>(&mut self) {
        assert!(T::ID < 64, "component id {} is past the 64 a signature can hold", T::ID);
        self.infos[T::ID as usize] = Some(T::INFO);
        self.component_count = self.component_count.max(T::ID + 1);
    }

Registering needs nothing but the type: w.register::<Position>(). Inside a generic function, T::ID and T::INFO work for whatever T is.

Step 6: signatures

A set of components is a u64 with a bit set per component in the set. What a thing is is a signature:

    let drone = mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>() | mask_of::<Health>();

Every question you'd ask about sets is a bit operation:

fn contains(signature: u64, wanted: u64) -> bool {
    (signature & wanted) == wanted
}

"Does this drone have what movement wants?" is contains(drone, moves), one AND and one compare. Adding a component is |, and removing one is & !:

    let put_out = burning_drone & !mask_of::<Burning>();

64 bits means at most 64 component types per world, which is plenty for learning and for most games. Larger ECSs use wider bitsets or sorted id lists; the idea is the same.

Run it

Read the bits as a table: each column is a component, each row a kind of thing. That table is the next three chapters. Each distinct row will become a table of its own.

In Rust, as in rin, & binds tighter than ==, so signature & wanted == wanted would also mean what it says. The program keeps the parentheses for anyone coming from C, where it doesn't.

Copy rules42// out anything that owns memory, a String or a Vec, so a component is its bytes43// and nothing else.44trait Component: Copy + 'static {45    const ID: u32;46    const INFO: &'static Info;47}48 49// One id per component type: its position in this enum.50#[derive(Clone, Copy)]51enum ComponentId {52    Position,53    Velocity,54    Health,55    Damage,56    Lifetime,57    Burning,58    Turret,59}60 61// Declares a component: the struct, and its Component impl. The id is the enum62// variant with the same name. The record is written by the compiler, at63// compile time: stringify! gives the name, Layout::new the size and alignment.64macro_rules! component {65    ($name:ident { $($field:ident: $ty:ty),* $(,)? }) => {66        #[derive(Clone, Copy, Default, Debug)]67        struct $name {68            $($field: $ty),*69        }70 71        impl Component for $name {72            const ID: u32 = ComponentId::$name as u32;73            const INFO: &'static Info = &Info { name: stringify!($name), layout: Layout::new::<$name>() };74        }75    };76}77 78// The components. Plain data, nothing else: no methods, no references to other79// entities, no knowledge of the world.80component!(Position { at: Vec2 });81component!(Velocity { per_second: Vec2 });82component!(Health { points: f32, max: f32 });83component!(Damage { amount: f32 });84component!(Lifetime { seconds: f32 });85component!(Burning { per_second: f32 });86component!(Turret { cooldown: f32, timer: f32 });87 88// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------89// The world's side: ids and bits, never types90// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------91 92// The registry. The world stores components as bytes, so per id it needs to93// know how many bytes, at what alignment, and a name for printing. A reflect94// record has all three.95struct World {96    infos: [Option<&'static Info>; 64],97    component_count: u32,98}99 100// One bit per component. A signature is a u64, so a world has at most 64.101fn bit(id: u32) -> u64 {102    1 << id103}104 105// The typed layer: from a type to the bit the world works in.106fn mask_of<T: Component>() -> u64 {107    bit(T::ID)108}109 110// Does a set contain every component of another? One AND and one compare.111fn contains(signature: u64, wanted: u64) -> bool {112    (signature & wanted) == wanted113}114 115impl World {116    fn new() -> World {117        World { infos: [None; 64], component_count: 0 }118    }119 120    // Hands the world T's record under T's id. Generic code can read T::INFO121    // for any component T, so registering needs nothing but the type.122    fn register<T: Component>(&mut self) {123        assert!(T::ID < 64, "component id {} is past the 64 a signature can hold", T::ID);124        self.infos[T::ID as usize] = Some(T::INFO);125        self.component_count = self.component_count.max(T::ID + 1);126    }127 128    fn info(&self, id: u32) -> &'static Info {129        self.infos[id as usize].expect("every component in a signature is registered")130    }131 132    // A signature as names, {Position Velocity}.133    fn names(&self, signature: u64) -> String {134        let names: Vec<&str> = (0..self.component_count)135            .filter(|&id| signature & bit(id) != 0)136            .map(|id| self.info(id).name)137            .collect();138        format!("{{{}}}", names.join(" "))139    }140 141    // A signature as bits, highest component first, so each column of the142    // output is one component.143    fn bits(&self, signature: u64) -> String {144        (0..self.component_count).rev().map(|id| if signature & bit(id) != 0 { '1' } else { '0' }).collect()145    }146}147 148fn yes(b: bool) -> &'static str {149    if b { "yes" } else { "no" }150}151 152fn main() {153    let mut w = World::new();154    w.register::<Position>();155    w.register::<Velocity>();156    w.register::<Health>();157    w.register::<Damage>();158    w.register::<Lifetime>();159    w.register::<Burning>();160    w.register::<Turret>();161 162    println!("the registry: {} components", w.component_count);163    println!("    id  name       size  align");164    for id in 0..w.component_count {165        let info = w.info(id);166        println!("    {id:2}  {:<9}  {:4}  {:5}", info.name, info.layout.size(), info.layout.align());167    }168 169    // What a thing is, written as the set of its components.170    let drone = mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>() | mask_of::<Health>();171    let bullet = mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>() | mask_of::<Damage>() | mask_of::<Lifetime>();172    let gun = mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Turret>();173    let burning_drone = drone | mask_of::<Burning>();174 175    println!("signatures, one bit per component, highest id first:");176    println!("    drone          {}  {}", w.bits(drone), w.names(drone));177    println!("    bullet         {}  {}", w.bits(bullet), w.names(bullet));178    println!("    turret         {}  {}", w.bits(gun), w.names(gun));179    println!("    burning drone  {}  {}", w.bits(burning_drone), w.names(burning_drone));180 181    // Which of them would a movement system want? Everything that contains182    // {Position Velocity}.183    let moves = mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>();184    println!("movement wants {}:", w.names(moves));185    println!("    drone {}, bullet {}, turret {}, burning drone {}",186        yes(contains(drone, moves)), yes(contains(bullet, moves)),187        yes(contains(gun, moves)), yes(contains(burning_drone, moves)));188 189    // Adding and removing a component is setting and clearing its bit.190    let put_out = burning_drone & !mask_of::<Burning>();191    println!("a burning drone with burning removed is a drone again: {}", yes(put_out == drone));192}

Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.2

Columns

ecs/src/2.components/2.2.columns/columns.rs

In the dojo: 4. a type-erased column, on its own, to watch and to practise.

1.4 kept components in typed Vecs: positions: Vec<Vec2>. A world that works for any component can't, because it doesn't know the types. It knows, from the registry, each component's size and alignment, and that's enough.

A column is one component's array, kept as bytes. Row r is the size bytes starting at r * size. Everything a table does with its data is a byte operation on columns: grow, copy one row over another, zero a new row. None of it depends on the type. The type comes back only at the edge, where game code reads a column as &[T].

This is also the one place in the course that needs unsafe, and the chapter is as much about how little of it there is as about columns. This chapter builds the column and exercises it by hand. 2.3 puts columns in a table.

Step 1: what a column is

struct Column {
    blocks: Vec<Block>,
    size: usize,
    id: u32,
    info: &'static Info,
}

Bytes, plus how many bytes make a row, plus which component it holds. No count: every column of a table has the same number of rows, so the table keeps that once (2.3).

The bytes live in a Vec of 16-byte blocks:

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Default)]
#[repr(C, align(16))]
struct Block([u8; 16]);

Why not a Vec<u8>? Alignment. A Vec<u8> only promises its bytes start at an address divisible by 1, and an f32 must start at a multiple of 4. align(16) makes every block, and so the start of the storage, a multiple of 16, which is enough for any component (the column checks that when it's made). Rows are packed from the start, so every row of every component lands on an address its type can live at.

Step 2: rows are byte ranges

    fn row(&self, row: usize) -> &[u8] {
        &self.bytes()[row * self.size..(row + 1) * self.size]
    }

That's the whole addressing scheme: row r is the bytes from r * size up to the next row. Copying and zeroing rows are ordinary slice operations:

    fn copy_row(&mut self, to: usize, from: usize) {
        let size = self.size;
        self.bytes_mut().copy_within(from * size..(from + 1) * size, to * size);
    }

    fn zero_row(&mut self, row: usize) {
        let size = self.size;
        self.bytes_mut()[row * size..(row + 1) * size].fill(0);
    }

copy_row is swap-remove's copy from 1.4, for any component.

Step 3: growing

    fn grow(&mut self, capacity: usize) {
        self.blocks.resize((capacity * self.size).div_ceil(16), Block::default());
    }

resize makes room for capacity rows, rounded up to whole blocks, with the new bytes zeroed. When the Vec needs a bigger allocation, it copies the rows into the new one and frees the old one. That's the difference from rin-dod's arena, which left the old block in place until the arena was cleared. Doubling the capacity each time keeps the copies to a few per table over a whole game.

Either way, the data moves when a column grows, so anything that pointed into the old block is left behind. In rin that's a silent bug. In Rust, a reference into a column borrows it, and grow needs &mut self, so the compiler won't let the two overlap. 2.5 comes back to this.

Step 4: the byte views, and the unsafe

Everything above works on &[u8] and &mut [u8], the column's bytes. Getting those from the blocks is one line, and it's unsafe:

    #[allow(unsafe_code)]
    fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
        // SAFETY: a Block is 16 initialised bytes with no padding, so the Vec's
        // buffer is `len * 16` initialised bytes.
        unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(self.blocks.as_ptr().cast::<u8>(), self.blocks.len() * 16) }
    }

unsafe doesn't turn off Rust's rules. It marks a place where you promise something the compiler can't check, here that the memory really is that many initialised bytes. The // SAFETY: comment says why the promise holds. The whole file starts with #![deny(unsafe_code)], so unsafe is an error everywhere except in items that say #[allow(unsafe_code)] by name. You can find every unsafe line with a search.

Step 5: the typed view, and why it's sound

    #[allow(unsafe_code)]
    fn slice<T: Component>(&self, count: usize) -> &[T] {
        assert!(self.id == T::ID, "a {} column read as {}", self.info.name, T::INFO.name);
        let bytes = &self.bytes()[..count * size_of::<T>()];
        // SAFETY: T is the column's component, so the bytes are `count` T's;
        // the storage is aligned to 16 and T needs at most 16; T is Pod, so
        // any bytes are a valid T.
        unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(bytes.as_ptr().cast::<T>(), count) }
    }

This is the untyped/typed split in one function. Below it, bytes. Above it, a &[T] that game code indexes like any slice. The assert catches the one mistake the byte level can't: reading a column as the wrong component.

Turning bytes into Ts is only sound if any bytes are a valid T. Some types have byte patterns that aren't valid values: a bool that's neither 0 nor 1, or a reference that's null. Components must be plain old data, promised by an unsafe trait:

/// Plain old data: what lets a column hold a component as bytes, zero a row,
/// copy a row with a byte copy, and hand the bytes back as the type.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// The type is Copy, has no padding bytes, and every bit pattern is a valid
/// value of it. That is a promise the compiler cannot check by itself, so the
/// trait is unsafe; pod! makes the promise only after checking it at compile
/// time.
#[allow(unsafe_code)]
unsafe trait Pod: Copy + 'static {}

f32, u32 and i32 are plain data. A struct is, if all its fields are and it has no padding (padding bytes are uninitialised, and reading them as bytes isn't allowed). The pod! macro declares a struct and checks both, at compile time:

        const _: () = {
            const fn field_is_pod<T: Pod>() {}
            $(field_is_pod::<$ty>();)*
            assert!(size_of::<$name>() == 0 $(+ size_of::<$ty>())*, "a component has padding");
        };

Calling field_is_pod::<bool>() doesn't compile, because bool isn't Pod. And a struct whose size isn't the sum of its fields' sizes stops the build with "a component has padding". component! now goes through pod!, so every component is checked.

That's the whole unsafe surface of the ECS: four one-line views (bytes, bytes_mut, slice, slice_mut), each with its reason, resting on one checked promise. The program also runs clean under Miri, Rust's interpreter for finding undefined behaviour (python tools/check.py --miri).

Step 6: rows stay rows across columns

Writing goes through the typed view:

        positions.slice_mut::<Position>(count)[row] = Position { at: Vec2 { x: i as f32, y: 1.0 } };
        healths.slice_mut::<Health>(count)[row] = Health { points: 50.0 + 10.0 * i as f32, max: 100.0 };

The program keeps two columns side by side, positions and healths, and moves them together:

    let last = count - 1;
    positions.copy_row(1, last);
    healths.copy_row(1, last);

Same operation, each column using its own row size. Row 1 is still one entity's data across both columns. That's a table in all but name.

Run it

a position column has 8-byte rows, a health column 8-byte rows
    grew to room for 2 rows
    grew to room for 4 rows
    grew to room for 8 rows
five rows, written through the typed view:
    row 0  position ( 0.00,  1.00)  health  50 / 100
    row 1  position ( 1.00,  1.00)  health  60 / 100
...
row 1's health as the column stores it, bytes: 00 00 70 42 00 00 c8 42
    that is 60.0 and 100.0 as little-endian f32s; the column never knew
swap-removed row 1: row 4 moved into it, in both columns

The byte line is the point of the chapter. 00 00 70 42 is 60.0 as an f32, and the column stored it without knowing it was a float, or a health, or anything at all.

Rust notes

rinRust
^u8 and an arena blockVec<Block>: the Vec allocates, grows and frees
c*.data[row * c*.size]&&bytes[row * size..(row + 1) * size]: a range of a slice, bounds-checked
memcpy, memsetcopy_within, fill: safe, checked slice methods
cast(c*.data, ^T); raw[0..count]std::slice::from_raw_parts, inside unsafe { }, with a // SAFETY: reason
any type can be cast to bytesonly Pod types, checked by pod! at compile time
#[repr(C)]the same: fields in declaration order, laid out as C would
#![deny(unsafe_code)]no rin equivalent: unsafe is an error unless an item allows it

Try

  1. Read the health column as Damage and run it. Read the panic message.
  2. Add a bool field to a component and build. Read the error. Then add an unsafe impl Pod for u8 {} and declare x: f32, n: u8: every field is Pod now, but the struct has 3 bytes of padding. Which check stops it?
  3. Start the capacity at 1 instead of 2. How many grows does it take to fit 5 rows? What if it grew by 1 each time instead of doubling?
  4. Print the bytes of a position row. Which bytes are x and which are y?

    row 1  position ( 4.00,  1.00)  health  90 / 100

Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.3

A table

ecs/src/2.components/2.3.tables/tables.rs

In the dojo: 2. swap-remove and the back-reference, 4. a type-erased column, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

The two halves meet. Part 1 built the entity index: handles, slots, packed rows, swap-remove. 2.1 and 2.2 built the component side: ids, a registry, columns of bytes. A table is 1.4's packed rows with the typed Vecs replaced by columns, one per component in its signature:

table {Position Velocity Health}
  entities  [ 0:1 | 3:1 | 2:1 | ... ]     who owns each row
  columns   Position [ ... ]  Velocity [ ... ]  Health [ ... ]
  capacity                                shared by every column

Row r is entity entities[r], and its components are row r of every column. This world still has a single table, so every entity has the same components; 2.4 gives each combination its own.

Step 1: the table

struct Table {
    signature: u64,
    capacity: usize,
    entities: Vec<Entity>,
    columns: [Option<Column>; 64],
}
  • signature says which components the table has.
  • columns[id] is Some when the signature has bit id, and None otherwise. 64 slots indexed by id means finding a column is an index, never a search. kayan in C looked columns up by name in a hash map, which is the thing this replaces.
  • The row count is entities.len(), and capacity is the table's, shared by every column. Neither can disagree with the columns, because there's only one of each.

A table is made from a signature and the registry:

    fn new(infos: &[Option<&'static Info>; 64], signature: u64) -> Table {
        let mut columns = [const { None }; 64];
        for id in 0..64 {
            if signature & bit(id) != 0 {
                let info = infos[id as usize]
                    .unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("signature {signature} uses component {id}, which was never registered"));
                columns[id as usize] = Some(Column::new(id, info));
            }
        }
        Table { signature, capacity: 0, entities: Vec::new(), columns }
    }

The signature is the column list. In your C kayan, the signature and the columns were written separately and could disagree (archetype D had position columns its signature didn't mention). Here one is made from the other.

[const { None }; 64] is how you fill an array with a value that isn't Copy. A Column owns a Vec, so it can't be copied, and [None; 64] won't compile; the const block makes 64 separate Nones instead.

Step 2: rows, for every column at once

Adding a row grows every column together when the table is full, then zeroes the new row in each:

    fn add_row(&mut self, e: Entity) -> usize {
        if self.count() == self.capacity {
            self.grow();
        }
        let row = self.count();
        self.entities.push(e);
        for c in self.columns.iter_mut().flatten() {
            c.zero_row(row);
        }
        row
    }

iter_mut().flatten() walks the 64 slots and skips the Nones, so the loop body sees only the table's real columns, as &mut Column.

Removing a row is 1.4's swap-remove, for every column:

    fn remove_row(&mut self, row: usize, slots: &mut [Slot]) {
        let last = self.count() - 1;
        if row != last {
            for c in self.columns.iter_mut().flatten() {
                c.copy_row(row, last);
            }
        }
        self.entities.swap_remove(row);
        if let Some(moved) = self.entities.get(row) {
            slots[moved.index as usize].row = row as u32;
        }
    }

Compare it with 1.4's despawn: the same moves and the same slot fix, but over columns of bytes instead of named Vecs. This function works for any table that will ever exist.

Why does it take slots as an argument? The slots belong to the world, and the table is a field of the world. In rin, kayan_table_remove_row took the whole world and reached into both. In Rust, a method on the table borrows the table, and nothing else; the world hands it the other thing it needs:

        self.table.remove_row(row, &mut self.slots);

self.table and self.slots are two fields, so the compiler lets them be borrowed at the same time, one by the method and one as its argument. Taking &mut World instead would borrow the table twice, and wouldn't compile. Passing what a function needs, rather than the world, is a habit you'll see for the rest of the course.

Step 3: the typed view of a table

    fn slice<T: Component>(&self) -> &[T] {
        self.column::<T>().slice::<T>(self.count())
    }

t.slice::<Position>() is the table's position column as a &[Position], cut to the rows in use. Systems will live on this in Part 3: get the slices, loop over rows. A table without the column stops the program with a message saying which one:

    fn column<T: Component>(&self) -> &Column {
        self.columns[T::ID as usize]
            .as_ref()
            .unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("the table has no {} column", T::INFO.name))
    }

Step 4: the world

struct World {
    infos: [Option<&'static Info>; 64],
    component_count: u32,
    slots: Vec<Slot>,
    free: Vec<u32>,
    live: usize,
    table: Table,
}

The registry from 2.1, the slots and free list from Part 1, and one table. Spawning is Part 1's spawn with the row coming from the table:

        let e = Entity { index, generation: self.slots[index as usize].generation };
        self.slots[index as usize].row = self.table.add_row(e) as u32;
        self.live += 1;
        e

and despawning is Part 1's despawn calling remove_row.

Step 5: writing a new entity's data

There's no typed get or set yet (that's 2.5), so the program finds the row and writes through the column slices:

        let row = w.row(e);
        w.table.slice_mut::<Position>()[row] = Position { at: Vec2 { x: 10.0 * i as f32, y: 0.0 } };
        w.table.slice_mut::<Velocity>()[row] = Velocity { per_second: Vec2 { x: 0.0, y: 1.0 } };
        w.table.slice_mut::<Health>()[row] = Health { points: 100.0, max: 100.0 };

Each line borrows the table, writes one row, and lets go, so the next line can borrow it again. Keeping all three slices at once would need three &mut borrows of one table, which the compiler refuses. 2.5 comes back to that.

Reading two columns at once is fine, since both are shared borrows. The printer zips them with the entities and walks all three together:

    for (row, ((e, p), h)) in t.entities.iter().zip(t.slice::<Position>()).zip(t.slice::<Health>()).enumerate() {

Row 0 went to 5:1 (the last row moved into the hole), then row 3 went to 4:1 the same way. Every column moved together, and the slots followed.

Try

  1. Remove Velocity from the table's signature and run it. Which line fails, and why is failing there the right behaviour?
  2. Make Table::grow start at 1 row. Count the grows for 6 drones.
  3. Delete the slot fix in remove_row and run verify.
  4. Change remove_row to take &mut World and call it from despawn as self.table.remove_row(row, self). Read the error.

Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.4

Many tables: archetypes

ecs/src/2.components/2.4.archetypes/archetypes.rs

In the dojo: 3. the slot map, on its own, to watch and to practise.

2.3's world had one table, so every entity had the same components. Real games mix: a turret has a position and a turret component, a drone has a position, velocity and health, a bullet has a position, velocity, damage and lifetime. Each combination gets a table of its own. Every row of a table has every component in its signature, so there are no holes and no flags. A table for one combination is called an archetype.

table 0 {Position Turret}                   0:1
table 1 {Position Velocity Health}          1:1 2:1 3:1
table 2 {Position Velocity Damage Lifetime} 4:1 5:1

Nobody declares the archetypes. The first time something spawns with a new combination, the world makes its table and remembers it by signature, so the next spawn finds it.

Step 1: slots say which table

struct Slot {
    generation: NonZeroU32,
    table: u32,
    row: u32,
}

Handle to slot to (table, row). That's the whole entity index from here on.

Step 2: the world keeps every table

struct World {
    infos: [Option<&'static Info>; 64],
    component_count: u32,
    tables: Vec<Table>,
    by_signature: HashMap<u64, u32>,
    slots: Vec<Slot>,
    free: Vec<u32>,
    live: usize,
}

tables holds them all, and by_signature maps a signature to its table's index. Tables are referred to by index, never by reference. Making a new table can grow the tables Vec and move every table in memory, and an index survives that. A reference is good until the next table is made, and Step 4 shows the compiler holding you to it.

Step 3: where archetypes come from

    fn table_for(&mut self, signature: u64) -> u32 {
        if let Some(&index) = self.by_signature.get(&signature) {
            return index;
        }
        let index = self.tables.len() as u32;
        self.tables.push(Table::new(&self.infos, signature));
        self.by_signature.insert(signature, index);
        index
    }

Found, or made. A game has tens of archetypes, maybe a few hundred, so a linear search would do too. HashMap is in the standard library, so the map costs nothing to add, and 2.6 makes the lookup rare anyway.

if let Some(&index) = ... is a pattern: get returns Option<&u32>, and Some(&index) matches the Some and copies the number out of the reference in one go.

Step 4: spawning takes a signature

    fn spawn(&mut self, signature: u64) -> Entity {

and puts the new entity in that signature's table:

        let table = self.table_for(signature);
        let row = self.tables[table as usize].add_row(e);
        self.slots[index as usize] = Slot { generation: e.generation, table, row: row as u32 };

The order matters: the table is reached after table_for, because finding the table can make one and move the rest. In rin, getting this order wrong is the classic archetype-ECS bug. It works until the first new archetype appears mid-game, and then a row goes into a table that no longer exists.

In Rust, the wrong order doesn't compile. Take the reference first:

        let t = &mut self.tables[0];
        let table = self.table_for(signature);
        let row = t.add_row(e);
error[E0499]: cannot borrow `*self` as mutable more than once at a time
    |
391 |         let t = &mut self.tables[0];
    |                      ----------- first mutable borrow occurs here
392 |         let table = self.table_for(signature);
    |                     ^^^^ second mutable borrow occurs here
393 |         let row = t.add_row(e);
    |                   - first borrow later used here

t borrows the world's tables, and table_for needs the whole world mutably, so the two can't overlap. The compiler doesn't know that table_for might move the tables; it only knows that it could change anything in the world, and that's enough to rule the bug out. This is the same rule that kept 2.2's references out of a growing column, applied one level up.

Despawning finds the table through the slot:

        let Slot { table, row, .. } = self.slots[e.index as usize];
        self.tables[table as usize].remove_row(row as usize, &mut self.slots);

let Slot { table, row, .. } = ... copies two fields out of the slot by name, and .. skips the rest. Then the call borrows one table and the slots, which are two different fields of the world, as in 2.3.

verify now walks every table: each row belongs to a live entity whose slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add up to the live count. Same invariant, one more field.

Step 6: one column, many tables

The end of the program reads every position in the world:

    for (ti, t) in w.tables.iter().enumerate() {
        for (row, (e, p)) in t.entities.iter().zip(t.slice::<Position>()).enumerate() {

The position column of each table, in turn. Positions are no longer one array; they're one array per archetype that has them. This is exactly what a query does in Part 3: visit the tables that have the right components, and stream their columns.

The borrow checker caught this bug because it's about references: a &mut Table that would have outlived its table. It still can't catch 1.2's bug, a stale number. An old table index stays a valid number after anything, as long as no tables are ever removed, which in this course they never are.

Try

  1. Spawn a "drone with damage" (Position, Velocity, Health, Damage). How many tables now?
  2. Spawn 100 entities with 100 different signatures (use the bits of a counter). What does that do to a system that visits tables? This is called archetype fragmentation.
  3. Swap the two lines in spawn so the table is reached first, as in Step 4, and read the error yourself. Then try to sneak past it: keep a raw pointer (*mut Table) instead of a reference. What does the compiler make you write before you can use it?

Typed access

ecs/src/2.components/2.5.typed_access/typed_access.rs

In the dojo: 4. a type-erased column, on its own, to watch and to practise.

The world stores any component in any combination, as bytes. Game code should never see the bytes. This chapter adds the typed layer on top:

w.get::<Position>(e)        -> Option<&Position>
w.get_mut::<Health>(e)      -> Option<&mut Health>
w.has::<Velocity>(e)        -> bool
w.set(e, value)             -> Ok, or Err(Dead), or Err(Missing)

Each is a few lines that turn the type into an id, find the entity's table and row through its slot, and hand the row back as a T. The byte-level core underneath doesn't change at all. This is the split from 2.2: byte work below, typed generic functions on top, each written once.

Step 1: get

    fn get<T: Component>(&self, e: Entity) -> Option<&T> {
        if !self.alive(e) {
            return None;
        }
        let t = self.table_of(e);
        if !t.has(T::ID) {
            return None;
        }
        Some(&t.slice::<T>()[self.row(e)])
    }

Handle, slot, table, row, typed view. It's the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component. Two ways to get None: the handle is dead, or the entity has no T. The caller checks once and then has a real reference.

get_mut is the same with &mut, so the caller can change the component in place:

    w.get_mut::<Health>(a).expect("a is a drone").points -= 25.0;

Step 2: has and set

    fn has<T: Component>(&self, e: Entity) -> bool {
        self.signature(e) & mask_of::<T>() != 0
    }

has doesn't touch the row at all. An entity's components are its table's signature, one AND away.

    fn set<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity, value: T) -> Result<(), Error> {
        if !self.alive(e) {
            return Err(Error::Dead);
        }
        *self.get_mut::<T>(e).ok_or(Error::Missing)? = value;
        Ok(())
    }

set writes a component the entity already has. Giving it a component it doesn't have changes which table it belongs in, and that's 2.6. So the error gains a second value:

enum Error {
    Dead,
    Missing,
}

The middle line of set packs three steps. ok_or(Error::Missing) turns the Option<&mut T> into a Result: the reference, or Err(Missing). The ? returns that error from set right away, or unwraps the reference. Then *... = value writes through it. ? is how Rust functions pass an error up without an if for every call.

set needs no type argument. w.set(e, Health { ... }) names Health by the value, and the compiler works out T from it.

Step 3: building things

With set, game code builds entities with small functions. Engines call these prefabs or archetype constructors:

fn spawn_drone(w: &mut World, x: f32, y: f32) -> Entity {
    let e = w.spawn(mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>() | mask_of::<Health>());
    w.set(e, Position { at: Vec2 { x, y } }).expect("just spawned");
    w.set(e, Velocity { per_second: Vec2 { x: -1.0, y: 0.0 } }).expect("just spawned");
    w.set(e, Health { points: 100.0, max: 100.0 }).expect("just spawned");
    e
}

expect("just spawned") says why each set can't fail: the entity was just spawned with exactly these components. If that's ever wrong, the program stops on the line that was wrong about it.

Reading two components at once is a match on both Options:

    match (w.get::<Position>(e), w.get::<Health>(e)) {
        (Some(p), Some(h)) => println!("    {e} at ({:5.2}, {:5.2}), health {:.0}", p.at.x, p.at.y, h.points),
        _ => println!("    {e} is not a live drone"),
    }

Both are shared borrows of the world, so they can be held at the same time.

Step 4: keep handles, borrow references

The reference get_mut returns points into a column. 2.2 showed what columns do when their table fills up: they move. So a reference is good until the next structural change: a spawn, a despawn, or (from 2.6) an add or remove.

In rin-dod, this is where the program kept a pointer to a drone's health, spawned 8 drones so the table grew, and wrote through the pointer. The write landed in the column's old block, and was lost without a sound. Here is the same thing in Rust:

    let kept = w.get_mut::<Health>(a).expect("a is a drone");
    let mut last = a;
    for i in 0..8 {
        last = spawn_drone(&mut w, 40.0 + i as f32, 0.0);
    }
    kept.points = 1.0;
error[E0499]: cannot borrow `w` as mutable more than once at a time
    |
606 |     let kept = w.get_mut::<Health>(a).expect("a is a drone");
    |                - first mutable borrow occurs here
...
609 |         last = spawn_drone(&mut w, 40.0 + i as f32, 0.0);
    |                            ^^^^^^ second mutable borrow occurs here
610 |     }
611 |     kept.points = 1.0;
    |     ----------------- first borrow later used here

kept borrows the world, and spawn_drone needs the world, so they can't overlap. The bug from rin-dod doesn't build. Nothing about columns moving is in the error; the compiler only knows that kept must not outlive anything that could change the world. That's enough.

So the program shows the bug that does build. Instead of a reference, it keeps a row number:

    let kept_row = w.row(a);
    w.despawn(a).expect("alive");
    w.table_of_mut(last).slice_mut::<Health>()[kept_row].points = 1.0;
kept 0:1's row number, 0, despawned 0:1, then wrote health 1 into row 0:
    9:1 at (47.00,  0.00), health 1
    the last drone moved into the hole, so the write hit 9:1; the handle 0:1 says dead

The despawn swap-removed 0:1's row, the last drone moved into it, and the write hit that drone instead. A row number is a number, like 1.2's entity number, and the borrow checker has nothing to say about numbers. Hence the rule every ECS has in some form:

Keep handles. Borrow references: get, use, forget.

In Rust, the "forget" half is enforced for references and not for row numbers. A handle is the one thing that's safe to keep, because the world checks it every time.

Run it

two drones and a bullet, built with set:
    0:1 at (20.00,  5.00), health 100
    1:1 at (30.00, -5.00), health 100
drone 0:1 is hit through get_mut::<Health>:
    0:1 at (20.00,  5.00), health 75
the bullet has a velocity: yes; a health: no
get::<Health> on the bullet is None: yes
set(Health) on the bullet: missing
despawned 1:1; set(Health) on it now: dead
    1:1 is not a live drone
...
verify: 0 problems

Try

  1. Write spawn_turret in the style of spawn_drone, for your own kind of thing.
  2. Take the ignore block from Step 4 and put it in the program. Read the error, then move the get_mut to after the loop. Why does it compile now?
  3. In the row-number demo, use w.get_mut::<Health>(a) instead of the kept row. What happens, and why is that the right answer?
  4. Make set add the component when it's missing, instead of returning Err(Missing). What would it need from 2.6?

Every component in the signature must be registered.248    fn new(infos: &[Option<&'static Info>; 64], signature: u64) -> Table {249        let mut columns = [const { None }; 64];250        for id in 0..64 {251            if signature & bit(id) != 0 {252                let info = infos[id as usize]253                    .unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("signature {signature} uses component {id}, which was never registered"));254                columns[id as usize] = Some(Column::new(id, info));255            }256        }257        Table { signature, capacity: 0, entities: Vec::new(), columns }258    }259 260    fn count(&self) -> usize {261        self.entities.len()262    }263 264    fn has(&self, id: u32) -> bool {265        self.signature & bit(id) != 0266    }267 268    // Double the room in `entities` and in every column at once.269    fn grow(&mut self) {270        self.capacity = if self.capacity == 0 { 4 } else { self.capacity * 2 };271        self.entities.reserve_exact(self.capacity - self.entities.len());272        for c in self.columns.iter_mut().flatten() {273            c.grow(self.capacity);274        }275    }276 277    // A new row at the end, owned by `e`, with every component zeroed.278    fn add_row(&mut self, e: Entity) -> usize {279        if self.count() == self.capacity {280            self.grow();281        }282        let row = self.count();283        self.entities.push(e);284        for c in self.columns.iter_mut().flatten() {285            c.zero_row(row);286        }287        row288    }289 290    // 1.4's swap-remove, for every column: the last row is copied over `row`,291    // and the slot of the entity that owned the last row is told where it292    // went. This371    // is where archetypes come from.372    fn table_for(&mut self, signature: u64) -> u32 {373        if let Some(&index) = self.by_signature.get(&signature) {374            return index;375        }376        let index = self.tables.len() as u32;377        self.tables.push(Table::new(&self.infos, signature));378        self.by_signature.insert(signature, index);379        index380    }381 382    // A new entity with the components in `signature`, all zeroed, in the383    // table for that signature.384    fn spawn(&mut self, signature: u64) -> Entity {385        let index = match self.free.pop() {386            Some(index) => index,387            None => {388                self.slots.push(Slot { generation: ONE, table: 0, row: 0 });389                self.slots.len() as u32 - 1390            }391        };392        let e = Entity { index, generation: self.slots[index as usize].generation };393        // table_for can make a table, and pushing onto `tables` can move every394        // table. Handle, slot, table, row, typed438    // view: the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component.439    fn get<T: Component>(&self, e: Entity) -> Option<&T> {440        if !self.alive(e) {441            return None;442        }443        let t = self.table_of(e);444        if !t.has(T::ID) {445            return None;446        }447        Some(&t.slice::<T>()[self.row(e)])448    }449 450    fn get_mut<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity) -> Option<&mut T> {451        if !self.alive(e) {452            return None;453        }454        let row = self.row(e);455        let t = self.table_of_mut(e);456        if !t.has(T::ID) {457            return None;458        }459        Some(&mut t.slice_mut::<T>()[row])460    }461 462    fn has<T: Component>(&self, e: Entity) -> bool {463        self.signature(e) & mask_of::<T>() != 0464    }465 466    // Write e's T.
