Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.6

Adding and removing components

ecs/src/2.components/2.6.add_remove/add_remove.rs

In the dojo: 2. swap-remove and the back-reference, on its own, to watch and to practise.

A drone catches fire: it gains a Burning component. The fire goes out: it loses it. Changing what an entity is, while the game runs, is the thing your C kayan couldn't do, because its archetypes were structs fixed at compile time. In an archetype ECS a table holds exactly one combination, so a drone that gains a component no longer belongs in its table. It moves:

  1. find the table for its signature plus (or minus) the component;
  2. add a row there, and copy every component the two tables share;
  3. swap-remove its old row, fixing whoever moves into the hole;
  4. point its slot at the new table and row.

Its handle doesn't change. Everything else about it is where it was, one table over.

Step 1: the move

    fn move_to(&mut self, e: Entity, to: u32) {
        let Slot { table: from, row, .. } = self.slots[e.index as usize];
        if from == to {
            return;
        }
        let [old, new] = self.tables.get_disjoint_mut([from as usize, to as usize]).expect("two different tables");
        let new_row = new.add_row(e);
        for (o, n) in old.columns.iter().zip(new.columns.iter_mut()) {
            if let (Some(o), Some(n)) = (o, n) {
                n.row_mut(new_row).copy_from_slice(o.row(row as usize));
            }
        }
        old.remove_row(row as usize, &mut self.slots);
        self.slots[e.index as usize] = Slot { generation: e.generation, table: to, row: new_row as u32 };
    }

Every piece is something you've already built: add_row (2.3), a byte copy per shared column (2.2), remove_row with its slot fix (1.4). Components only the new table has start zeroed (add_row zeroes them). Components only the old table has disappear with the old row.

The column loop zips the two tables' 64 column slots, id by id, and if let (Some(o), Some(n)) matches only the ids both tables have. That's the "components the two tables share" from the list above, as a pattern.

A move costs one row copy in and one row copy out. That's cheap, but not free, and it's why components that flip on and off every frame are sometimes better as a field (an on_fire: f32 inside Health) than as a component.

Step 2: two tables at once

The move reads one table and writes another, so it needs both at the same time, mutably. The obvious way doesn't compile:

        let old = &mut self.tables[from as usize];
        let new = &mut self.tables[to as usize];
error[E0499]: cannot borrow `self.tables` as mutable more than once at a time
    |
534 |         let old = &mut self.tables[from as usize];
    |                        ----------- first mutable borrow occurs here
535 |         let new = &mut self.tables[to as usize];
    |                        ^^^^^^^^^^^ second mutable borrow occurs here

The compiler doesn't know from and to are different numbers. If they were the same, old and new would be two &mut to one table, and that's the one thing &mut promises never happens. So it refuses two &mut borrows of one Vec, whatever the indices.

get_disjoint_mut is the standard answer. It takes the indices, checks at run time that they're different (and in range), and hands back both:

        let [old, new] = self.tables.get_disjoint_mut([from as usize, to as usize]).expect("two different tables");

It returns a Result, and expect stops the program if the check fails. It can't fail here, because move_to returned early when from == to. One compare at run time, where the compiler couldn't prove it. You'll see this trade again: when the borrow checker can't see that something is fine, Rust usually has a checked way to say so, rather than an unsafe one.

old.remove_row(row, &mut self.slots) still works with old borrowed: old borrows self.tables, and the slots are another field.

Step 3: add and remove, typed

    fn add<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity, value: T) -> Result<(), Error> {
        if !self.alive(e) {
            return Err(Error::Dead);
        }
        if !self.has::<T>(e) {
            let from = self.slots[e.index as usize].table;
            let to = self.table_with(from, T::ID);
            self.move_to(e, to);
        }
        self.set(e, value)
    }

If the entity already has a T, adding is just setting. Otherwise it moves to the table with T, then sets it. remove::<T> is the mirror image: Err(Missing) if it has no T, otherwise a move to the table without T.

Step 4: the archetype graph

Which table is "the table with T"? Its signature is the old one plus T's bit, so it could be looked up in by_signature every time. But a game toggling components does that constantly, always between the same few tables. So each table remembers its neighbours:

struct Table {
    signature: u64,
    capacity: usize,
    entities: Vec<Entity>,
    columns: [Option<Column>; 64],
    add_edges: [Option<u32>; 64],
    remove_edges: [Option<u32>; 64],
}

add_edges[id] is where this table's entities go when they gain component id. remove_edges[id] is where they go when they lose it. None means "not known yet". rin-dod stored index + 1 so a zeroed table meant "not known"; Option<u32> says it directly.

    fn table_with(&mut self, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 {
        if let Some(to) = self.tables[from as usize].add_edges[id as usize] {
            self.edge_hits += 1;
            return to;
        }
        self.lookups += 1;
        let to = self.table_for(self.tables[from as usize].signature | bit(id));
        self.tables[from as usize].add_edges[id as usize] = Some(to);
        self.tables[to as usize].remove_edges[id as usize] = Some(from);
        to
    }

The first move from {Position Velocity Health} with Burning looks the table up (and makes it). It then writes the answer on both tables: an add edge one way and a remove edge back. After that, catching fire and putting it out both follow edges. The tables and their edges form a graph, the archetype graph, and flecs is built around it.

table_for can push a table and move them all, so each line after it indexes self.tables afresh rather than keeping a reference from before. In rin that was a comment saying so. Here it's the only way that compiles (2.4).

Run it

4 drones:
    table 0 {Position Velocity Health}: 0:1 1:1 2:1 3:1
frame 1
    0:1 catches fire: ok
    2:1 catches fire: ok
    table 0 {Position Velocity Health}: 3:1 1:1
    table 1 {Position Velocity Health Burning}: 0:1 2:1
frame 2
    0:1 is put out: ok
    1:1 catches fire: ok
    2:1 catches fire: ok
...
frame 3
    1:1 is put out: ok
    2:1 is put out: ok
    3:1 is put out: missing
    3:1 catches fire: ok
...
2:1 moved tables twice and kept its data: at (30.00, 0.00), health 100
moves that looked up a table by signature: 1; that followed an edge: 6
verify: 0 problems

Watch row order shuffle as entities move: 3:1 jumps to row 0 of table 0 when 0:1 leaves. Order is never promised, and swap-remove is why. And one lookup for seven moves: that's the graph working.

Rust notes

rinRust
from: *kayan_table = ...; to: *kayan_table = ...;get_disjoint_mut([from, to]): two &mut at once, checked different at run time
if (has(from, id) && has(to, id)) { memcpy(...) }zip the column slots, if let (Some(o), Some(n)), then copy_from_slice
add_edges: [64]u32, stored as index + 1[Option<u32>; 64]: None is "not known yet"
kayan_remove<burning>(w, e)w.remove::<Burning>(e): no value to pass, so the type is named
kayan_add<burning>(w, e, { ... })w.add(e, Burning { ... }): the type comes from the value

copy_from_slice panics if the two slices have different lengths. They can't here (same component, same size), but if a bug ever made them differ, the copy would stop the program instead of writing past a row.

Try

  1. Add a Stunned component and stun a burning drone. How many tables exist now, and which edges were written?
  2. Print every table's known edges after frame 3.
  3. Make add on a drone that's already burning add to the rate instead of replacing it. Where does that logic belong: in kayan or in the game?
  4. Call move_to(e, from) without the early return and see what get_disjoint_mut says. Why is a panic better here than two &mut to one table?

Asking for a component the table does not have is a bug, so it329    // stops.330    fn slice<T: Component>(&self) -> &[T] {331        self.column::<T>().slice::<T>(self.count())332    }333 334    fn slice_mut<T: Component>(&mut self) -> &mut [T] {335        let count = self.count();336        self.columns[T::ID as usize]337            .as_mut()338            .unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("the table has no {} column", T::INFO.name))339            .slice_mut::<T>(count)340    }341}342 343// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------344// The world345// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------346 347// The world: the registry, the slots and free list, and every table, with a348// map from signature to table index so finding one is a lookup, not a search.349// Tables are referred to by index, never by reference: making a table can grow350// `tables` and move all of them, and an index survives that.351struct World {352    infos: [Option<&'static Info>; 64],353    component_count: u32,354    tables: Vec<Table>,355    by_signature: HashMap<u64, u32>,356    slots: Vec<Slot>,357    free: Vec<u32>,358    live: usize,359    // How table moves found their destination, for this chapter's output.360    lookups: u32,361    edge_hits: u32,362}363 364impl World {365    fn new() -> World {366        World {367            infos: [None; 64],368            component_count: 0,369            tables: Vec::new(),370            by_signature: HashMap::new(),371            slots: Vec::new(),372            free: Vec::new(),373            live: 0,374            lookups: 0,375            edge_hits: 0,376        }377    }378 379    fn register<T: Component>(&mut self) {380        assert!(T::ID < 64, "component id {} is past the 64 a signature can hold", T::ID);381        self.infos[T::ID as usize] = Some(T::INFO);382        self.component_count = self.component_count.max(T::ID + 1);383    }384 385    fn alive(&self, e: Entity) -> bool {386        self.slots.get(e.index as usize).is_some_and(|s| s.generation == e.generation)387    }388 389    // The table for a signature: found if it exists, made if it does not. This390    // is where archetypes come from.391    fn table_for(&mut self, signature: u64) -> u32 {392        if let Some(&index) = self.by_signature.get(&signature) {393            return index;394        }395        let index = self.tables.len() as u32;396        self.tables.push(Table::new(&self.infos, signature));397        self.by_signature.insert(signature, index);398        index399    }400 401    // A new entity with the components in `signature`, all zeroed, in the402    // table for that signature.403    fn spawn(&mut self, signature: u64) -> Entity {404        let index = match self.free.pop() {405            Some(index) => index,406            None => {407                self.slots.push(Slot { generation: ONE, table: 0, row: 0 });408                self.slots.len() as u32 - 1409            }410        };411        let e = Entity { index, generation: self.slots[index as usize].generation };412        // table_for can make a table, and pushing onto `tables` can move every413        // table. A reference to a table cannot live across that call (the414        // borrow checker refuses), so the index comes first and the table after.415        let table = self.table_for(signature);416        let row = self.tables[table as usize].add_row(e);417        self.slots[index as usize] = Slot { generation: e.generation, table, row: row as u32 };418        self.live += 1;419        e420    }421 422    fn despawn(&mut self, e: Entity) -> Result<(), Error> {423        if !self.alive(e) {424            return Err(Error::Dead);425        }426        let Slot { table, row, .. } = self.slots[e.index as usize];427        self.tables[table as usize].remove_row(row as usize, &mut self.slots);428        let slot = &mut self.slots[e.index as usize];429        slot.generation = slot.generation.checked_add(1).expect("a number has lived 4 billion lives");430        self.free.push(e.index);431        self.live -= 1;432        Ok(())433    }434 435    fn table_of(&self, e: Entity) -> &Table {436        &self.tables[self.slots[e.index as usize].table as usize]437    }438 439    fn table_of_mut(&mut self, e: Entity) -> &mut Table {440        &mut self.tables[self.slots[e.index as usize].table as usize]441    }442 443    fn row(&self, e: Entity) -> usize {444        self.slots[e.index as usize].row as usize445    }446 447    // The components a live entity has: its table's signature. 0 for a dead448    // one.449    fn signature(&self, e: Entity) -> u64 {450        if !self.alive(e) {451            return 0;452        }453        self.table_of(e).signature454    }455 456    // e's T, or None if e is dead or has no T. Handle, slot, table, row, typed457    // view: the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component.458    fn get<T: Component>(&self, e: Entity) -> Option<&T> {459        if !self.alive(e) {460            return None;461        }462        let t = self.table_of(e);463        if !t.has(T::ID) {464            return None;465        }466        Some(&t.slice::<T>()[self.row(e)])467    }468 469    fn get_mut<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity) -> Option<&mut T> {470        if !self.alive(e) {471            return None;472        }473        let row = self.row(e);474        let t = self.table_of_mut(e);475        if !t.has(T::ID) {476            return None;477        }478        Some(&mut t.slice_mut::<T>()[row])479    }480 481    fn has<T: Component>(&self, e: Entity) -> bool {482        self.signature(e) & mask_of::<T>() != 0483    }484 485    // Write e's T. It must already have one: giving an entity a component it486    // does not have changes its table, which is 2.6.487    fn set<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity, value: T) -> Result<(), Error> {488        if !self.alive(e) {489            return Err(Error::Dead);490        }491        *self.get_mut::<T>(e).ok_or(Error::Missing)? = value;492        Ok(())493    }494 495    // The table an entity of table `from` moves to when it gains component496    // `id`. The first time, it is found by signature, which can make the497    // table; the answer is written on both tables, as from's add edge and the498    // destination's remove edge, so neither direction is looked up again.499    fn table_with(&mut self, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 {500        if let Some(to) = self.tables[from as usize].add_edges[id as usize] {501            self.edge_hits += 1;502            return to;503        }504        self.lookups += 1;505        let to = self.table_for(self.tables[from as usize].signature | bit(id));506        self.tables[from as usize].add_edges[id as usize] = Some(to);507        self.tables[to as usize].remove_edges[id as usize] = Some(from);508        to509    }510 511    // The same for losing component `id`.512    fn table_without(&mut self, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 {513        if let Some(to) = self.tables[from as usize].remove_edges[id as usize] {514            self.edge_hits += 1;515            return to;516        }517        self.lookups += 1;518        let to = self.table_for(self.tables[from as usize].signature & !bit(id));519        self.tables[from as usize].remove_edges[id as usize] = Some(to);520        self.tables[to as usize].add_edges[id as usize] = Some(from);521        to522    }523 524    // Move a live entity to table `to`. Components both tables have are525    // copied, byte for byte; components only the new table has start zeroed;526    // components only the old table has are dropped with its old row.527    // get_disjoint_mut lends out two tables of the Vec at once, after528    // checking at run time that they are two different tables.529    fn move_to(&mut self, e: Entity, to: u32) {530        let Slot { table: from, row, .. } = self.slots[e.index as usize];531        if from == to {532            return;533        }534        let [old, new] = self.tables.get_disjoint_mut([from as usize, to as usize]).expect("two different tables");535        let new_row = new.add_row(e);536        for (o, n) in old.columns.iter().zip(new.columns.iter_mut()) {537            if let (Some(o), Some(n)) = (o, n) {538                n.row_mut(new_row).copy_from_slice(o.row(row as usize));539            }540        }541        old.remove_row(row as usize, &mut self.slots);542        self.slots[e.index as usize] = Slot { generation: e.generation, table: to, row: new_row as u32 };543    }544 545    // Give e a T. If it already has one, this is set; if not, it moves to the546    // table with T and then sets it.547    fn add<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity, value: T) -> Result<(), Error> {548        if !self.alive(e) {549            return Err(Error::Dead);550        }551        if !self.has::<T>(e) {552            let from = self.slots[e.index as usize].table;553            let to = self.table_with(from, T::ID);554            self.move_to(e, to);555        }556        self.set(e, value)557    }558 559    // Take e's T away, moving it to the table without T.560    fn remove<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity) -> Result<(), Error> {561        if !self.alive(e) {562            return Err(Error::Dead);563        }564        if !self.has::<T>(e) {565            return Err(Error::Missing);566        }567        let from = self.slots[e.index as usize].table;568        let to = self.table_without(from, T::ID);569        self.move_to(e, to);570        Ok(())571    }572 573    // The invariant, over every table: each row belongs to a live entity whose574    // slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add575    // up to the live count.576 t.entities.iter().enumerate() {581                if !self.alive(e) {582                    println!("verify: table {ti} row {row} holds dead entity {e}");583                    problems += 1;584 println!("verify: {e} is in table {ti} row {row}, its slot says table {} row {}", s.table, s.row);589                    problems += 1;590                }591            }592            rows += t.count();593        }594        if rows != self.live {595            println!("verify: {rows} rows in tables, {} live entities", self.live);596            problems += 1;597        }598        problems599    }600 601    fn info(&self, id: u32) -> &'static Info {602        self.infos[id as usize].expect("every component in a signature is registered")603    }604 605    // A signature as names, {Position Velocity}.606    fn names(&self, signature: u64) -> String {607        let names: Vec<&str> = (0..self.component_count)608            .filter(|&id| signature & bit(id) != 0)609 self.tables.iter().enumerate() {616            print!("    table {ti} {}:", self.names(t.signature));617            for e in &t.entities {618                print!(" {e}");619            }620 Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.7

Inspecting the world

ecs/src/2.components/2.7.inspecting/inspecting.rs

The world can store, copy and move any component, but it can't show you one. When something goes wrong at frame 3,000, you want to see an entity: every component it has, every field, with names. In C that means writing a printer per component and keeping each in step with its struct. rin's compiler writes a reflect record for every struct: its fields, with their names, types and byte offsets. Rust has no such records built in, but the macro that already declares each component can write one. The world registered the records back in 2.1 to learn component sizes. Here they pay off a second time.

w.inspect(e)          every component of e, field by field
w.print_layout()      every table, its columns, and their memory

Neither names a single component type. Add a component tomorrow and both print it.

Step 1: records with fields

2.1's record had a name and a layout. Now it lists the fields too:

struct Info {
    name: &'static str,
    layout: Layout,
    fields: &'static [Field],
}

struct Field {
    name: &'static str,
    offset: usize,
    size: usize,
    ty: &'static str,
    info: Option<&'static Info>,
    hidden: bool,
}

A field's record says where its bytes are in the struct (offset, size), and what they are. info is the field type's own record when it's a struct (at: Vec2 inside Position), and None when it's a builtin like f32, which tools read by its type's name, ty.

Step 2: the compiler fills them in

pod! writes the record, one Field per field it declares:

        impl Reflect for $name {
            const RECORD: Option<&'static Info> = Some(&Info {
                name: stringify!($name),
                layout: Layout::new::<$name>(),
                fields: &[$(Field {
                    name: stringify!($field),
                    offset: std::mem::offset_of!($name, $field),
                    size: size_of::<$ty>(),
                    ty: stringify!($ty),
                    info: <$ty as Reflect>::RECORD,
                    hidden: is_hidden!($($attr)?),
                }),*],
            });
        }

$( ... ),* repeats once per field. Every value in it comes from the compiler: offset_of! is the field's byte offset, as the compiler laid it out, so the record can't disagree with the struct.

<$ty as Reflect>::RECORD is the field type's record, and that's how nesting works. Every type a component is made of implements Reflect. Structs made with pod! have a record; builtins say they don't:

trait Reflect {
    const RECORD: Option<&'static Info>;
}

impl Reflect for f32 {
    const RECORD: Option<&'static Info> = None;
}

The whole record, nested records included, is a constant built at compile time. Nothing is computed when the program starts.

Step 3: a component as bytes

Tools work from records, not types, so they need the byte view:

    fn get_bytes(&self, e: Entity, id: u32) -> Option<&[u8]> {
        if !self.alive(e) || id >= self.component_count {
            return None;
        }
        let row = self.row(e);
        self.table_of(e).columns[id as usize].as_ref().map(|c| c.row(row))
    }

It's get::<T>'s path, stopping one step early: the row's bytes as a slice, sized by the column. .map(|c| c.row(row)) turns the Option<&Column> into an Option<&[u8]>: None stays None, and a column becomes its row. Game code uses the typed layer; tools use this.

Step 4: walking fields

fn print_fields(info: &Info, base: &[u8], depth: usize) {
    for f in info.fields.iter().filter(|f| !f.hidden) {
        let at = &base[f.offset..f.offset + f.size];
        print!("{:indent$}{}:", "", f.name, indent = depth * 4);
        match f.info {
            Some(inner) => {
                println!();
                print_fields(inner, at, depth + 1);
            }
            None => {
                print!(" ");
                print_builtin(f.ty, at);
                println!();
            }
        }
    }
}

For each field the record lists, cut its bytes out of the component by offset and size. A struct field has a record of its own, so the printer recurses into it. A builtin is printed by its type's name:

        "f32" => print!("{:.2}", f32::from_ne_bytes(at.try_into().expect("4 bytes"))),

at.try_into() turns the &[u8] slice into a [u8; 4] array, failing if it isn't 4 bytes long, and f32::from_ne_bytes turns 4 bytes into a float. No pointer cast, so no unsafe: the inspector reads any component through safe code.

Because each field's bytes are cut with a bounds-checked slice, a record that disagreed with the data would stop the program instead of printing garbage.

Step 5: hiding bookkeeping

A field can be marked #[hidden]:

component!(Turret { cooldown: f32, #[hidden] timer: f32 });

That looks like a Rust attribute, but it's only text the macro matches. The pattern $(#[$attr:ident])? takes an optional #[word] before a field, and is_hidden! turns it into the record's hidden flag:

macro_rules! is_hidden {
    () => {
        false
    };
    (hidden) => {
        true
    };
}

No attribute gives false; #[hidden] gives true; any other word is a compile error, because no rule matches it. The inspector skips hidden fields. The component decides what a tool shows; the tool doesn't need to know the component.

Step 6: an entity, and the layout

inspect walks the entity's signature and prints each component with print_fields:

        for id in (0..self.component_count).filter(|&id| signature & bit(id) != 0) {
            let info = self.info(id);
            println!("    {}", info.name);
            print_fields(info, self.get_bytes(e, id).expect("e has it"), 2);
        }

print_layout walks every table and prints each column's row size and bytes used out of bytes allocated, which shows where memory goes.

Run it

table 1 {Position Velocity Health}: 0 rows, room for 4

    Health     8 bytes a row,    0 of   32 bytes in use

The turret's timer isn't printed. Table 1 is empty but keeps its capacity: drone 1:1 was its only remaining row after 2:1 caught fire and moved out, and then 1:1 was despawned. Tables never shrink in this course. A real engine might trim empty ones between levels.

Part 2 in one picture

handle 2:1 ──> slots[2] { generation 1, table 2, row 0 }
                                         │
table 2 {Position Velocity Health Burning}
  entities  [ 2:1 ]
  Position  [ (30, -5) ]     Velocity [ (-1, 0) ]     Health [ 60/100 ]     Burning [ 10 ]
  add_edges / remove_edges ──> neighbouring tables in the archetype graph

The storage half of the ECS is done: identity (Part 1), and any component, in any combination, changing at run time (Part 2). Part 3 is the behaviour: queries to find tables, and systems to run over them.

Rust notes

rinRust
position<>, a record the compiler writes for every structa record pod! writes, from stringify!, offset_of! and size_of
f*.info, the field type's record, or null<$ty as Reflect>::RECORD: Some for a pod! struct, None for a builtin
timer: f32 @ "hidden"#[hidden] timer: f32, matched by the macro, not a real attribute
reflect_field_has_attr(f, "hidden")f.hidden, a bool the macro set
cast(at.data, *f32)*f32::from_ne_bytes(at.try_into()...): bytes to a number, no unsafe
printf("%*s", depth * 4, "")print!("{:indent$}", "", indent = depth * 4)

Rust crates like bevy_reflect do this with derive macros, which can read a whole struct definition and write any code about it. macro_rules! is simpler and in the language itself, at the cost of declaring components in the macro's own syntax.

Try

  1. Add a field to Health and run it. Nothing in the inspector changes.
  2. Mark Health's max as #[hidden]. Then try #[secret] and read the error.
  3. Write w.set_f32_by_name(e, "Health", "points", 10.0) with the records: find the component by name, the field by name, check its ty is "f32", and write it with copy_from_slice(&value.to_ne_bytes()). That's the core of an editor or a console. It needs a get_bytes_mut.

Build an ECS · part 3, systems · 3.1

Queries

ecs/src/3.systems/3.1.queries/queries.rs

Part 2 finished the storage. Everything from here on is behaviour, and in an ECS behaviour lives in systems: code that runs over every entity with some set of components. "Every entity with a position and a velocity" isn't in one place. It's spread over every table whose signature has both bits. So a system's first job is finding those tables, and the thing that finds them is a query:

all {Position Velocity}, none {}   ->   tables 1, 2, 3

A query matches tables, not entities. A game has a handful of tables and rarely makes new ones, so the matching is done once and kept. Each frame, a system walks the kept list, and inside each table streams the columns.

Step 1: the query

struct Query {
    all: u64,
    none: u64,
    tables: Vec<u32>,
    checked: usize,
}
  • all: a table must have every one of these components.
  • none: and none of these. "Drones that aren't burning" is all {Health}, none {Burning}.
  • tables: the matching tables, by index. Indices, as always, because a reference to a table can't outlive the next new table.
  • checked: how many of the world's tables the query has looked at.

Matching is two ANDs on the signature:

fn matches(signature: u64, all: u64, none: u64) -> bool {
    (signature & all) == all && (signature & none) == 0
}

Step 2: keeping it up to date

Tables are only ever added, always at the end of w.tables, and never removed. So a query that has checked the first checked tables only needs to look at the ones after that:

    fn update(&mut self, tables: &[Table]) {
        for (ti, t) in tables.iter().enumerate().skip(self.checked) {
            if matches(t.signature, self.all, self.none) {
                self.tables.push(ti as u32);
            }
        }
        self.checked = tables.len();
    }

The first update checks every table. After that, a frame with no new tables costs one comparison. A new table is checked once, by each query, the next time each is updated. flecs does the same thing in reverse: when a table is made, it tells the queries.

update takes &[Table], the world's tables as a slice, not the world. The query lives outside the world, in the game's own variables, and borrows only what it reads.

Step 3: walking a query

This is the shape of every system:

    movers.update(&w.tables);
    for &ti in &movers.tables {
        let (ps, vs) = w.tables[ti as usize].pair_mut::<Position, Velocity>();
        for (p, v) in ps.iter_mut().zip(vs.iter()) {
            p.at.x += v.per_second.x * 0.5;
            p.at.y += v.per_second.y * 0.5;
        }
    }

Two loops. The outer one is over tables, a few iterations. The inner one is over rows: two dense slices, read and written in order. That's lesson 1's move_soa. The query's job is to hand you the slices; what you do with them is the same data-oriented loop as always.

The drones and the bullet are in different tables, and the loop doesn't care. The turret isn't matched (no velocity), and the loop never sees it, not even to skip it.

Step 4: two columns of one table

The system writes positions and reads velocities, both columns of the same table. 2.3 noted that two slice_mut calls on one table can't be held at once: each borrows the whole table. 2.6 met the same problem with two tables of one Vec, and the same answer works here, one level down:

    fn pair_mut<A: Component, B: Component>(&mut self) -> (&mut [A], &mut [B]) {
        const { assert!(A::ID != B::ID, "pair_mut needs two different components") };
        let count = self.count();
        let [a, b] = self.columns.get_disjoint_mut([A::ID as usize, B::ID as usize]).expect("two different columns");
        let a = a.as_mut().unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("the table has no {} column", A::INFO.name));
        let b = b.as_mut().unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("the table has no {} column", B::INFO.name));
        (a.slice_mut::<A>(count), b.slice_mut::<B>(count))
    }

get_disjoint_mut lends out two columns of the 64. And since the column indices are the components' ids, which are constants, the "two different columns" check can run at compile time: const { assert!(...) } is evaluated when the program is built, for each A and B it's called with. pair_mut::<Position, Position>() doesn't build.

The two slices are &mut, so a system that only reads one takes it as &: vs.iter() above.

Run it

movers: all {Position Velocity}, none {}; tables: 2, entities: 4
    table 1 {Position Velocity Health}: 1:1 2:1 3:1
    table 2 {Position Velocity Damage Lifetime}: 4:1
targets: all {Position Health}, none {Burning}; tables: 1, entities: 3
    table 1 {Position Velocity Health}: 1:1 2:1 3:1
on_fire: all {Health Burning}, none {}; tables: 0, entities: 0

Then drone 2:1 catches fire, which makes table 3, after the queries were made:

2:1 catches fire, and the world makes table 3 for it
the queries have checked 3 tables; updating them checks the new one only
movers: all {Position Velocity}, none {}; tables: 3, entities: 4
    table 1 {Position Velocity Health}: 1:1 3:1
    table 2 {Position Velocity Damage Lifetime}: 4:1
    table 3 {Position Velocity Health Burning}: 2:1
targets: all {Position Health}, none {Burning}; tables: 1, entities: 2
    table 1 {Position Velocity Health}: 1:1 3:1
on_fire: all {Health Burning}, none {}; tables: 1, entities: 1
    table 3 {Position Velocity Health Burning}: 2:1

movers picked up the new table, targets refused it (none {Burning}), and on_fire got its first. Nobody re-scanned the old tables.

Last, the bullet is despawned. Its table is now empty, and stays in movers. Walking an empty table costs one look at its length.

Why this is fast

A query's cost doesn't depend on how many entities there are. It depends on how many tables match, and that number is small and stable. 10,000 drones in one table is one table to visit. That's the payoff of grouping entities by signature back in 2.4: the "which entities have X and Y?" question gets answered per table, once, instead of per entity, every frame.

The flip side is archetype fragmentation (2.4's Try): if every entity had a unique signature, every query would match thousands of one-row tables.

Try

  1. Write a query for "everything with a position that isn't a turret" and print it.
  2. Make 100 drones and walk movers. How many times does the outer loop run?
  3. Add any: u64 to the query: at least one of these components. Where in matches does it go?
  4. Add let _ = w.tables[1].pair_mut::<Position, Position>(); to main and read the build error. Then try pair_mut::<Position, Damage>() on the drones' table. When does that one fail, and why can't it be caught at compile time?

Take `&`395    // of either one to only read it.396    fn pair_mut<A: Component, B: Component>(&mut self) -> (&mut [A], &mut [B]) {397        const { assert!(A::ID != B::ID, "pair_mut needs two different components") };398        let count = self.count();399        let [a, b] = self.columns.get_disjoint_mut([A::ID as usize, B::ID as usize]).expect("two different columns");400        let a = a.as_mut().unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("the table has no {} column", A::INFO.name));401        let b = b.as_mut().unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("the table has no {} column", B::INFO.name));402        (a.slice_mut::<A>(count), b.slice_mut::<B>(count))403    }404}405 406// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------407// The world408// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------409 410// The world: the registry, the slots and free list, and every table, with a411// map from signature to table index so finding one is a lookup, not a search.412// Tables are referred to by index, never by reference: making a table can grow413// `tables` and move all of them, and an index survives that.414struct World {415    infos: [Option<&'static Info>; Build an ECS · part 3, systems · 3.2

Systems

ecs/src/3.systems/3.2.systems/systems.rs

3.1's movement loop had the shape of every system: bring a query up to date, then for each of its tables take the columns as slices and loop over the rows. This chapter names that shape and splits it in two:

  • the kernel: a plain loop over plain slices. It knows nothing about tables, entities or worlds. This is lessons 1 to 7: streaming, aliasing, vectorization.
  • the system: a query, plus a small function kayan calls on each table the query matches. It takes the table's columns and calls the kernel.

A frame runs the systems in order, each over all of its tables. The order is the schedule, and it's written down once, as data.

Step 1: the kernels

fn integrate(ps: &mut [Position], vs: &[Velocity], dt: f32) {
    for (p, v) in ps.iter_mut().zip(vs) {
        p.at.x += v.per_second.x * dt;
        p.at.y += v.per_second.y * dt;
    }
}

That's the whole thing, and it's the code you'd want to write if there were no ECS at all. Kernels are where you profile, read assembly and reach for SIMD (the lessons). Everything else in this course exists to hand them the right slices. burn and age look the same.

rin writes ps: noalias []position to promise the compiler that nothing else reaches ps, so it can vectorize without checking for overlap. In Rust, every &mut slice already makes that promise, and the borrow checker is what keeps it true. There's nothing to write.

Step 2: what a system gets

struct Iter<'a> {
    tables: &'a mut [Table],
    table: usize,
    dt: f32,
}

type SystemFn = fn(&mut Iter<'_>);

One struct instead of three parameters. It's the same idea as flecs' ecs_iter_t: adding to it later (3.3 adds a field) changes no system's signature.

Iter<'a> holds a borrow, so it carries a lifetime, 'a: the struct can't outlive the tables it borrows. You write 'a on the struct and '_ ("some lifetime, whichever") where it's used, and the compiler does the rest. This is the first struct in the course that holds a reference; the rest own their data.

Note what's not in it: the world. rin's kayan_iter had a world pointer, and through it a system could call kayan_despawn in the middle of a frame. Here a system gets the tables, and spawn, despawn, add and remove are methods of World, which it can't reach. A system can change values, never structure, and that's a rule of the types now, not a convention. 3.3 is about what to do when a system needs to change structure.

The system itself is the adapter:

fn move_system(it: &mut Iter) {
    let (ps, vs) = it.tables[it.table].pair_mut::<Position, Velocity>();
    integrate(ps, vs, it.dt);
}

Columns out, kernel in. No loop here: the kernel has it. ps and vs borrow it.tables, and it.dt is another field, so reading it alongside is fine.

Step 3: a system is data

struct System {
    name: &'static str,
    query: Query,
    run: SystemFn,
    calls: usize,
    rows: usize,
}

A name, a query, a function pointer. calls and rows count the work, for the output. The schedule is an array of these:

    let mut systems = [
        System::new("burn", mask_of::<Health>() | mask_of::<Burning>(), 0, burn_system),
        System::new("age", mask_of::<Lifetime>(), 0, age_system),
        System::new("move", mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>(), 0, move_system),
    ];

move_system without parentheses is the function itself, as a value of type SystemFn. No allocation, no trait object: a plain pointer to code, as in rin.

Step 4: a frame

fn progress(w: &mut World, systems: &mut [System], dt: f32) {
    for s in systems.iter_mut() {
        s.query.update(&w.tables);
        for &ti in &s.query.tables {
            let rows = w.tables[ti as usize].count();
            if rows > 0 {
                s.calls += 1;
                s.rows += rows;
                (s.run)(&mut Iter { tables: &mut w.tables, table: ti as usize, dt });
            }
        }
    }
}

progress is flecs' name for the same thing. For each system in order, for each of its tables, one call. (s.run)(...) calls the function in the run field; the parentheses tell Rust it's a field, not a method named run. The game loop becomes:

    for frame in 1..=8 {
        progress(&mut w, &mut systems, dt);

The systems live outside the world, in main's own array, so progress can borrow a system's query while lending the world's tables to the system. If the schedule were a field of the world, the two borrows would overlap.

Order is data flow

Systems run one after another, never interleaved, and each sees everything the earlier ones wrote this frame. So the order is a statement about data: a system that reads what another writes runs after it. Move before collide means bullets hit where they are now, not where they were. Damage before death means a drone dies in the frame its health hits zero, not the next. 3.4's schedule has nine systems, and each position in it is one of these decisions.

Bigger engines go further. Each system declares what it reads and writes, and the scheduler uses that to run systems that don't conflict at the same time, on other threads. Underneath, the order is still a list like this one. In Rust, "doesn't conflict" is exactly the borrow checker's question: two systems can run at once if neither needs &mut of what the other touches.

Run it

the schedule, run in this order every frame:
burn: all {Health Burning}, none {}; tables: 1, entities: 1
    table 2 {Position Velocity Health Burning}: 2:1
age: all {Lifetime}, none {}; tables: 1, entities: 3
    table 3 {Position Velocity Damage Lifetime}: 4:1 5:1 6:1
move: all {Position Velocity}, none {}; tables: 3, entities: 6
    table 1 {Position Velocity Health}: 1:1 3:1
    table 2 {Position Velocity Health Burning}: 2:1
    table 3 {Position Velocity Damage Lifetime}: 4:1 5:1 6:1
...
after frame 8, 2.00 seconds:
    0:1 at ( 0.00,  0.00)
    1:1 at (18.00,  4.00)  health 100
    3:1 at (26.00, -4.00)  health 100
    2:1 at (22.00,  0.00)  health 84, burning
    4:1 at (17.00,  0.00)  lifetime -1.50
    5:1 at (17.00,  4.00)  lifetime -1.00
    6:1 at (17.00, -4.00)  lifetime -0.50

8 frames, one call per table per frame:
    burn called  8 times, over  8 rows
    age  called  8 times, over 24 rows
    move called 24 times, over 48 rows
3 bullets are out of time and still in the world

move made 24 calls in 8 frames, three tables a frame, and each call is one tight loop. Call overhead is per table, never per entity.

And the last line is the cliffhanger. Each bullet's lifetime ran out, and nothing removed it, because a system in this chapter changes values, never structure. Despawning from inside a system looks like a one-line fix. It isn't, and 3.3 shows why.

Try

  1. Swap burn and move in the schedule. Does anything change? Now think of a pair where it would.
  2. Add a heal system for drones that aren't burning (all {Health}, none {Burning}).
  3. Build in Release (python tools/check.py --release systems) and find integrate in the assembly. Is it vectorized? (Lesson 1 shows how to look.)
  4. Try to despawn from age_system. What would it need that Iter doesn't have?

A reference to a table cannot live across that call (the473        // borrow checker refuses), so the index comes first and the table after.474        let table = self.table_for(signature);475        let row = self.tables[table as usize].add_row(e);476        self.slots[index as usize] = Slot { generation: e.generation, table, row: row as u32 };477        self.live += 1;478        e479    }480 481    fn despawn(&mut self, e: Entity) -> Result<(), Error> {482        if !self.alive(e) {483            return Err(Error::Dead);484        }485        let Slot { table, row, .. } = self.slots[e.index as usize];486        self.tables[table as usize].remove_row(row as usize, &mut self.slots);487        let slot = &mut self.slots[e.index as usize];488        slot.generation = slot.generation.checked_add(1).expect("a number has lived 4 billion lives");489        self.free.push(e.index);490        self.live -= 1;491        Ok(())492    }493 494    fn table_of(&self, e: Entity) -> &Table {495        &self.tables[self.slots[e.index as usize].table as usize]496    }497 498    fn table_of_mut(&mut self, e: Entity) -> &mut Table {499        &mut self.tables[self.slots[e.index as usize].table as usize]500    }501 502    fn row(&self, e: Entity) -> usize {503        self.slots[e.index as usize].row as usize504    }505 506    // The components a live entity has: its table's signature. 0 for a dead507    // one.508    fn signature(&self, e: Entity) -> u64 {509        if !self.alive(e) {510            return 0;511        }512        self.table_of(e).signature513    }514 515    // e's T, or None if e is dead or has no T. Handle, slot, table, row, typed516    // view: the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component.517    fn get<T: Component>(&self, e: Entity) -> Option<&T> {518        if !self.alive(e) {519            return None;520        }521        let t = self.table_of(e);522        if !t.has(T::ID) {523            return None;524        }525        Some(&t.slice::<T>()[self.row(e)])526    }527 528    fn get_mut<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity) -> Option<&mut T> {529        if !self.alive(e) {530            return None;531        }532        let row = self.row(e);533        let t = self.table_of_mut(e);534        if !t.has(T::ID) {535            return None;536        }537        Some(&mut t.slice_mut::<T>()[row])538    }539 540    fn has<T: Component>(&self, e: Entity) -> bool {541        self.signature(e) & mask_of::<T>() != 0542    }543 544    // Write e's T. It must already have one: giving an entity a component it545    // does not have changes its table, which is 2.6.546    fn set<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity, value: T) -> Result<(), Error> {547        if !self.alive(e) {548            return Err(Error::Dead);549        }550        *self.get_mut::<T>(e).ok_or(Error::Missing)? = value;551        Ok(())552    }553 554    // The table an entity of table `from` moves to when it gains component555    // `id`. The first time, it is found by signature, which can make the556    // table; the answer is written on both tables, as from's add edge and the557    // destination's remove edge, so neither direction is looked up again.558    fn table_with(&mut self, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 {559        if let Some(to) = self.tables[from as usize].add_edges[id as usize] {560            return to;561        }562        let to = self.table_for(self.tables[from as usize].signature | bit(id));563        self.tables[from as usize].add_edges[id as usize] = Some(to);564        self.tables[to as usize].remove_edges[id as usize] = Some(from);565        to566    }567 568    // The same for losing component `id`.569    fn table_without(&mut self, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 {570        if let Some(to) = self.tables[from as usize].remove_edges[id as usize] {571            return to;572        }573        let to = self.table_for(self.tables[from as usize].signature & !bit(id));574        self.tables[from as usize].remove_edges[id as usize] = Some(to);575        self.tables[to as usize].add_edges[id as usize] = Some(from);576        to577    }578 579    // Move a live entity to table `to`. Components both tables have are580    // copied, byte for byte; components only the new table has start zeroed;581    // components only the old table has are dropped with its old row.582    // get_disjoint_mut lends out two tables of the Vec at once, after583    // checking at run time that they are two different tables.584    fn move_to(&mut self, e: Entity, to: u32) {585        let Slot { table: from, row, .. } = self.slots[e.index as usize];586        if from == to {587            return;588        }589        let [old, new] = self.tables.get_disjoint_mut([from as usize, to as usize]).expect("two different tables");590        let new_row = new.add_row(e);591        for (o, n) in old.columns.iter().zip(new.columns.iter_mut()) {592            if let (Some(o), Some(n)) = (o, n) {593                n.row_mut(new_row).copy_from_slice(o.row(row as usize));594            }595        }596        old.remove_row(row as usize, &mut self.slots);597        self.slots[e.index as usize] = Slot { generation: e.generation, table: to, row: new_row as u32 };598    }599 600    // Give e a T. If it already has one, this is set; if not, it moves to the601    // table with T and then sets it.602    fn add<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity, value: T) -> Result<(), Error> {603        if !self.alive(e) {604            return Err(Error::Dead);605        }606        if !self.has::<T>(e) {607            let from = self.slots[e.index as usize].table;608            let to = self.table_with(from, T::ID);609            self.move_to(e, to);610        }611        self.set(e, value)612    }613 614    // Take e's T away, moving it to the table without T.615    fn remove<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity) -> Result<(), Error> {616        if !self.alive(e) {617            return Err(Error::Dead);618        }619        if !self.has::<T>(e) {620            return Err(Error::Missing);621        }622        let from = self.slots[e.index as usize].table;623        let to = self.table_without(from, T::ID);624        self.move_to(e, to);625        Ok(())626    }627 628    // e's component `id` as its bytes: None if e is dead or has no such629    // component. ecs/src/3.systems/3.3.commands/commands.rs

In the dojo: 5. a command buffer, on its own, to watch and to practise.

3.2's systems change values, never structure, so bullets whose time ran out stay in the world. The obvious fix is to despawn them from inside the loop that walks their table. It's wrong, and seeing exactly why is most of this chapter. Rust catches part of it, which makes the part it doesn't catch easier to see.

Step 1: the bug

The natural way to write it is a loop over the table's rows that despawns as it goes:

fn expire_now(w: &mut World, table: usize) {
    let t = &w.tables[table];
    for (&e, l) in t.entities.iter().zip(t.slice::<Lifetime>()) {
        if l.seconds <= 0.0 {
            w.despawn(e).expect("alive");
        }
    }
}

It doesn't compile:

error[E0502]: cannot borrow `*w` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
     |
1061 |     let t = &w.tables[table];
     |              -------- immutable borrow occurs here
1062 |     for (&e, l) in t.entities.iter().zip(t.slice::<Lifetime>()) {
     |                    -------------------------------------------- immutable borrow later used here
1063 |         if l.seconds <= 0.0 {
1064 |             w.despawn(e).expect("alive");
     |             ^^^^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here

The loop borrows the table, and despawn needs the whole world, table included. The compiler doesn't know what despawn does to the table; it only knows it could change it while the loop is reading it. In rin, this version compiles and has the bug. So the program writes the version that compiles in Rust too, a loop over row numbers:

fn expire_now(w: &mut World, table: usize) {
    let mut row = 0;
    while row < w.tables[table].count() {
        if w.tables[table].slice::<Lifetime>()[row].seconds <= 0.0 {
            let e = w.tables[table].entities[row];
            w.despawn(e).expect("alive");
        }
        row += 1;
    }
}

Each line borrows the table for a moment and lets go, so nothing is borrowed when despawn runs. Four bullets, three of them out of time:

1. an expire loop that despawns as it goes
    lifetimes:  0:1 0.00  1:1 1.00  2:1 0.00  3:1 0.00
after one pass:
    lifetimes:  3:1 0.00  1:1 1.00
verify: 0 problems. The world is fine; the loop missed one.

Row by row:

row 0: 0:1 is out of time. Despawn: the last row, 3:1, moves into row 0.
row 1: 1:1 has time left.
row 2: 2:1 is out of time. Despawn: it's the last row, so nothing moves.
row 3: the table has 2 rows now. Stop.

3:1 moved into row 0, which the loop had already passed, so it was never looked at. The world is perfectly consistent (verify agrees). The loop is what's wrong: a despawn swap-removes from the table the loop is walking. A row number is a number, and 2.5 already showed what the borrow checker says about those: nothing.

Walking backwards fixes this case (lesson 2 does it), because the row that moves in has already been looked at. But it doesn't fix the general problem:

  • Adding or removing a component moves the entity to another table. If the query matches that table too and visits it later, the entity is processed twice.
  • If that table is new, making it can grow w.tables and move every table. In rin, the table pointer the loop holds then points at the old copy, and every write after that is lost. In Rust, a reference couldn't survive that (2.4), but a table index would, and so would the confusion.
  • One system's despawn can land in a table another system is halfway through, if a system despawns entities it found through a second query.

Step 2: record now, apply later

So a system doesn't change structure. It records a command saying what should change, and the world applies every command after the frame's last system:

during the frame   values change; tables, rows and borrows do not
after the frame    spawns, despawns, adds and removes, in order
enum Command {
    Spawn { signature: u64, entity: Option<Entity> },
    Despawn(Entity),
    Add { target: Target, id: u32, start: usize, len: usize },
    Remove { entity: Entity, id: u32 },
}

A Rust enum can carry different data in each variant, so each command holds exactly what it needs. rin's kayan_command was one struct with every field, and a kind saying which fields meant something. An add carries its value as bytes: len bytes at start in the buffer's byte store.

struct Commands {
    list: Vec<Command>,
    bytes: Vec<u8>,
}

This is the frame arena, made of Vecs. After the commands are applied, both are cleared. clear keeps the memory, so after a few frames the Vecs are big enough for any frame, and recording a command allocates nothing. rin's memops_arena_clear did the same thing for one block of memory.

Step 3: recording

The typed methods a system calls copy the value's bytes into the store and push a command:

    fn add<T: Component>(&mut self, target: impl Into<Target>, value: T) {
        let start = self.bytes.len();
        self.bytes.extend_from_slice(bytes_of(&value));
        self.list.push(Command::Add { target: target.into(), id: T::ID, start, len: size_of::<T>() });
    }

bytes_of is the course's fifth and last unsafe line: a Pod value as its bytes, the opposite direction from 2.2's slice.

fn bytes_of<T: Pod>(value: &T) -> &[u8] {
    // SAFETY: T is Pod, so it has no padding and all its bytes are
    // initialised; the slice borrows `value` and cannot outlive it.
    unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts((value as *const T).cast::<u8>(), size_of::<T>()) }
}

rin's frame arena pushed each value at its type's alignment. Here the bytes go into a Vec<u8> at whatever offset comes next, which is fine, because they're only ever copied as bytes into a column, never read as a T where they lie.

The fixed expire system is the broken loop with the despawn recorded:

fn expire_system<C>(it: &mut Iter, _ctx: &mut C) {
    let t = &it.tables[it.table];
    for (&e, l) in t.entities.iter().zip(t.slice::<Lifetime>()) {
        if l.seconds <= 0.0 {
            it.commands.despawn(e);
        }
    }
}

It's the version that didn't compile in Step 1, and now it does. t borrows it.tables, and it.commands is a different field of the Iter, so the loop can read the table and record at the same time. The table doesn't change while the loop runs, so every row is looked at once.

struct Iter<'a> {
    tables: &'a mut [Table],
    table: usize,
    commands: &'a mut Commands,
    dt: f32,
}

3.2 noted that Iter has no world. That's what makes this the only way: a system has the tables and the command buffer, and no method that changes structure is in reach.

Step 4: applying, by id

Commands hold bytes and ids, not types. So applying an add needs 2.6's add by id:

    fn add_id(&mut self, e: Entity, id: u32, value: &[u8]) -> Result<(), Error> {

It's the same move-then-write as before, with the write a copy_from_slice of the value's bytes into the row. Once that exists, the typed add from 2.6 shrinks to a one-line wrapper. That's the pattern from the start of the course: byte work written once, a typed generic layer on top.

    fn add<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity, value: T) -> Result<(), Error> {
        self.add_id(e, T::ID, bytes_of(&value))
    }

flush applies the list in order, and progress calls it after the frame's last system:

    fn flush(&mut self) {
        let mut cmds = std::mem::take(&mut self.commands);
        for i in 0..cmds.list.len() {
            let result = match cmds.list[i] {
                Command::Spawn { signature, .. } => {
                    let e = self.spawn(signature);
                    cmds.list[i] = Command::Spawn { signature, entity: Some(e) };
                    Ok(())
                }
                Command::Despawn(e) => self.despawn(e),
                Command::Add { target, id, start, len } => {
                    let e = cmds.resolve(target);
                    self.add_id(e, id, &cmds.bytes[start..start + len])
                }
                Command::Remove { entity, id } => self.remove_id(entity, id),
            };

The commands live in the world, and applying them calls &mut self methods on the world. Reading self.commands while calling self.spawn would be two overlapping borrows. std::mem::take moves the buffer out of the world, leaving an empty one in its place, so the loop owns it outright. At the end, it goes back, cleared, with its memory:

        cmds.list.clear();
        cmds.bytes.clear();
        self.commands = cmds;

Moving a Commands is copying two Vec headers, 48 bytes. The contents stay where they are.

Step 5: commands that arrive too late

By the time a command is applied, its entity may be gone. The usual case is two systems both asking to despawn the same thing. Applying in order handles that for free: the first despawn works, and the second finds a dead handle. Part 1's generations make that check one comparison, and every method already returns a Result that says so:

            match result {
                Ok(()) => self.applied += 1,
                Err(_) => self.skipped += 1,
            }

Step 6: spawning from a system

A turret firing is a spawn in the middle of a frame. The new entity doesn't exist until the commands are applied, so there's no handle to give its components to. commands.spawn returns a pending spawn instead: the spawn command's place in the list.

struct Pending(usize);

Components are given to that:

            let shot = it.commands.spawn(bullet_signature());
            it.commands.add(shot, *p);
            it.commands.add(shot, Velocity { per_second: Vec2 { x: 8.0, y: 0.0 } });
            it.commands.add(shot, Damage { amount: 25.0 });
            it.commands.add(shot, Lifetime { seconds: 2.0 });

add takes target: impl Into<Target>, "anything that converts into a Target", and both Entity and Pending do:

enum Target {
    Entity(Entity),
    Pending(usize),
}

So add(e, value) and add(shot, value) are one method. rin needed two, kayan_defer_add and kayan_pending_set.

When the flush reaches the spawn, it makes the entity and writes the handle into the command (entity: Some(e) in Step 4). The adds after it look the handle up there, through resolve. The bullet is spawned with its full signature, so the adds land in the table it's already in: no moves. And it doesn't move until the next frame, because no system ran over it this one.

Step 7: a system with a context

A bullet that reaches a target damages it. The hit system walks the bullets (its own query) and, for each, the targets (a second query). It needs that second query from somewhere, so a system now gets a context, whatever the game passes to progress:

type SystemFn<C> = fn(&mut Iter<'_>, &mut C);

C is a type parameter: the context is whatever type the schedule chooses. This schedule's context is the targets query, so the hit system takes it typed:

fn hit_system(it: &mut Iter, targets: &mut Query) {

rin's ctx was a *void, cast back to *kayan_query inside the system, and nothing checked the cast. Here a system in a System<Query> schedule that asked for some other context wouldn't compile. Systems that don't use the context are generic over it (expire_system<C>), so they fit any schedule. The program's second demo has no context to pass, so it passes &mut (), the empty type.

The hit system needs the bullets' table and a target's table at once, which is 2.6's get_disjoint_mut again:

            let Ok([bullets, t]) = it.tables.get_disjoint_mut([it.table, ti as usize]) else {
                continue;
            };

let ... else is a pattern that must match, or the else runs (and must leave the block: here, continue). If a table matched both queries, the two indices would be the same, and the loop skips that pair instead of stopping.

The damage is a value, so it's written now. The bullet's despawn is structure, so it's recorded. Walking a second query in the middle of a frame is safe because of commands: no table is made or moved until the frame is over, so the indices both queries hold stay good.

Run it

2. an expire system that records despawns
    lifetimes:  0:1 0.00  1:1 1.00  2:1 0.00  3:1 0.00
    despawn 0:1
    despawn 2:1
    despawn 3:1
after one frame:
    lifetimes:  1:1 1.00

All three. Then the turret, with two targets 0.25 apart in its line of fire and a third out of it:

3. a turret, two targets in its line of fire, one out of it
frame 1
    spawn {Position Velocity Damage Lifetime} -> 4:1
frame 2
frame 3
    spawn {Position Velocity Damage Lifetime} -> 5:1
frame 4
    despawn 4:1
    despawn 4:1: skipped, dead
frame 5
    spawn {Position Velocity Damage Lifetime} -> 4:2
...
health: 1:1 50, 2:1 50, 3:1 100
commands applied: 17, skipped: 2

In frame 4, bullet 4:1 is close enough to both targets. Both lose 25, and both hits record a despawn. The first applies; the second finds 4:1 already dead and is skipped. In frame 5 the next bullet gets number 4 back with generation 2: Part 1, working.

17 commands, for three bullets and two despawns: each spawn is five, the spawn and its four components.

Rust notes

rinRust
a loop holding the table, calling kayan_despawn: compiles, misses rowsthe same loop: E0502, doesn't compile
a loop over row numbers, calling kayan_despawnthe same: compiles, misses rows
kayan_command { kind, entity, spawn, id, signature, value }enum Command: each variant carries only its own fields
frame: memops_arena, cleared after the flushtwo Vecs, cleared after the flush: same memory reused, no allocation
kayan_defer_add and kayan_pending_setone add(target: impl Into<Target>, value)
ctx: *void, cast in the systemC, a type parameter: hit_system(it, targets: &mut Query)
it*.world, for kayan_defer_*it.commands: the only structural change a system can reach

Try

  1. Walk the rows backwards in expire_now ((0..count).rev()). Does it catch all three now? Does that fix the problem for adds and removes?
  2. Write a system that records an add of Burning for every target it walks. Then flush after each system instead of after the frame. What does that change about what later systems see? (flecs calls these sync points.)
  3. Print c.commands.list.capacity() after each frame. When does it stop growing?
  4. Give a pending spawn a component that isn't in its signature (add a Burning to the bullet). Does it work? What does it cost?

64],444    component_count: u32,445    tables: Vec<Table>,446    by_signature: HashMap<u64, u32>,447    slots: Vec<Slot>,448    free: Vec<u32>,449    live: usize,450    // The frame's commands. `trace` prints each one as it is applied.451    commands: Commands,452    applied: usize,453    skipped: usize,454    trace: bool,455}456 457impl World {458    fn new() -> World {459        World {460            infos: [None; There is no entity yet, so878// it is named by its place in the command list; give it components with879// `commands.add(pending, value)`.880#[derive(Clone, Copy)]881struct Pending(usize);882 883// Who an add is for: a live entity, or one spawned earlier in the same frame.884// Both convert into a Target, so `add` takes either.885#[derive(Clone, Copy)]886enum Target {887    Entity(Entity),888    Pending(usize),889}890 891impl From<Entity> for Target {892    fn from(e: Entity) -> Target {893        Target::Entity(e)894    }895}896 897impl From<Pending> for Target {898    fn from(p: Pending) -> Target {899        Target::Pending(p.0)900    }901}902 903// A structural change recorded during a frame and applied after it. A spawn's entity905// is filled in when it is applied, which is how a pending add finds it.906#[derive(Clone, Copy)]907enum Command {908    Spawn { signature: u64, entity: Option<Entity> },909    Despawn(Entity),910    Add { target: Target, id: u32, start: usize, len: usize },911    Remove { entity: Entity, id: u32 },912}913 914// The frame's commands, and the bytes of their values. There is no world here, so a system has963// no way to change structure except through a command.964struct Iter<'a> {965    tables: &'a mut [Table],966    table: usize,967    commands: &'a mut Commands,968    dt: f32,969}970 971// A system's function gets the Iter, and the context the game passes to972// progress: whatever its systems share, such as another query or a score.973type SystemFn<C> = fn(&mut Iter<'_>, &mut C);974 975// A system: a name, the query that finds its tables, and the function run on976// each of those tables that has rows. `calls` and `rows` count what it has run977// over.978struct System<C> {979    name: &'static str,980    query: Query,981    run: SystemFn<C>,982    calls: usize,983    rows: usize,984}985 986impl<C> System<C> {987    fn new(name: &'static str, all: u64, none: u64, run: SystemFn<C>) -> System<C> {988        System { name, query: Query::new(all, none), run, calls: 0, rows: 0 }989    }990}991 992// One frame: every system in order, each over every table it matches that has993// rows, then the commands they recorded. Written with an1057// iterator over the table, this would not compile: the iterator borrows the1058// table, and despawn needs the whole world. Written over row numbers, it1059// borrows nothing between despawns, so it compiles, and is wrong.1060fn expire_now(w: &mut World, table: usize) {1061    let mut row = 0;1062    while row < w.tables[table].count() {1063        if w.tables[table].slice::<Lifetime>()[row].seconds <= 0.0 {1064            let e = w.tables[table].entities[row];1065            w.despawn(e).expect("alive");1066        }1067        row += 1;1068    }1069}1070 1071// The right way: record the despawn. The table does not change until the1072// frame is over, so every row is looked at once.1073fn expire_system<C>(it: &mut Iter, _ctx: &mut C) {1074    let t = &it.tables[it.table];1075    for (&e, l) in t.entities.iter().zip(t.slice::<Lifetime>()) {1076        if l.seconds <= 0.0 {1077            it.commands.despawn(e);1078        }1079    }1080}1081 1082fn age_system<C>(it: &mut Iter, _ctx: &mut C) {1083    age(it.tables[it.table].slice_mut::<Lifetime>(), it.dt);1084}1085 1086fn move_system<C>(it: &mut Iter, _ctx: &mut C) {1087    let (ps, vs) = it.tables[it.table].pair_mut::<Position, Velocity>();1088    integrate(ps, vs, it.dt);1089}1090 1091// A turret whose timer is up spawns a bullet where it stands. The bullet does1092// not exist until the frame ends, so it first moves next frame.1093fn turret_system<C>(it: &mut Iter, _ctx: &mut C) {1094    let (ps, ts) = it.tables[it.table].pair_mut::<Position, Turret>();1095    for (p, t) in ps.iter().zip(ts.iter_mut()) {1096        if t.timer <= 0.0 {1097            let shot = it.commands.spawn(bullet_signature());1098            it.commands.add(shot, *p);1099            it.commands.add(shot, Velocity { per_second: Vec2 { x: 8.0, y: 0.0 } });1100            it.commands.add(shot, Damage { amount: 25.0 });1101            it.commands.add(shot, Lifetime { seconds: 2.0 });1102            t.timer += t.cooldown;1103        }1104        t.timer -= it.dt;1105    }1106}1107 1108// A bullet within half a unit of a target hits it. The damage is a value, so1109// it is written now; the bullet's despawn is structure, so it is recorded. The1110// targets are another query, which this schedule passes as its context. The1111// bullets' table and a target table are borrowed together with1112// get_disjoint_mut; during a frame no table is made or moved, so the indices1113// stay good.1114fn hit_system(it: &mut Iter, targets: &mut Query) {1115    targets.update(it.tables);1116    for b in 0..it.tables[it.table].count() {1117        for &ti in &targets.tables {1118            let Ok([bullets, t]) = it.tables.get_disjoint_mut([it.table, ti as usize]) else {1119                continue;1120            };1121            let p = bullets.slice::<Position>()[b];1122            let d = bullets.slice::<Damage>()[b];1123            let e = bullets.entities[b];1124            let (tps, ths) = t.pair_mut::<Position, Health>();1125            for (tp, th) in tps.iter().zip(ths.iter_mut()) {1126                let dx = tp.at.x - p.at.x;1127                let dy = tp.at.y - p.at.y;1128                if dx * dx + dy * dy < 0.25 {1129                    th.points -= d.amount;1130                    it.commands.despawn(e);1131                }1132            }1133        }1134    }1135}1136 1137fn make_world() -> World {1138    let mut w = World::new();1139    w.register::<Position>();1140    w.register::<Velocity>();1141    w.register::<Health>();1142    w.register::<Damage>();1143    w.register::<Lifetime>();1144    w.register::<Turret>();1145    w.register::<Burning>();1146    w1147}1148 1149// Four bullets, three of them out of time.1150fn four_bullets(w: &mut World) {1151    spawn_bullet(w, 1.0, 0.0);1152    spawn_bullet(w, 2.0, 1.0);1153    spawn_bullet(w, 3.0, 0.0);1154    spawn_bullet(w, 4.0, 0.0);1155}1156 1157fn print_lifetimes(w: &World) {1158    let t = &w.tables[w.by_signature[&bullet_signature()] as usize];1159    print!("    lifetimes:");1160    for (e, l) in t.entities.iter().zip(t.slice::<Lifetime>()) {1161        print!("  {e} {:.2}", l.seconds);1162    }1163    println!();1164}1165 1166fn main() {1167    println!("1. an expire loop that despawns as it goes");1168    let mut a = make_world();1169    four_bullets(&mut a);1170    print_lifetimes(&a);1171    let bullets = a.by_signature[&bullet_signature()] as usize;1172    expire_now(&mut a, bullets);1173    println!("after one pass:");1174    print_lifetimes(&a);1175    println!("verify: {} problems. The world is fine; the loop missed one.", a.verify());1176 1177    println!();1178    println!("2. an expire system that records despawns");1179    let mut b = make_world();1180    b.trace = true;1181    four_bullets(&mut b);1182    print_lifetimes(&b);1183    let mut right = [System::new("expire", mask_of::<Lifetime>(), 0, expire_system)];1184    progress(&mut b, &mut right, &mut (), 0.25);1185    println!("after one frame:");1186    print_lifetimes(&b);1187 1188    println!();1189    println!("3. a turret, two targets in its line of fire, one out of it");1190    let mut c = make_world();1191    c.trace = true;1192    let gun = c.spawn(mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Turret>());1193    c.set(gun, Turret { cooldown: 0.5, timer: 0.0 }).expect("just spawned");1194    let near = spawn_target(&mut c, 4.0, 0.0);1195    let far = spawn_target(&mut c, 4.25, 0.0);1196    let aside = spawn_target(&mut c, 4.0, 3.0);1197    let mut targets = Query::new(mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Health>(), 0);1198    let lifetime_only = mask_of::<Lifetime>();1199    let mut systems = [1200        System::new("turret", mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Turret>(), 0, turret_system),1201        System::new("age", lifetime_only, 0, age_system),1202        System::new("expire", lifetime_only, 0, expire_system),1203        System::new("hit", mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Damage>(), 0, hit_system),1204        System::new("move", mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>(), 0, move_system),1205    ];1206    for frame in 1..=6 {1207        println!("frame {frame}");1208        progress(&mut c, &mut systems, &mut targets, 0.25);1209    }1210    let health = |e| c.get::<Health>(e).expect("alive").points;1211    println!("health: {near} {:.0}, {far} {:.0}, {aside} {:.0}", health(near), health(far), health(aside));1212    println!("commands applied: {}, skipped: {}", c.applied, c.skipped);1213    c.print_tables();1214    println!("verify: {} problems", c.verify());1215}

Build an ECS · part 3, systems · 3.4

A game

ecs/src/3.systems/3.4.game/game.rs

In the dojo: this chapter puts all five building blocks together; the dojo has each one on its own, to watch and to practise.

Everything together. Three lanes, a turret at the left end of each, and drones coming from the right in waves:

  • a turret fires down its lane while there's a drone in it;
  • a bullet that reaches a drone damages it;
  • a drone below half health catches fire;
  • a drone with no health left is destroyed;
  • a drone that gets to the left end has reached the base.

The top of the file is kayan, exactly as 3.3 left it. The game is the bottom: kernels, systems, a schedule and a level script. Every rule of the game is a system over a query. Every structural change a system makes is a command.

The pieces

The components are the same seven from 2.1. A drone is a signature:

fn drone_signature() -> u64 {
    mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>() | mask_of::<Health>()
}

A burning drone is that plus Burning, which puts it in another table. There is no Drone type anywhere in the program. A drone is whatever lives in a table with these columns.

What the systems share (the drones query, the clock, the score) is one struct, the schedule's context (3.3):

struct Game {
    drones: Query,
    time: f32,
    fired: u32,
    hits: u32,
    fires: u32,
    kills: u32,
    breaches: u32,
    came: u32,
}

Every system in the schedule gets &mut Game. The ones that use it name it (g: &mut Game); the rest are generic and ignore it.

The schedule

    let mut systems = [
        System::new("turret", shooting, 0, turret_system),
        System::new("age", mask_of::<Lifetime>(), 0, age_system),
        System::new("expire", mask_of::<Lifetime>(), 0, expire_system),
        System::new("move", movers, 0, move_system),
        System::new("hit", bullets, 0, hit_system),
        System::new("ignite", mask_of::<Health>(), mask_of::<Burning>(), ignite_system),
        System::new("burn", mask_of::<Health>() | mask_of::<Burning>(), 0, burn_system),
        System::new("die", mask_of::<Health>(), 0, die_system),
        System::new("breach", mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Health>(), 0, breach_system),
    ];

Read it as the frame, top to bottom. Each line's position is a data-flow decision (3.2):

  • move before hit: bullets hit where they are, not where they were.
  • hit before ignite, burn and die: a drone takes damage, catches fire and is destroyed in the same frame its health drops.
  • die before breach: only a drone that survived the frame can reach the base. breach also checks points > 0 itself, because both run in the same frame and die's despawn hasn't been applied yet.
  • ignite has none {Burning}: a drone catches fire once. The add is a command, so next frame it's in the burning table and the query no longer matches it.

The array's type is [System<Game>; 9], and nobody wrote that down. The compiler works it out from turret_system, which takes &mut Game, and then picks C = Game for every generic system in the list.

The rules

Each one is a few lines. The ones that only change values call kernels:

fn burn_system<C>(it: &mut Iter, _ctx: &mut C) {
    let (hs, fires) = it.tables[it.table].pair_mut::<Health, Burning>();
    burn(hs, fires, it.dt);
}

The ones that change structure record commands:

        if h.points < 0.5 * h.max && h.points > 0.0 {
            it.commands.add(e, Burning { per_second: 10.0 });
            g.fires += 1;
        }

The turret is the most involved. It asks the drones query whether anything is ahead of it in its lane, then spawns a bullet with a pending spawn (3.3). It needs its own row and the drones' tables, which are all in it.tables, so it takes them one after another: copy the row's values out, look at the drones, then borrow the row again to write the timer.

        let p = it.tables[it.table].slice::<Position>()[row];
        let ready = it.tables[it.table].slice::<Turret>()[row].timer <= 0.0;
        if ready && drone_ahead(it.tables, &g.drones, p.at.x, p.at.y) {

p is a copy, not a reference (components are Copy), so nothing is borrowed when drone_ahead reads all the tables. rin's version held a pointer into the turret column across the call; Rust makes you say which borrow comes first. Here it costs nothing, and the order is clearer.

hit is 3.3's hit system, with one extra thought about speed. A bullet moves a unit a frame and a fast drone a quarter, so they close by at most 1.25 a frame. A hit window of ±0.75 is 1.5 wide, so no bullet can pass through a drone between two frames:

                if dx * dx < 0.5625 && dy * dy < 0.25 {

The level

The waves aren't a system. They're the level script, and it runs between frames, in the game loop, where spawning directly is safe:

    for frame in 0..frames {
        g.time = frame as f32 * dt;
        if frame % 32 == 0 && frame / 32 < 8 {
            send_wave(&mut w, &mut g, frame / 32);
        }
        progress(&mut w, &mut systems, &mut g, dt);
        problems += w.verify();

verify runs after every frame: 512 checks of Part 1's invariant over the whole world.

Drawing by table

The picture of the lanes walks a query of everything with a position. What an entity is drawn as comes from its table's signature, decided once per table, not per entity:

fn glyph_of(signature: u64) -> char {
    if signature & mask_of::<Turret>() != 0 {
        'T'
    } else if signature & mask_of::<Burning>() != 0 {
        '*'
    } else if signature & mask_of::<Health>() != 0 {
        'd'
    } else {
        '-'
    }
}

In an OOP engine this would be a virtual draw() per object, or in Rust a dyn Draw trait object. Here it's a property of a table, and the inner loop is a plain loop over positions.

Exact on purpose

Every speed and time step is a power of two: dt is 1/16, drones move 2 or 4 units a second, bullets 16, fire burns 10 a second (0.625 a frame). So every position, health and timer is exactly representable, and no rounding ever happens. Rust also never fuses a multiply and an add into one instruction on its own (C compilers may). That's why a Debug build and a Release build print the same game, and why it matches rin-dod's line for line. Real games give that up for nicer numbers. Rounding differences usually don't matter, but they do the day you want a replay or a lockstep network game.
