What you built

Part 1  entities       handles, generations, slots, swap-remove, verify
Part 2  components     ids, columns, tables, archetypes, typed access,
                       moving between tables, the archetype graph, reflection
Part 3  systems        queries, kernels and schedules, commands, a game

That's a working archetype ECS, about 700 lines of kayan without comments, with five one-line unsafe blocks, no dependencies, and a clean run under Miri. It's the design flecs is built on (tables, the archetype graph, cached queries, command buffers), and Bevy and Unity DOTS are close cousins, minus their years of features.

What Rust changed

Across the course, the borrow checker turned three of rin-dod's quiet bugs into compile errors:

chapterthe bugin rinin Rust
2.4a table pointer kept across table_fora row in a table that movedE0499
2.5a component pointer kept across a spawna write lost in an old blockE0499
3.3despawning while iterating a tablea row skippedE0502

And it caught none of the bugs about numbers: 1.2's reused entity number, 2.5's stale row number, 3.3's loop over row numbers. Those are what generations, handles and commands are for, in either language. The borrow checker tracks who may touch memory; it doesn't know what a number means.

It also turned two conventions into types: a system can't change structure, because Iter has no world (3.2), and a system's context is checked, not cast (3.3). And it cost three things rin didn't have: get_disjoint_mut where two tables or columns are needed at once, std::mem::take to apply commands to the world that owns them, and a few borrows taken one after another instead of held together (the turret, 2.3's writes).

Next

Things worth adding, roughly in order of how much they teach:

  • Relationships: ChildOf(parent) as a component, flecs' big idea.
  • Change detection: a per-column version number, so a system can skip tables nothing wrote to.
  • Parallel systems: systems that don't write what others read can run at the same time. In Rust, that's two &mut borrows that don't overlap, so std::thread::scope and split_at_mut (or get_disjoint_mut) are most of what's needed, and the compiler checks the split.
  • Removing empty tables, and the queries' table lists with them.
  • Serialization: the reflect records already describe every byte; write the tables out and read them back.

Try

  1. Add a fourth lane. What changes? (Only the level: LANES, the picture.)
  2. Make bullets pierce: they don't despawn on a hit, but each drone can only be hit by a bullet once. Where does "once" live? (A component on the bullet? On the drone?)
  3. Add a Shield component that absorbs the next hit, then removes itself. Which systems change?
  4. Call w.inspect on a drone the frame it catches fire. Where in the main loop can you call it, and why not from ignite_system?

64],440    component_count: u32,441    tables: Vec<Table>,442    by_signature: HashMap<u64, u32>,443    slots: Vec<Slot>,444    free: Vec<u32>,445    live: usize,446    // The frame's commands. `trace` prints each one as it is applied.447    commands: Commands,448    applied: usize,449    skipped: usize,450    trace: bool,451}452 453impl World {454    fn new() -> World {455        World {456            infos: [None; This481    // is where archetypes come from.482    fn table_for(&mut self, signature: u64) -> u32 {483        if let Some(&index) = self.by_signature.get(&signature) {484            return index;485        }486        let index = self.tables.len() as u32;487        self.tables.push(Table::new(&self.infos, signature));488        self.by_signature.insert(signature, index);489        index490    }491 492    // A new entity with the components in `signature`, all zeroed, in the493    // table for that signature.494    fn spawn(&mut self, signature: u64) -> Entity {495        let index = match self.free.pop() {496            Some(index) => index,497            None => {498                self.slots.push(Slot { generation: ONE, table: 0, row: 0 });499                self.slots.len() as u32 - 1500            }501        };502        let e = Entity { index, generation: self.slots[index as usize].generation };503        // table_for can make a table, and pushing onto `tables` can move every504        // table. Handle, slot, table, row, typed548    // view: the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component.549    fn get<T: Component>(&self, e: Entity) -> Option<&T> {550        if !self.alive(e) {551            return None;552        }553        let t = self.table_of(e);554        if !t.has(T::ID) {555            return None;556        }557        Some(&t.slice::<T>()[self.row(e)])558    }559 560    fn get_mut<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity) -> Option<&mut T> {561        if !self.alive(e) {562            return None;563        }564        let row = self.row(e);565        let t = self.table_of_mut(e);566        if !t.has(T::ID) {567            return None;568        }569        Some(&mut t.slice_mut::<T>()[row])570    }571 572    fn has<T: Component>(&self, e: Entity) -> bool {573        self.signature(e) & mask_of::<T>() != 0574    }575 576    // Write e's T. The first time, it is found by signature, which can make the588    // table; the answer is written on both tables, as from's add edge and the589    // destination's remove edge, so neither direction is looked up again.590    fn table_with(&mut self, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 {591        if let Some(to) = self.tables[from as usize].add_edges[id as usize] {592            return to;593        }594        let to = self.table_for(self.tables[from as usize].signature | bit(id));595        self.tables[from as usize].add_edges[id as usize] = Some(to);596        self.tables[to as usize].remove_edges[id as usize] = Some(from);597        to598    }599 600    // The same for losing component `id`.601    fn table_without(&mut self, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 {602        if let Some(to) = self.tables[from as usize].remove_edges[id as usize] {603            return to;604        }605        let to = self.table_for(self.tables[from as usize].signature & !bit(id));606        self.tables[from as usize].remove_edges[id as usize] = Some(to);607        self.tables[to as usize].add_edges[id as usize] = Some(from);608        to609    }610 611    // Move a live entity to table `to`. The buffer is taken out of the world while it is applied, so676    // applying it can change the world freely, and put back after, emptied but677    // with its capacity.678    fn flush(&mut self) {679        let mut cmds = std::mem::take(&mut self.commands);680        for i in 0..cmds.list.len() {681            let result = match cmds.list[i] {682                Command::Spawn { signature, .. } => {683                    let e = self.spawn(signature);684                    cmds.list[i] = Command::Spawn { signature, entity: Some(e) };685                    Ok(())686                }687                Command::Despawn(e) => self.despawn(e),688                Command::Add { target, id, start, len } => {689                    let e = cmds.resolve(target);690                    self.add_id(e, id, &cmds.bytes[start..start + len])691                }692                Command::Remove { entity, id } => self.remove_id(entity, id),693            };694            match result {695                Ok(()) => self.applied += 1,696                Err(_) => self.skipped += 1,697            }698            if self.trace {699                self.print_command(&cmds, i, result);700            }701        }702        cmds.list.clear();703        cmds.bytes.clear();704        self.commands = cmds;705    }706 707    // One applied command. The components given to a new entity are part of708    // its spawn line, so they are not printed on their own.709    fn print_command(&self, cmds: &Commands, i: usize, result: Result<(), Error>) {710 row belongs to a live entity whose726    // slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add727    // up to the live count.728    fn verify(&self) -> usize {729        let mut problems = 0;730        let mut rows = 0;731        for (ti, t) in self.tables.iter().enumerate() {732            for (row, &e) in t.entities.iter().enumerate() {733                if !self.alive(e) }789}790 791// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------792// The inspector: reflect records, no component types793// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------794 795// One value of a builtin type, read from its bytes by its type's name.796// from_ne_bytes turns bytes into a number, so this needs no unsafe.797fn print_builtin(ty: &str, at: &[u8]) {798    match ty {799        "f32" => print!("{:.2}", f32::from_ne_bytes(at.try_into().expect("4 bytes"))),800        "u32" => 806// Every field of a struct whose bytes are `base`, nested structs indented807// under their field. A field's bytes are cut from `base` by its offset and808// size, both from the reflect record.809fn print_fields(info: &Info, base: &[u8], depth: usize) {810    for f in info.fields.iter().filter(|f| !f.hidden) {811        let at = &base[f.offset..f.offset + f.size];812        print!("{:indent$}{}:", "", f.name, indent = depth * 4);813        match f.info {814            Some(inner) => {815                println!();816                print_fields(inner, at, depth + 1);817            }818            None => {819                print!(" ");820                print_builtin(f.ty, at);821                println!();822            }823        }824    }825}826 827// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------828// Queries829// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------830 831// The tables a system runs over: every table whose signature has all of `all`832// and none of `none`, kept by index. Tables are only ever added, at the end of833// the world's `tables`, so the query remembers how many it has checked and,834// brought up to date, looks at the new ones only.835struct Query {836    all: u64,837    none: u64,838    tables: Vec<u32>,839    checked: usize,840}841 842fn matches(signature: u64, all: u64, none: u64) -> bool {843    (signature & all) == all && (signature & none) == 0844}845 846impl Query {847    fn new(all: u64, none: u64) -> Query {848        Query { all, none, tables: Vec::new(), checked: 0 }849    }850 851    // Check the tables made since the query last looked. With none new, this852    // is one comparison, so call it before every walk.853    fn update(&mut self, tables: &[Table]) {854        for (ti, t) in tables.iter().enumerate().skip(self.checked) {855            if matches(t.signature, self.all, self.none) {856                self.tables.push(ti as u32);857            }858        }859        self.checked = tables.len();860    }861 862    // How many entities the query matches: the rows of its tables.863    fn count(&mut self, tables: &[Table]) -> usize {864        self.update(tables);865        self.tables.iter().map(|&ti| tables[ti as usize].count()).sum()866    }867}868 869// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------870// Commands871// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------872 873// A spawn that has been recorded and not applied. There is no entity yet, so874// it is named by its place in the command list; give it components with875// `commands.add(pending, value)`.876#[derive(Clone, Copy)]877struct Pending(usize);878 879// Who an add is for: a live entity, or one spawned earlier in the same frame.880// Both convert into a Target, so `add` takes either.881#[derive(Clone, Copy)]882enum Target {883    Entity(Entity),884    Pending(usize),885}886 887impl From<Entity> for Target {888    fn from(e: Entity) -> Target {889        Target::Entity(e)890    }891}892 893impl From<Pending> for Target {894    fn from(p: Pending) -> Target {895        Target::Pending(p.0)896    }897}898 899// A structural change recorded during a frame and applied after it. An add's900// value is `len` bytes at `start` in the buffer's byte store. A spawn's entity901// is filled in when it is applied, which is how a pending add finds it.902#[derive(Clone, Copy)]903enum Command {904    Spawn { signature: u64, entity: Option<Entity> },905    Despawn(Entity),906    Add { target: Target, id: u32, start: usize, len: usize },907    Remove { entity: Entity, id: u32 },908}909 910// The frame's commands, and the bytes of their values. Both Vecs are cleared911// after every flush and keep their capacity, so once a game has run a few912// frames, recording a command allocates nothing: a frame arena, made of Vecs.913#[derive(Default)]914struct Commands {915    list: Vec<Command>,916    bytes: Vec<u8>,917}918 919impl Commands {920    fn spawn(&mut self, signature: u64) -> Pending {921        self.list.push(Command::Spawn { signature, entity: None });922        Pending(self.list.len() - 1)923    }924 925    fn despawn(&mut self, e: Entity) {926        self.list.push(Command::Despawn(e));927    }928 929    fn add<T: Component>(&mut self, target: impl Into<Target>, value: T) {930        let start = self.bytes.len();931        self.bytes.extend_from_slice(bytes_of(&value));932        self.list.push(Command::Add { target: target.into(), id: T::ID, start, len: size_of::<T>() });933    }934 935    fn remove<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity) {936        self.list.push(Command::Remove { entity: e, id: T::ID });937    }938 939    // The entity a command is for: the one it names, or the one its spawn made.940    fn resolve(&self, target: Target) -> Entity {941        match target {942            Target::Entity(e) => e,943            Target::Pending(i) => match self.list[i] {944                Command::Spawn { entity: Some(e), .. } => e,945                _ => unreachable!("a spawn is applied before the commands that name it"),946            },947        }948    }949}950 951// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------952// Systems953// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------954 955// What a system gets for each table it runs on: every table, which one to956// work on, the frame's command buffer, and its time step. Its fields are957// separate borrows, so a system can take `&mut it.tables[it.table]` and record958// into `it.commands` at the same time. There is no world here, so a system has959// no way to change structure except through a command.960struct Iter<'a> {961    tables: &'a mut [Table],962    table: usize,963    commands: &'a mut Commands,964    dt: f32,965}966 967// A system's function gets the Iter, and the context the game passes to968// progress: whatever its systems share, such as another query or a score.969type SystemFn<C> = fn(&mut Iter<'_>, &mut C);970 971// A system: a name, the query that finds its tables, and the function run on972// each of those tables that has rows. `calls` and `rows` count what it has run973// over.974struct System<C> {975    name: &'static str,976    query: Query,977    run: SystemFn<C>,978    calls: usize,979    rows: usize,980}981 982impl<C> System<C> {983    fn new(name: &'static str, all: u64, none: u64, run: SystemFn<C>) -> System<C> {984        System { name, query: Query::new(all, none), run, calls: 0, rows: 0 }985    }986}987 988// One frame: every system in order, each over every table it matches that has989// rows, then the commands they recorded. A system sees every value the systems990// before it wrote this frame, and no structural change until the next.991fn progress<C>(w: &mut World, systems: &mut [System<C>], ctx: &mut C, dt: f32) {992    for s in systems.iter_mut() {993        s.query.update(&w.tables);994        for &ti in &s.query.tables {995            let rows = w.tables[ti as usize].count();996            if rows > 0 {997                s.calls += 1;998                s.rows += rows;999                let mut it = Iter { tables: &mut w.tables, table: ti as usize, commands: &mut w.commands, dt };1000                (s.run)(&mut it, ctx);1001            }1002        }1003    }1004    w.flush();1005}1006 1007fn print_schedule<C>(w: &World, systems: &mut [System<C>]) {1008    for s in systems.iter_mut() {1009        w.print_query(s.name, &mut s.query);1010    }1011}1012 1013// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------1014// The program1015// The dojo · five building blocks

The dojo

dojo/README.md

An ECS is mostly a few small building blocks put together. None of them is specific to an ECS: a renderer's texture handles are a slot map, a particle system is swap-remove over packed arrays, undo and network replication are command buffers. The course meets each block for the first time in the middle of building something bigger, which is why its chapters can feel dense. The dojo takes the blocks out and gives each one two halves:

  • a playground, to understand it: a small program that runs the block step by step and draws its insides, with one switch at the top that breaks it the way it most often breaks. Step through it in a debugger, flip the switch, watch what goes wrong.
  • a kata, to own it: you write the block yourself, and a harness checks it. Reading and stepping through code feels like learning, but writing it from a blank page, getting it wrong, and doing it again a few days later is what makes it yours.
blockwhat it isin the course
1free list and generationshandles that are safe to keep after what they name is gone1.2, 1.3
2swap-remove and the back-referencevalues packed with no holes, found by id: a sparse set1.4, 2.3, 2.6
3the slot map1 and 2 together: handles into packed values1.4, 2.4
4a type-erased columnan array of any type as bytes, viewed as a typed slice2.2, 2.3, 2.5
5a command bufferstructural changes recorded now and applied later3.3, 3.4

Do them in order the first time: 3 is 1 and 2 put together, and 5 applies its commands to something like 3. They can come before the course, alongside it, or after it.

Each block

dojo/3.slot_map/
  README.md              the block, its invariant, the levels, the variations
  play_slot_map.rs       the playground
  harness.rs             fixed: a scenario, then a fuzz run against a model
  levels/1.rs ... 3.rs   where a kata starts
  solution/kata.rs       the reference, out of the way
  kata.rs                yours: made by `start`, ignored by git

The harness doesn't know how your kata works, only what it must do. First it runs a short scenario, the playground's steps, and prints each as it passes. Then it runs 20,000 random operations from a seed against a simple model of the right answers, and checks after each one. A failure says which operation, which seed, and how to stop just before it in a debugger.

Levels, so the reps get harder:

  1. One function in an otherwise finished file: the one with the idea in it, usually the one people forget.
  2. Every function body, with the fields and signatures given.
  3. A blank page, with only a list of what the harness calls.
  4. Variations: the same harness, different insides, listed in each block's README.

Each README gives a target time for levels 1 to 3.

Doing reps

python tools/dojo.py                      the blocks, your reps, and what is due
python tools/dojo.py play slot_map        the playground
python tools/dojo.py start slot_map 2     a fresh kata.rs from level 2; the clock starts
python tools/dojo.py slot_map             build the harness with your kata.rs and run it

A block can be named by its number, its name or the start of its name: 3, slot_map and slot are the same. While the kata fails, fix it and run it again. When it passes, the time since start goes into dojo/log.md, and the block is due again 1, 3, 7, 14 and then 30 days after each pass. python tools/dojo.py with no arguments says what is due. Spacing reps out is what makes them stick, much more than doing many in one day.

start won't overwrite a kata.rs you've changed unless you add --force. Your log is a plain markdown table; commit it or don't.

When a kata fails, the harness says where:

FAIL at operation 64 (seed 1): row 4 holds 43's value 37043, but get(43) gives 43020
    debug it: build/dojo/swap_remove/harness --seed 1 --stop 64
    with a breakpoint on stop_here, which runs just before that operation

Run that binary under a debugger with a breakpoint on stop_here. It stops just before the failing operation, with your structure in the state that leads to the failure. A panic in your kata reports the operation it happened in the same way. --seed N reruns a different fuzz run, and --release builds it optimised, for big --ops. Block 4's kata needs unsafe, and python tools/dojo.py column --miri runs it under Miri.

How it's built

A harness is an ordinary program, and your kata is one of its modules:

#[path = "../dojo.rs"]
mod dojo;
mod kata;

mod kata; is kata.rs beside the harness, so the kata uses what the harness provides as crate::Handle, crate::Dead or crate::Pod. dojo/dojo.rs holds what every harness shares: those types, the run's settings, the random number generator, and the reporting. The runner builds with rustc directly, with the warnings for unused code off, since a kata in progress is full of it.

python tools/check.py dojo keeps the dojo honest: every reference solution must pass its harness and print its harness.expected, level 1 must fail (its gap must be a gap), level 2 must compile, and the playgrounds must print their .expected. The harnesses were also checked against broken solutions, the mistakes each block is about, and catch each one.

The same dojo exists in rin, in rin-dod. The random number generator is the same, so a seed is the same run in both, and the playgrounds print the same thing.

The dojo · block 1

Free list and generations

dojo/1.free_list/play_free_list.rs

Handles name things that come and go: entities, textures, sounds, network connections. A handle is two numbers, index:generation, and two small ideas make it safe to keep:

  • A free list. A freed index is reused before a new one is made, so the arrays an index points into stay as long as the most things ever alive at once, not the most things ever made.
  • A generation per index. Freeing bumps the index's generation, so every handle made for the old life stops matching. A reused index can't be mistaken for whatever had it before.

The invariant: a handle is alive exactly when its generation is the one its index holds now. A free index already holds its next generation, which no handle has yet, so "free" needs no flag of its own. Every index is either alive or on the free list, once.

In the course: 1.2 builds the free list and meets its bug, 1.3 adds generations, and every later chapter keeps both.

Watch it: the playground

cargo run --bin play_free_list
python tools/dojo.py play free_list

It allocates four handles, frees two, reuses one, and draws both arrays after each step:

free b, then d: their generations go up now, before anyone reuses them
    generations  0:1  1:2  2:1  3:2
    free list    [1 3]
alloc e: alloc takes from the end of the free list, so index 3, in its next life
    e 3:2

Step through it: break on alloc and free, and watch generations and free change. Then flip the switch at the top, BUMP_ON_FREE, to false and run it again. The freed b is still alive, the reused index comes back with the old generation so d and e are the same handle, and freeing d again frees e and puts index 3 on the free list twice. That's the bug from 1.2, in four lines of output.

Do reps: the kata

You write Handles, an allocator of handles:

    pub fn alloc(&mut self) -> Handle {
    pub fn free(&mut self, h: Handle) -> Result<(), Dead> {
    pub fn alive(&self, h: Handle) -> bool {

plus new(), live() (how many are alive) and slots() (how many indices have been handed out). Handle and Dead are given, in dojo/dojo.rs: Handle { index: u32, generation: NonZeroU32 }, shown as index:generation.

The harness first runs a short scenario, the playground's steps, and prints each as it passes. Then it runs 20,000 random allocs and frees from a seed, against a model that keeps every handle ever handed out. It checks what your allocator does, not how: a handle is never handed out twice, a freed index is reused before a new one is made, alive agrees with the model for every handle, live and dead.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Keep the free list inside the dead slots: no free Vec, but a slot that is either Alive { generation } or Free { generation, next }, and a first_free: Option<u32>. Rust enums are made for this.
  • 16-bit generations in the slots, stored as u16, that wrap from 65535 back to 1, never 0. What does wrapping give up?
  • Reuse in first-in, first-out order (VecDeque), so an index rests as long as possible before it comes back. Why might a game want that?

The dojo · block 2

Swap-remove and the back-reference

dojo/2.swap_remove/play_swap_remove.rs

Systems loop over values, so values are kept packed: one after another, no holes, nothing to skip. Removing one from the middle would leave a hole, so the last value moves into it instead. That's swap-remove: one copy, however many values there are, at the price of order.

Values move, so an id can't be the position of its value. Two arrays keep track:

  • sparse, by id: rows[id] is the row id's value is in now;
  • packed, by row: ids[row] is the id that owns the row. This is the back-reference: when the last row moves into a hole, it says whose entry in rows to fix.

The whole structure is what EnTT calls a sparse set.

The invariant: the rows are packed, and the two arrays point at each other: for every row, rows[ids[row]] == row, and an id with no value has no row.

In the course: 1.4 packs entities into rows this way, 2.3 does it for every column of a table, and 2.6 does it when an entity moves between tables.

Watch it: the playground

cargo run --bin play_swap_remove
python tools/dojo.py play swap_remove

It inserts four values, removes one from the middle, and draws both sides after each step:

remove 7, in row 1: the last row, 5's, moves into the hole
    row         0    1    2
    ids         3    5    1
    values     30   50   10
    rows    1->2  3->0  5->1  (id -> row)

Step through it: break on remove, and watch ids and rows as the last row moves. Then flip the switch at the top, FIX_BACK_REFERENCE, to false and run it again. Id 5's row still says 3, past the end, so get 5 finds nothing. Then insert 9 puts 9's value in row 3, and get 5 returns 90, another id's value, with nothing to say it's wrong. That's the bug every packed array invites, and the reason the back-reference exists.

Do reps: the kata

You write SparseSet<T>. The heart of it is remove:

    pub fn remove(&mut self, id: u32) -> Option<T> {
        let row = self.rows.get_mut(id as usize)?.take()? as usize;
        let value = self.values.swap_remove(row);
        self.ids.swap_remove(row);
        if let Some(&moved) = self.ids.get(row) {
            self.rows[moved as usize] = Some(row as u32);
        }
        Some(value)
    }

That's the reference, so don't read it before level 1 if you'd rather not know. The full API:

    pub fn insert(&mut self, id: u32, value: T) -> Option<T> {
    pub fn get(&self, id: u32) -> Option<&T> {

plus new(), get_mut, len(), values() (the packed values, in row order) and ids() (ids()[row] owns values()[row]).

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random inserts and removes over a small range of ids, so the same ids come and go many times, against a plain map from id to value. Every 64 operations it checks the packed rows themselves: as many as the map has, and each row's owner holding exactly that row's value.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Pages: rows as Vec<Option<Box<[u32; 64]>>>, 64 ids a page, a page made only when an id in it gets a value. A big id no longer means a big rows. This is what EnTT does.
  • **No Option:** rows: Vec<u32> with u32::MAX for "no row". Compare size_of::<Option<u32>>() with size_of::<u32>(). Then try Option<NonZeroU32> holding row + 1: same size as u32, and still an Option.
  • By hand: swap-remove without Vec::swap_remove: copy the last row over the hole, then pop. Where does the "removing the last row" case go?

And one that fails on purpose: a remove that keeps order, shifting every later row down and fixing each one's back-reference. The scenario stops it at the first ids line. Why does the harness insist on swap-remove's order, and what does keeping order cost?

When it fails

A forgotten back-reference often shows up as a panic in a get that is right, not in the remove that is wrong:

FAIL in the scenario: it panicked after "values" passed
    panicked at dojo/2.swap_remove/kata.rs:46:26:
index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 3

The line says where the panic happened, and the first line says which step was last to pass, so the bug is in what ran between them. In the fuzz run, a failure gives the operation and the seed:

FAIL at operation 64 (seed 1): row 4 holds 43's value 37043, but get(43) gives 43020
    debug it: build/dojo/swap_remove/harness --seed 1 --stop 64

Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on stop_here, which runs just before that operation.

The dojo · block 3

The slot map

dojo/3.slot_map/play_slot_map.rs

Dojos 1 and 2, put together. Values live packed in rows, so a loop over them has no holes (dojo 2). The rest of the program keeps handles, which survive rows moving and say when their value is gone (dojo 1). In between is a slot per index:

handle 1:2  ->  slots[1] { generation 2, row 0 }  ->  values[0]

A lookup is two steps: the handle's generation must be the slot's, and the slot says the row. A remove is both dojos' work: bump the generation and free the index, then swap-remove the row and fix the slot of whoever moved. Game engines keep textures, meshes and sounds this way, and it is the ECS's entity index.

The invariant: dojo 1's and dojo 2's together. A handle is alive exactly when its generation is its slot's; the rows are packed; and for every row, the slot of the row's handle points back at that row.

In the course: 1.4 is a slot map with an entity's components as its value, and every chapter after keeps it, with a table number added to the slot in 2.4.

Watch it: the playground

cargo run --bin play_slot_map
python tools/dojo.py play slot_map

It keeps three textures, removes one, reuses its index, and draws the slots and the rows after each step:

remove stone: free index 1 in its next life, and water moves into row 1
    slots    0: generation 1, row 0 | 1: generation 2, free | 2: generation 1, row 1
    rows     0:1 grass | 2:1 water

Step through it: break on remove, and watch the slot, the free list and the rows change in that order. Then flip the switch at the top, CHECK_GENERATION, to false and run it again. The removed stone still finds slot 1, and reads whatever is in slot 1's row now: water, then lava. In a game, that's a sound that plays the wrong sample, or a mesh drawn with another mesh's texture.

Do reps: the kata

You write SlotMap<T>. Its two-step lookup:

    pub fn get(&self, h: Handle) -> Option<&T> {
        self.contains(h).then(|| &self.values[self.slots[h.index as usize].row as usize])
    }

and the API around it:

    pub fn insert(&mut self, value: T) -> Handle {
    pub fn remove(&mut self, h: Handle) -> Option<T> {

plus new(), contains, get_mut, len(), values() (the packed values, in row order) and handles() (handles()[row] owns values()[row]). Handle comes from dojo/dojo.rs, as in dojo 1.

Level 3 is the one to come back to. Once you can write a slot map from a blank page in fifteen minutes, dojos 1 and 2 are in your hands too.

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random inserts, removes, reads and writes against a model that maps every live handle to its value and keeps every dead one. It checks dojo 1's rules for the handles (never handed out twice, a freed index reused before a new one is made, a removed handle never alive again) and dojo 2's for the rows (packed, each row's handle holding that row's value).

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Free list inside the slots: a slot is Alive { generation, row } or Free { generation, next: Option<u32> }, and the map keeps first_free: Option<u32>. No free Vec, and a slot can't be alive and free at once.
  • **remove without contains**: look the slot up once, with get_mut, and bail out with ? and a generation check. How many times does the reference look at the slot?
  • **retain(|h, v| keep)**: remove every value the closure rejects, in one pass, keeping the rows packed. Which way should the loop walk? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL at operation 233 (seed 1): remove(33:1) returned 214, the model says 210
    debug it: build/dojo/slot_map/harness --seed 1 --stop 233

The wrong value usually means a slot pointing at the wrong row: an earlier remove moved a row and didn't fix its slot. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on stop_here, which runs just before that operation, then look at the slot of the handle being removed.

The dojo · block 4

A type-erased column

dojo/4.column/play_column.rs

A column is one component's rows, kept as bytes. It doesn't know the type it holds, only how many bytes make a row and how they must be aligned. That is enough to grow, to zero a new row, and to move the last row into a hole, which is everything a table does to its columns. The type comes back only at the edge: a typed view turns the bytes into a &[T], for a T of the column's size and alignment.

Two things make it work:

  • Aligned storage. The bytes start on a 16-byte boundary, so every row of any type aligned to 16 or less lands where that type may live.
  • Growing by a factor. A full column doubles, so the copies that growing costs add up to about one per push, however many rows there are.

The invariant: the column holds len rows of size bytes each, packed from the start of a 16-byte-aligned allocation with room for capacity rows. A typed view is only handed out for a T that is plain data, of exactly size bytes, aligned to exactly align.

In the course: 2.2 builds the column, 2.3 puts columns in a table, and 2.5 is about what happens to a reference into a column that grows.

Watch it: the playground

cargo run --bin play_column
python tools/dojo.py play column

It fills a column of Vec2s and draws each row's bytes next to the value they are:

push 3 zeroed rows, and write each through the typed view
    capacity 4, 3 rows in use, 2 blocks of storage
    row 0  00 00 80 3f 00 00 00 40   as a Vec2 (1, 2)
    row 1  00 00 40 40 00 00 80 40   as a Vec2 (3, 4)

Then it grows the column, swap-removes from it, and asks for the rows as two wrong types. Step through it: break on grow and watch the rows move to the new allocation.

The switch at the top, DOUBLE, picks how a full column grows. Set it to false, so the column grows by one row, and run it again. The last line is the point: the same 1000 pushes copy 1,020 rows when the column doubles, and 499,494 when it grows by one.

1000 pushes into a u32 column, growing by doubling
    9 grows, 1020 rows copied to make room

Do reps: the kata

You write Column. Its bytes come from a Vec of 16-byte blocks:

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Default)]
#[repr(C, align(16))]
struct Block([u8; 16]);

and the typed views are the only place the column needs unsafe:

    pub fn slice<T: Pod>(&self) -> &[T] {
    pub fn slice_mut<T: Pod>(&mut self) -> &mut [T] {

plus new(size, align), len(), capacity(), push_zeroed() (a zeroed row at the end, and its row number), swap_remove(row), and row(row) and row_mut(row), a row's bytes. Pod is given, in the harness: an unsafe trait for plain data, which slice needs before it may turn bytes into a T. The harness denies unsafe code except in functions marked #[allow(unsafe_code)], as the course does.

The harness first runs a short scenario: three Vec3s written through slice_mut and read back as bytes, a swap-remove, a row past the end, two types the column must refuse, a column aligned to 16, and a column of tags, zero-byte rows. Then it runs 20,000 random pushes, writes and swap-removes, shared between four row types: 3 bytes aligned to 1, a u32, a 12-byte Vec3, and a 16-byte Vec4 aligned to 16. Each is checked against a Vec of that type, through slice and through row, along with the alignment of every view, and that a full column grows by at least half.

Miri is worth the wait here. A typed view over storage that isn't aligned often works on your machine, because the allocator happened to return an aligned address. Miri doesn't let it happen by luck.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Grow by 1.5 instead of 2. Count the grows and the rows copied for 1000 pushes. Why do some allocators prefer it?
  • Allocate with **std::alloc** and the exact Layout (size * capacity, aligned to align) instead of a Vec of blocks: alloc_zeroed, realloc, and dealloc in a Drop. More unsafe, so run it with --miri. The tag column in the scenario will find the catch: a zero-size allocation is undefined behaviour.
  • Shrink: when a swap-remove leaves the column less than a quarter full, halve its capacity. Why a quarter and not a half? (Push and remove one row, over and over, at the boundary.)

The dojo · block 5

A command buffer

dojo/5.commands/play_commands.rs

Systems walk tables, and while they walk, they decide to change which things exist: a bullet's time is up, a turret fires, a drone catches fire. Doing it on the spot breaks the walk. A despawn swap-removes, so the last row moves into the hole, behind the loop, and is never looked at. So a system records the change instead, as a command, and the frame applies every command, in order, once nothing is walking anything.

Three details make it work:

  • Pending spawns. A spawn has no handle until it is applied, so recording one hands back a pending number, and later commands in the same buffer can name the spawn by it.
  • Skipping the dead. Two systems may both despawn the same thing, or set a value on something an earlier command removed. Applied in order, the second finds a dead handle and is skipped. Generations make that one comparison.
  • A frame arena. After the buffer is applied it is cleared, and keeps its memory, so once a game has run a few frames, recording a command allocates nothing.

The invariant: recording changes nothing but the buffer. Applying it has exactly the effect of running every command straight away, in the order it was recorded, with each pending number meaning the handle its spawn made.

In the course: 3.3 builds the buffer and shows the bug it fixes, and 3.4's game runs on it. The Advanced lesson 6 has one too.

Watch it: the playground

cargo run --bin play_commands
python tools/dojo.py play commands

A packed world of five things, and one frame of three systems. The expire system records a despawn for each thing whose life is up, the spawner records a replacement and sets its life through its pending number, and a second system despawns something the first already did. Then the buffer is applied:

apply the buffer, in the order it was recorded
    despawn 0:1: ok, 4:1 moves into 0:1's row
    despawn 2:1: ok, 3:1 moves into 2:1's row
    despawn 3:1: ok, it was the last row
    spawn with life 1: pending 0 is 3:2
    set pending 0 life 5: ok, 3:2 has life 5
    despawn 2:1: skipped, 2:1 is dead

Step through it: break on apply and walk the list. Then flip the switch at the top, DEFER, to false, so every system changes the world on the spot, and run it again. The expire system despawns 0:1, 4:1 moves into its row behind the loop, and when the loop ends, 3:1 is still there with no life:

things left with no life: none

becomes things left with no life: 3:1, moved behind the loop and never looked at. That's 3.3's bug.

Do reps: the kata

You write Commands. A command names its target either way:

pub enum Target {
    Entity(Handle),
    Pending(Pending),
}

and From conversions let set and despawn take a Handle or a Pending alike:

    pub fn set(&mut self, target: impl Into<Target>, value: u32) {
    pub fn apply(&mut self, w: &mut World) -> Applied {

plus new(), spawn(value), which returns a Pending, despawn(target), and len(), the commands waiting. The world is given, in the harness: a generational store of numbers with spawn, despawn, set and get, where despawn and set return Err(Dead) for a dead handle. apply returns Applied { applied, skipped }.

The harness first runs a short scenario: a set, a despawn, a spawn that reuses the despawned index, a set through the spawn's pending number, and two commands that find their target dead. Then a fuzz run, frame after frame: random commands recorded against live handles, dead handles and the frame's own pending spawns, then applied. A model runs the same commands straight away on a copy of the world from before the frame, and the harness checks the two worlds match, the applied and skipped counts match, and the buffer is empty afterwards.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Keep the spawned handles in the command list itself, as 3.3 does: a spawn command holds an Option<Handle> that apply fills in, and a pending number finds its spawn through it.
  • Record the whole buffer as **one Vec<u8>**: a tag byte, then the command's fields as bytes. One allocation for any mix of commands, read back in order.
  • Let the values be any plain-data type, not just u32: store each value's bytes in a byte store, as the course's bytes_of does, and keep the harness's u32 as one case of it.

Advanced · seven lessons

Layout and SIMD

docs/README.md

Seven lessons for after Build an ECS. The course builds the ECS. These go underneath it, to the memory and the machine code:

  • Lesson 1, aos vs soa. The same particles in three layouts: what a loop fetches per cache line, what a &mut slice promises the compiler, which loops it vectorizes, and how to check that in the assembly.
  • Lessons 2 to 6 build an archetype ECS again, compressed into five steps, and end with a small game. They came first and move fast. After the course, read them as a recap, or as a second take on the same design. Lesson 4 builds the world in includes/kayan.rs, and lessons 5 and 6 bring it in unchanged with #[path].
  • Lesson 7, layout follows access. Four layouts under streams and under random lookups, timed, and how an ECS decides where each component lives.
  • Lesson 0, from kayan, reviews the original C kayan: what these lessons kept from it, what they changed, and why.
lessonabout
0from kayanwhat was kept from the C kayan, what changed, and why
1aos vs soathe same particles in three layouts, what a loop fetches, and what SIMD needs
2archetype tableone table: columns, rows, spawn, swap-remove, systems over slices
3many archetypesone table type for every archetype: ids, signatures, queries
4entity handlesgenerational handles, slots, moving between archetypes
5inspectorprinting and editing any entity from reflect records
6kayana small game, and deferring structural changes to a command buffer
7access patternsfour layouts under streams and lookups, and how an ECS decides

How to read them

Read each lesson's .rs file from the top. It opens with the problem it solves, and the code follows in the order it runs. Then run it and read the output against the code: every lesson prints what it does, step by step. The guides here give the background that doesn't fit in a file header, and end with exercises.

Timings only mean something in a Release build:

python tools/check.py --release aos_vs_soa
build/check/release/aos_vs_soa --time

or cargo run --release --bin aos_vs_soa -- --time.

Debug builds check every slice index and every integer for overflow, and don't vectorize. Lesson 1's guide shows how to read the assembly, and what to look for in it.

Advanced · lesson 0 · review

From kayan

docs/0_from_kayan.md

kayan is a sketch of an archetype entity component system in C, about 200 lines in src/kayan.h, with haikal generating its containers. These lessons start from its idea and rebuild the rest, first in rin (rin-dod) and here in Rust. This page says what was kept, what was changed, and why, so the lessons can be read as a review of it as much as a rewrite.

What kayan does

Components are bits in an enum, positions = 1 << 0, velocities = 1 << 1 and so on. Each archetype is a C struct written by hand (A, B, C, D) that starts with an ArchetypeHeader and then holds one haikal Array_T per component. The header has a u64 signature and a Map_u64 from column name to the column's byte offset in the struct.

A query walks an array of void * pointing at the archetypes, reads each header, and tests (signature & want) == want. For a match it looks up "positions" and "velocities" in the offset map, adds the offsets to the struct's address, and runs the loop over the two columns.

Kept

  • An archetype is a struct of arrays. Each component is a contiguous column and every entity in the table has every column. That is the whole point, and kayan had it right from the start.
  • A signature is a u64 of component bits, and a query is the test (signature & all) == all. Lesson 3 adds a none mask beside it.
  • Arena-style memory. kayan and rin-dod allocate from arenas and never free one thing at a time. Here the world's data lives in Vecs that only grow while the game runs (tables are never removed), and the frame's commands live in Vecs that are cleared after every frame and keep their memory. That is an arena's allocation pattern, with the Vec doing the bookkeeping and freeing everything when the world is dropped.

Changed

  • One table type for every archetype (lesson 3). kayan needs a new C struct, a new signature line and new offset-map lines for every archetype. Here an archetype is data: a signature, and the world makes its table the first time something needs it (lesson 4).
  • Columns by component id, not by name (lesson 3). kayan hashes the strings "positions" and "velocities" on every query. Here a table's columns are an array indexed by component id, so finding one is an index. Names are kept for tools, through reflect records (lesson 5).
  • The signature comes from the columns (lesson 3). In kayan they are written separately and can disagree. In D they do: it has positions and velocities columns, but its signature is health | damage | alive, so the movement query never visits it.
  • A row is added and removed in one place (lesson 2). kayan appends to each column at the call site, and keeps entity_count apart from the columns. For B and D it increments a's count instead of their own (kayan.h lines 142, 145, 168, 174), so A reports seven entities and the others report none. Nothing breaks only because the query loop happens to use the column's own length. In Rust the row count is a length, of the table's entities Vec, so there is no second count to get wrong.
  • Entities have handles (lesson 4). kayan's entity id is the value of an archetype's entity_count before it is bumped: meant per table, in practice A's, as above. Nothing records where an entity lives, so there is no way to refer to one entity from elsewhere, to remove it, or to move it to another archetype. The lessons use an {index, generation} handle and a slot list that tracks each entity's table and row.
  • Entities move between archetypes (lesson 4). Adding or removing a component moves the entity to the matching table, copying the components both tables share.
  • Structural changes wait for the end of the frame (lesson 6), through a command buffer. kayan never changes structure while a query runs, but only because it never changes structure at all.
  • Reflect records replace hand-written tables (lessons 3 to 5). A component's size, alignment, field names and offsets are written down by the macro that declares it, from what the compiler knows. The offset map goes away entirely.

What Rust adds

  • Components are checked to be plain data. Columns hold bytes, and turning bytes back into a component is only sound if any bytes are a valid value. pod! checks at compile time that every field is plain data and the struct has no padding. kayan, like C, trusts you.
  • **unsafe is fenced in.** Every program starts with #![deny(unsafe_code)]. Lessons 1, 2 and 7 have no unsafe at all. Lessons 3 to 6 have the byte views of a column, four one-line blocks, and lessons 4 to 6 add one more, bytes_of, all with a // SAFETY: reason, and they run clean under Miri (python tools/check.py --miri).
  • Some of kayan's quiet bugs don't compile. A pointer to a table kept across the creation of another, a slice kept across a spawn, two &mut to one column: each is a borrow-checker error in these lessons, where in C or rin the write would just go somewhere stale. What the borrow checker can't see is a stale number, a row or an entity index, and handles and the command buffer are still how those are handled.

Not carried over

  • **vec4s for positions.** kayan pads 3D vectors to 16 bytes, which suits SIMD loads. The lessons use Vec2 and Vec3 and plain loops, and leave vectorizing to the compiler. Every &mut slice in Rust promises that nothing else reaches its memory, which is what rin's noalias and C's restrict say, so kernels that take slices vectorize without run-time overlap checks. Lesson 1 adds a third layout, one f32 array per coordinate, which is the one SIMD runs cleanly over. Lesson 7 weighs that layout against lookups, which it is bad at.
  • cglm and the haikal containers. Rust's standard library (Vec, HashMap, slices) covers what they did, and the lessons have no dependencies at all.

Small things in kayan.h

  • The query's inner loop declares i32 i, shadowing the outer i (line 201). The Rust lessons mostly avoid the question: a loop over an iterator, or two zipped together, has no index to shadow.
  • Each lookup on lines 199 and 200 hashes and compares a string, once per column per archetype per query. That is cheap next to a large loop, but it is work that an array index does for nothing.

Advanced · lesson 1

AoS vs SoA

src/1.aos_vs_soa/aos_vs_soa.rs

src/1.aos_vs_soa/aos_vs_soa.rs

The same 262,144 particles, stored three times: as a Vec of 68-byte Particle structs (AoS), as seven Vecs, one per field (SoA), and with position and velocity split one step further into six Vec<f32>, one per coordinate (split). Sixty steps of movement run over each, and the program checks that all three end with the same positions.

What the loop fetches

Memory reaches the CPU in 64-byte cache lines. A loop that reads 24 bytes of each 68-byte particle still pulls every byte of every line those particles sit in, so about two thirds of what movement fetches in the AoS loop is tint, age, lifetime, size and name. In the SoA loop the two arrays it reads are the only thing it fetches, and the hardware prefetcher sees two simple streams. The split loop fetches the same 24 bytes per particle as SoA, as six streams.

The program prints that arithmetic:

bytes fetched per step: 17825792     (AoS: 68 bytes x 262144)
bytes fetched per step: 6291456      (SoA: 24 bytes x 262144)
bytes fetched per step: 6291456      (split: 6 x 4 bytes x 262144)

Particle is #[repr(C)], so its fields sit in the order they're written. Without it Rust may reorder a struct's fields to save padding. Here there's none to save, so the size would be 68 either way.

What the CPU does with each layout

SSE registers hold four floats, AVX registers eight. One instruction adds four (or eight) pairs of floats at once, but only if they arrive side by side. Here is what rustc 1.97 at -C opt-level=3 (Release) makes of each loop on x86-64 Linux, read from the assembly:

loopparticles per passinstructions per passper particleshuffles
move_aos229about 152
move_soa477about 1930
move_split42050
move_split, -C target-cpu=native814under 20
  • AoS goes one particle at a time. LLVM unrolls the loop twice and does each particle's x and y as a pair, but the next particle's fields are 68 bytes away, so there is nothing to load four of. At opt-level=2 it's plainly scalar, 17 instructions a particle.
  • SoA is vectorized, four particles per pass, but each Vec3 keeps x, y and z side by side. To get four x's into one register the compiler loads them one float at a time and stitches them together, then takes them apart again to store. About a tenth of the loop is arithmetic, and per particle it costs about what AoS does.

  • Split is what SIMD wants. Each line of move_split becomes one load of four consecutive floats, one multiply, one add, one store:

    movups (%rcx,%rbx), %xmm3 four vx mulps %xmm1, %xmm3 vx * dt movups (%rdi,%rbx), %xmm4 four px addps %xmm3, %xmm4 px + vx * dt movups %xmm4, (%rdi,%rbx) four px back

The SoA and split loops are the ones clang made of rin-dod's C, instruction for instruction: rustc and clang share LLVM, and the layout decides the code, not the language.

A layout is right for SIMD when its vector loop is mostly full-width loads, math and stores. When it is mostly movss, unpcklps and shufps, the data is fighting the registers.

Split is right for this loop, which runs over every particle in order. It is wrong for a loop that reaches particles by index, where x, y and z in three arrays are three trips to memory instead of one. Lesson 7 measures both kinds of loop over four layouts.

Reading the assembly

Ask rustc for it:

rustc --edition 2024 -C opt-level=3 -C debug-assertions=off --emit asm -o aos_vs_soa.s src/1.aos_vs_soa/aos_vs_soa.rs

and search the .s file for move_split:. Rust mangles names, so the label is _RNv...10move_split:, but the plain name is in it. Each kernel is marked #[inline(never)] so it stays a function you can find; inlined into main, the three would blend into one block of code.

objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn on a Release binary works too. The third-party cargo-show-asm (cargo asm --bin aos_vs_soa move_split) prints one function at a time; it's a convenience, and nothing in the course needs it.

Timings

--time prints how long each layout took. Release builds, best of seven runs, on the 2.8 GHz Xeon these lessons were checked on, ms:

buildAoSSoAsplit
-C opt-level=371.037.418.8
-C opt-level=292.137.718.6
-C opt-level=3 -C target-cpu=native160.721.018.2

The same loops with 8,192 particles, so everything stays in L2, and 1,920 steps so the work is the same:

buildAoSSoAsplit
-C opt-level=324.236.69.0
-C opt-level=232.836.79.1
-C opt-level=3 -C target-cpu=native123.916.48.6
  • Split is the fastest everywhere, by two to four times.
  • In cache, SoA is slower than AoS. Its 30 shuffles cost more than AoS's wasted bytes, once the bytes come from L2 instead of memory. The SoA loop is vectorized, and that's not the same as fast.
  • From the 6 MB case, SoA's smaller footprint shows. That machine has 33 MB of L3, so the data stays in cache between steps, but SoA and split still move a third of the bytes AoS does.
  • **target-cpu=native made AoS two to five times slower.** This Xeon has AVX-512, and with it LLVM "vectorizes" move_aos eight particles at a time with vgatherdps and vscatterdps: instructions that load and store eight floats from eight different addresses. They work one lane at a time inside the CPU, and the loop is slower than doing it by hand. SoA gained, because wider shuffles cost less. Split barely moved: it was already waiting on memory, not on arithmetic.

target-cpu=native builds for the CPU you're on, so a binary built that way may not run on another machine, and what it does to these loops depends on which CPU that is. The course's builds use the default target, which every x86-64 CPU runs.

The machine is shared; expect about 20 percent noise between runs, and more for AoS, which went anywhere from 70 to 125 ms. rin-dod's C, built with clang -O2 and run turn about with the Rust build on the same day, came out the same within that noise: they are the same loops. Both were slower that day than rin-dod's own tables, which is the machine, not the language.

Debug numbers are not worth comparing: Debug checks every index and every add for overflow, and vectorizes nothing.

For a Release build, python tools/check.py --release aos_vs_soa leaves one in build/check/release/aos_vs_soa; run it with --time. Or cargo run --release --bin aos_vs_soa -- --time.

The parameter list is the data

move_aos(ps: &mut [Particle], ...) says it needs particles. move_soa(positions: &mut [Vec3], velocities: &mut [Vec3], ...) and move_split(px, py, pz, vx, vy, vz, ...) say exactly which data they read and write, and with &mut or &, which of the two. In lessons 2 and 3 every system is written that way. In lesson 6 each system runs its own query, then works only on the columns it named.

Naming the columns is what lets a scheduler see that two systems touch different data, and it is what makes a system easy to test: hand it two small arrays.

Every &mut is noalias

As far as a C compiler can tell, two float * arrays could overlap. So before it works on several particles at once, it checks at run time that the two are apart, and keeps a one-at-a-time copy of the loop for when they are not. rin's noalias on a parameter promises that nothing else reaches the memory behind it, and the check goes away.

In Rust, every &mut makes that promise, and the borrow checker is what keeps it true. rustc passes it on to LLVM as noalias on every &mut parameter, so the check is never there. move_soa starts with two instructions that take the shorter of the two lengths, for zip, and goes straight to the vector loop:

cmpq   %rsi, %rcx
cmovbq %rcx, %rsi

rin checked the promise in Debug, and a Release build ran on with wrong results. Rust checks it when the program is built. Pass soa.positions as both arguments and it doesn't compile:

error[E0499]: cannot borrow `soa.positions` as mutable more than once at a time
    |
218 |         move_soa(&mut soa.positions, &mut soa.positions, DT);
    |         -------- ------------------  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ second mutable borrow occurs here
    |         |        |
    |         |        first mutable borrow occurs here
    |         first borrow later used by call

rin-dod's lesson also needed noalias on move_aos's one slice, because on Windows a slice was passed by reference, and a float written through it might have been the slice's own length. Rust passes a slice as two values, its pointer and its length, in registers, so there's nothing in memory for a write to change.

**And GRAVITY is a const.** rin-dod made gravity static, so that gcc would know no write through a slice could change it. A Rust const is a value, not a place in memory: it's written into the code where it's used, and there's nothing to change.

Bounds checks

What Rust adds is a bounds check on every index, Release included. A check that might fail inside a loop is a problem for SIMD: the loop must stop at exactly the right particle, so it can't do four at once past a check it hasn't made. move_soa has no index at all, because zip walks both slices and stops at the shorter. move_split indexes six slices, so it cuts them to one length first:

    let n = px.len();
    let (py, pz, vx, vy, vz) = (&mut py[..n], &mut pz[..n], &vx[..n], &mut vy[..n], &vz[..n]);
    for i in 0..n {

Now every slice is exactly n long, i < n is in bounds for all six, and the checks are five compares at the top of the function, none in the loop. If a slice is too short, the program stops before anything is written.

Without the cut, LLVM still vectorized this loop on this machine: it worked out the shortest of the six lengths, ran the vector loop up to there, and kept a checked one-at-a-time loop for the rest. The cut makes that certain rather than lucky.

Fused multiply-add

A fused multiply-add computes p + v * dt in one instruction that rounds once instead of twice. C compilers fuse on their own when allowed to (rin-dod's checksums moved with -mfma). Rust never fuses on its own. With -C target-cpu=native on this AVX-512 machine, move_split is eight floats a pass with separate vmulps and vaddps, and the output is byte for byte the same as the default build's.

To get the fused instruction you ask for it, v.x.mul_add(dt, p.x), and then the checksum's last digits move. Without FMA in the target, mul_add calls a much slower software routine to round once anyway.

When AoS is right

When the code that touches a record touches most of its fields, AoS fetches nothing wasted, and keeping a record together is simpler. Data-oriented design does not mean SoA everywhere. It means choosing the layout from the loops that run over it. An entity component system is the case where many small loops each touch a few fields.

Try

  1. Run with --time in Release. Then remove tint, age, lifetime and name from Particle and run again. The AoS loop should close most of the gap, because the struct shrinks toward what the loop reads.
  2. Build with -C target-cpu=native and compare --time. Then find move_aos in the assembly and count the vgatherdps. On a CPU without AVX-512 you'll see something else; what?
  3. kayan stored positions as 16-byte vec4s. Give Vec3 a fourth float and see what it does to the bytes-per-step line, to move_soa's assembly and to the timing.
  4. Store the split columns in blocks of eight, struct Block { x: [f32; 8], y: [f32; 8], ... }, and write the loop over blocks. Each block is a whole AVX register per coordinate, and a particle's coordinates stay near each other. (Lesson 7 does this, and finds a surprise with target-cpu=native.)
  5. Pass &mut soa.positions as both arguments to move_soa, and read the error.
  6. Delete the line that cuts the slices in move_split and compare its assembly. Then index vx[i + 1] instead of vx[i] (and stop one early). Does the loop still vectorize?
  7. Write p.x = v.x.mul_add(dt, p.x) in move_soa, build with -C target-cpu=native, and watch the checksums.

Advanced · lesson 2

One archetype table

src/2.archetype_table/archetype_table.rs

src/2.archetype_table/archetype_table.rs

Eight sparks in one table with three component columns, positions, velocities and lives, plus a numbers column that exists only so the output can say which spark is which. Each frame they move, they age, and the ones that ran out are removed.

Two rules

Columns never disagree. spawn and despawn are the only places rows come and go, and each touches every column. A new component means a new column, one line in each of those two methods, and one more argument to spawn. A call site cannot add a row to some columns and forget the others.

        self.numbers.push(number);
        self.positions.push(position);
        self.velocities.push(velocity);
        self.lives.push(life);

Each column is a Vec, and its length is the number of rows in use. There's no separate count to keep in step: count() is numbers.len(), and the two rules keep every other column the same length.

Rows are packed. Systems loop over every row and never test whether a row is alive. Removing a row moves the last row into the hole, which Vec does with swap_remove:

    spark 0 in row 0 expired; spark 7 moved from row 7 into it

That one move per column is the whole cost of a despawn, whatever the table's size. The price is that a row number is not a name for a spark. After that line, "row 0" means spark 7. Lesson 4 adds names that don't move.

Removing while iterating

expire_system walks the rows backwards. When it removes row i, the row that moves in comes from the end, and the end has already been tested:

    for i in (0..t.count()).rev() {

(0..t.count()) is computed once, before the loop starts, and .rev() hands out its numbers from the top. A forward loop would have to stay on i after a removal, and it's easy to get wrong. Lesson 6 removes the question entirely by not removing anything during a loop.

Why numbers, and not an iterator over lives? Because an iterator borrows the column for as long as it runs, and despawn needs the whole table:

    for (i, life) in t.lives.iter().enumerate().rev() {
        if *life <= 0.0 {
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `*t` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
    |
111 |     for (i, life) in t.lives.iter().enumerate().rev() {
    |                      --------------------------------
    |                      |
    |                      immutable borrow occurs here
    |                      immutable borrow later used here
...
114 |             let moved = t.despawn(i);
    |                         ^^^^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here

The compiler doesn't know that walking backwards makes the despawn harmless. It only knows the column could change under the iterator, and refuses. A loop over row numbers borrows nothing between iterations, so it compiles, and getting its order right is up to you. The ECS course meets the same choice in 3.3.

Systems take slices

fn move_system(positions: &mut [Vec2], velocities: &[Vec2], dt: f32) {
    for (p, v) in positions.iter_mut().zip(velocities) {
        p.x += v.x * dt;
        p.y += v.y * dt;
    }
}

move_system gets the rows in use and knows nothing about tables. &[Vec2] says it only reads velocities. The call hands it two fields of the table at once, one mutably and one shared, which the compiler allows because they're different fields:

        move_system(&mut sparks.positions, &sparks.velocities, dt);

zip walks the two slices together and stops at the shorter one, so the loop has no index and nothing to bounds-check. Indexing positions[i] would be checked in every build, Release included, against the slice's length, which is the row count. There's no way to reach the spare capacity behind it.

&mut [Vec2] also makes a promise to the compiler: while the call runs, nothing else reaches the memory positions covers. rin writes that promise as noalias, and has to remember to. In Rust every &mut makes it, and the borrow checker is what keeps it true. So the compiler vectorizes the loop with no run-time check that the columns are apart.

rin needed noalias even on age_system's one slice, because on Windows a slice arrives by reference, and without the promise clang-cl assumed a float written through it might be the slice's own pointer or length. Rust passes a slice as a pointer and a length in two registers, on every platform, and a &mut is the only way to its memory in any case, so there's nothing to add. The loop is eight floats per pass:

movups (%r9,%rdi,4), %xmm0       four lives
movups 16(%r9,%rdi,4), %xmm1     four more
addps  %xmm2, %xmm0              plus -dt
addps  %xmm2, %xmm1
movups %xmm0, (%r9,%rdi,4)
movups %xmm1, 16(%r9,%rdi,4)

The systems were inlined into main and dt folded into a constant, so the subtraction became an add of -0.5. To look yourself: rustc --edition 2024 -C opt-level=3 --emit asm src/2.archetype_table/archetype_table.rs, then search the .s file for addps.

positions and velocities are Vec2, x and y side by side. Lesson 1 measures what that costs when x and y are treated differently. Here they aren't: both get += v * dt, so the compiler treats each column as one run of floats, and move_system is also a plain mulps and addps loop, four sparks per pass, with no shuffling.

Status codes

spawn returns Result<usize, Full>: the new row, or why there wasn't one. A Result is must-use, so calling spawn and ignoring it is a warning, and this course builds with warnings as errors. rin's spawn_status was an enum[must_use] with the row through an out-parameter; Rust puts both in the return value. The ninth spark shows the Full case:

        if let Err(Full) = sparks.spawn(i, Vec2 { x: f, y: 0.0 }, Vec2 { x: 1.0, y: f }, life) {
            println!("spark {i} did not fit: the table is full");
        }

Try

  1. Rewrite expire_system to walk forwards with for i in 0..t.count(). Run it: it panics in frame 1. Why? (The range was computed before the loop despawned anything.) Now write it as a while i < t.count() loop that rereads the count, like rin's forward loop. It runs, and the output doesn't change, because no frame here expires a spark together with the one in the last row. Change two lives so that one does, and find the spark that outlives its life by a frame. Then fix the loop.
  2. Delete the line in despawn that swap-removes lives. What does the output show, and how long did it take to notice?
  3. Call sparks.spawn(...) as a statement, ignoring its result, and build. Read the error. Then discard it on purpose with let _ = sparks.spawn(...).
  4. Make the table grow instead of returning Full. With Vecs, that's deleting two lines. What did the fixed capacity give you that growing doesn't? (Hint: what happens to a reference into a column when it grows? Lesson 4.)

It is lesson 1's struct of arrays with two rules added.6//7// Every column has the same length, always. Spawn pushes to every column in8// one place and despawn removes from every column in one place. kayan appended9// to each column at the call site, and three appends that must happen together10// are three chances to forget one.11//12// Rows are packed. Despawn moves the last row into the hole it leaves (a13// swap-remove), so a system loops over every row with no gaps and no "alive"14// flag to test. The price is that a row is not a stable name for an entity: the15// last entity changes rows every time something before it dies. Lesson 4 deals16// with that.17//18// The sparks here have a position, a velocity and a life in seconds. Each frame19// they move, they age, and the ones whose life ran out are removed. Removal20// walks the rows backwards, so the row swapped into a hole has already been21// looked at this frame.22 23// `unsafe` is an error, except where an item allows it by name. Nothing here24// needs it: every column is a Vec of its own type.25#![deny(unsafe_code)]26 27#[derive(Clone, Copy, Default)]28struct Vec2 {29    x: f32,30    y: f32,31}32 33// The table for the archetype {position, velocity, life}. Each column is a Vec,34// and its length is the number of rows in use, the same for every column.35// `numbers` is not a component: it only lets the output say which spark sits in36// which row.37struct SparkTable {38    capacity: usize,39    numbers: Vec<u32>,40    positions: Vec<Vec2>,41    velocities: Vec<Vec2>,42    lives: Vec<f32>,43}44 45// Why a spawn did not happen.46#[derive(Debug)]47struct Full;48 49impl SparkTable {50    // Every column gets room for `capacity` rows once, up front.51    fn new(capacity: usize) -> SparkTable {52        SparkTable {53            capacity,54            numbers: Vec::with_capacity(capacity),55            positions: Vec::with_capacity(capacity),56            velocities: Vec::with_capacity(capacity),57            lives: Vec::with_capacity(capacity),58        }59    }60 61    fn count(&self) -> usize {62        self.numbers.len()63    }64 65    // The only place a row is added: every column gets its value here. Returns66    // the new row, or Full when there is no room.67    fn spawn(&mut self, number: u32, position: Vec2, velocity: Vec2, life: f32) -> Result<usize, Full> {68        if self.count() == self.capacity {69            return Err(Full);70        }71        self.numbers.push(number);72        self.positions.push(position);73        self.velocities.push(velocity);74        self.lives.push(life);75        Ok(self.count() - 1)76    }77 78    // The only place a row is removed. Returns the row that moved, which is80    // `row` itself when the removed row was the last one.81    fn despawn(&mut self, row: usize) -> usize {82        let last = self.count() - 1;83        self.numbers.swap_remove(row);84        self.positions.swap_remove(row);85        self.velocities.swap_remove(row);86        self.lives.swap_remove(row);87        last88    }89}90 91// Systems. Each takes the columns it reads and writes, as slices, and knows92// nothing about tables. A `&mut` slice is the only way to reach its memory93// while the call runs, so the loop can be vectorized without checking whether94// the columns overlap.95fn move_system(positions: &mut [Vec2], velocities: &[Vec2], dt: f32) {96    for (p, v) in positions.iter_mut().zip(velocities) {97        p.x += v.x * dt;98        p.y += v.y * dt;99    }100}101 102fn age_system(lives: &mut [f32], dt: f32) {103    for life in lives {104        *life -= dt;105    }106}107 108// Structural change: rows leave the table. Backwards, so the row a swap-remove109// pulls in has already been tested.110fn expire_system(t: &mut SparkTable) {111    for i in (0..t.count()).rev() {112        if t.lives[i] <= 0.0 {113            let number = t.numbers[i];114            let moved = t.despawn(i);115            if moved != i {116                println!("    spark {number} in row {i} expired; spark {} moved from row {moved} into it", t.numbers[i]);117            } else {118                println!("    spark {number} in row {i} expired; it was the last row");119            }120        }121    }122}123 124fn print_table(t: &SparkTable) {125    for (row, ((n, p), life)) in t.numbers.iter().zip(&t.positions).zip(&t.lives).enumerate() {126        println!("    row {row}  spark {n}  position ({:6.2}, {:6.2})  life {life:.2}", p.x, p.y);127    }128}129 130fn main() {131    let mut sparks = SparkTable::new(8);132    println!("a table with room for {} sparks, {} bytes of components a row",133        sparks.capacity, size_of::<Vec2>() * 2 + size_of::<f32>());134 135    // Eight sparks with lives of 0.5s to 4s, plus one more than fits.136    for i in 0..9 {137        let f = i as f32;138        let life = 0.5 + ((i * 5) % 8) as f32 * 0.5;139        if let Err(Full) = sparks.spawn(i, Vec2 { x: f, y: 0.0 }, Vec2 { x: 1.0, y: f }, life) {140            println!("spark {i} did not fit: the table is full");141        }142    }143    print_table(&sparks);144 145    let dt = 0.5;146    for frame in 1..=4 {147        println!("frame {frame}");148        move_system(&mut sparks.positions, &sparks.velocities, dt);149        age_system(&mut sparks.lives, dt);150        expire_system(&mut sparks);151        print_table(&sparks);152    }153    println!("{} sparks left", sparks.count());154}
