Advanced · lesson 3

Many archetypes

src/3.many_archetypes/many_archetypes.rs

src/3.many_archetypes/many_archetypes.rs

Four archetypes (rock, ship, bullet, turret) and four components (Position, Velocity, Health, Damage). One Table type holds all four archetypes, and two queries decide which tables each system visits.

A table without a type

Lesson 2's table had one typed field per column. That can't work for every archetype at once, so the columns become bytes:

struct Table {
    name: &'static str,
    signature: u64,
    count: usize,
    capacity: usize,
    columns: [Option<Column>; 64],
}

columns[id] is None when the table has no such component. A column is a run of 16-byte blocks and the component's reflect record:

struct Column {
    blocks: Vec<Block>,
    info: &'static Info,
}

The record says how many bytes make a row, info.layout.size(). add_row, and lesson 4's moves, work only from sizes, so they never need to know a component's type:

    fn zero_row(&mut self, row: usize) {
        let size = self.info.layout.size();
        self.bytes_mut()[row * size..(row + 1) * size].fill(0);
    }

Types come back at the edges. column::<T>() finds T's column by T's id and returns it as a &[T] of the rows in use. Systems take &mut [Position], &[Velocity] and so on, exactly as in lesson 2.

    fn column<T: Component>(&self) -> &[T] {
        self.columns[T::INFO.id as usize]
            .as_ref()
            .unwrap_or_else(|| panic!("table {} has no {} column", self.name, T::INFO.name))
            .slice::<T>(self.count)
    }

Turning bytes back into Ts is the one thing the compiler can't check, so it is unsafe: four one-line views in Column, each with a // SAFETY: comment, resting on the Pod promise that pod! checks at compile time. The ECS course's 2.2 builds the same column step by step, and explains why the blocks are 16 bytes. The program runs clean under Miri.

One list, and nothing to check

rin keeps three things in step by hand: the component enum, the component_info array of records, and a component_of<T> specialisation per type. It sizes the arrays by the enum's reflected member count, and a components_check at startup stops the program if the enum and the records were written in different orders.

Rust has no reflection to count an enum's members or read their names. It doesn't need them here. The component! macro writes each component's record as a constant of its type, with the id taken from the enum member that has the struct's own name:

        impl Component for $name {
            const INFO: &'static Info = &Info {
                id: ComponentId::$name as u32,
                name: stringify!($name),
                layout: Layout::new::<$name>(),
            };
        }

So the record can't belong to the wrong type, and nothing is looked up by position. A table is made from records, not ids:

        Table::new("ship", &[Position::INFO, Velocity::INFO, Health::INFO], 16),

The enum is the only list left, and a component that isn't in it doesn't compile:

error[E0599]: no variant, associated function, or constant named `Armor` found for enum `ComponentId` in the current scope
...
111 | component!(Armor { points: f32 });
    |            ^^^^^ variant, associated function, or constant not found in `ComponentId`

There's no count either. columns has 64 slots, one per bit a signature can hold, and the unused ones are None. A slot is 32 bytes, a Vec and a reference, so that's 2 KB a table, and nothing next to its columns.

Two columns of one table

move_system writes positions and reads velocities, two columns of the same table. rin takes the velocities first and then the positions. The same in Rust doesn't compile:

                let velocities = t.column::<Velocity>();
                move_system(t.column_mut::<Position>(), velocities, dt);
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `*t` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
    |
352 |                 let velocities = t.column::<Velocity>();
    |                                  - immutable borrow occurs here
353 |                 move_system(t.column_mut::<Position>(), velocities, dt);
    |                             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^  ---------- immutable borrow later used here
    |                             |
    |                             mutable borrow occurs here

This isn't a bug in rin. The two columns really are separate memory. But column borrows the whole table, and the compiler can't see which column inside it a call reaches. So the table hands out both at once, through get_disjoint_mut, which lends two slots of the columns array after checking they're different:

    fn pair_mut<A: Component, B: Component>(&mut self) -> (&mut [A], &mut [B]) {
        const { assert!(A::INFO.id != B::INFO.id, "pair_mut needs two different components") };
        let count = self.count;
        let [a, b] = self.columns.get_disjoint_mut([A::INFO.id as usize, B::INFO.id as usize])
            .expect("two different columns");

The ids are constants, so pair_mut::<Position, Position>() is stopped by the const assert when the program builds. The query loop then reads like rin's:

                let (positions, velocities) = t.pair_mut::<Position, Velocity>();
                move_system(positions, velocities, dt);

Different types, the same loop

rin's guide found that clang vectorized this lesson's move_system without a run-time overlap check, and lesson 2's only with one, before either had noalias. Here the columns are different struct types, and clang reads C's type rules as saying those can't share memory. In lesson 2 both were vec2.

Rust has no rules about types sharing memory. It has &mut: the positions slice is the only way to its memory, whatever the types. So the two lessons compile to the same loop, four rows a pass, with no overlap check. The only extra work is pair_mut's, once per table before the loop: the two column ids and the two slice lengths.

Queries

    let moving = Query { all: mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>(), none: 0 };
    // Turrets have health too, but they repair by other means: no regen for
    // anything that deals damage.
    let healing = Query { all: mask_of::<Health>(), none: mask_of::<Damage>() };

A table matches when it has every bit in all and none in none. moving visits ships and bullets. healing visits ships but not turrets, which have health but also deal damage. The output prints each visit:

frame 1
    move visits ship
    regen visits ship
    move visits bullet

The signature cannot lie

Table::new builds the signature from the same list it makes columns from:

        for &info in components {
            t.signature |= bit(info.id);
            t.columns[info.id as usize] = Some(Column::new(info, capacity));
        }

kayan wrote them separately, and archetype D's signature left out two of its columns (see 0_from_kayan.md).

Four tables at once

Setting up the world needs a &mut to each of the four tables. rin takes tables[0]&, tables[1]& and so on. Rust takes the array apart with a pattern:

    let [rocks, ships, bullets, turrets] = &mut tables;

Four names, four &mut Tables, and the compiler knows they're four different elements, because the pattern says so. Indexing &mut tables[1] twice would be two borrows of the array, and only one may be held at a time.

Rust notes

rinRust
columns: [component<>.count]^u8, null if absentcolumns: [Option<Column>; 64], None if absent
component_info[id]*.sizeinfo.layout.size(), from Layout::new::<T>() in the macro
component_of: proc<position>() -> component per typeT::INFO.id, a constant of the type
components_check() at startupnothing to check: the id comes from the enum member with the type's name
cast(t*.columns[c], ^T); raw[0..count]slice::<T>(count), one unsafe line with its reason
column<velocity>(t) in a local, then column<position>(t)t.pair_mut::<Position, Velocity>()
tables[0]&, tables[1]&, ...let [rocks, ships, bullets, turrets] = &mut tables;
printfmt(...); exit(1);assert! and panic!, with the same messages

Try

  1. Add an Armor component, give it to turrets, and make a query that visits only tables with both Health and Armor. What did you have to touch?
  2. Ask the rock table for column::<Velocity>(). Read the message, then find where it comes from.
  3. Change columns to [Option<Column>; 4], then add a fifth component. Where does it fail, and when: building or running?
  4. Write remove_row with the swap-remove from lesson 2, working only from the columns' record sizes and copy_within on their bytes.

That is a promise the compiler cannot check by itself, so the41/// trait is unsafe; pod! makes the promise only after checking it at compile42/// time.43#[allow(unsafe_code)]44unsafe trait Pod: Copy + 'static {}45 46#[allow(unsafe_code)]47unsafe impl Pod for f32 {}48 49macro_rules! pod {50    ($name:ident { $($field:ident: $ty:ty),* $(,)? }) => {51        #[derive(Clone, Copy, Default, Debug)]52        #[repr(C)]53        struct $name {54            $($field: $ty),*55        }56 57        #[allow(unsafe_code)]58        unsafe impl Pod for $name {}59 60        const _: () = {61            const fn field_is_pod<T: Pod>() {}62            $(field_is_pod::<$ty>();)*63            assert!(size_of::<$name>() == 0 $(+ size_of::<$ty>())*, "a component has padding");64        };65    };66}67 68// A component's reflect record: its id, its name, and the size and alignment a69// column needs to store it as bytes.70struct Info {71    id: u32,72    name: &'static str,73    layout: Layout,74}75 76trait Component: Pod {77    const INFO: &'static Info;78}79 80// The components, one member each. A component's id is its member's position.81#[derive(Clone, Copy)]82enum ComponentId {83    Position,84    Velocity,85    Health,86    Damage,87}88 89// Declares a component and its record. The id is the enum member with the90// struct's own name, so a component missing from the enum does not compile,91// and a record cannot belong to the wrong type.92macro_rules! component {93    ($name:ident { $($field:ident: $ty:ty),* $(,)? }) => {94        pod!($name { $($field: $ty),* });95 96        impl Component for $name {97            const INFO: &'static Info = &Info {98                id: ComponentId::$name as u32,99                name: stringify!($name),100                layout: Layout::new::<$name>(),101            };102        }103    };104}105 106pod!(Vec2 { x: f32, y: f32 });107component!(Position { at: Vec2 });108component!(Velocity { per_second: Vec2 });109component!(Health { points: f32, max: f32 });110component!(Damage { per_hit: f32 });111 112fn bit(id: u32) -> u64 {113    1 << id114}115 116fn mask_of<T: Component>() -> u64 {117    bit(T::INFO.id)118}119 120// 16 bytes, aligned to 16: the unit a column's storage comes in, so the start121// of every column is aligned for any component.122#[derive(Clone, Copy, Default)]123#[repr(C, align(16))]124struct Block([u8; 16]);125 126// One component's rows, as bytes, with room for a fixed number of rows. The127// record says how many bytes make a row.128struct Column {129    blocks: Vec<Block>,130    info: &'static Info,131}132 133impl Column {134    fn new(info: &'static Info, capacity: usize) -> Column {135        assert!(info.layout.align() <= 16, "{} needs more alignment than a column has", info.name);136        Column { blocks: vec![Block::default(); (info.layout.size() * capacity).div_ceil(16)], info }137    }138 139    #[allow(unsafe_code)]140    fn bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {141        // SAFETY: a Block is 16 initialised bytes with no padding, so the Vec's142        // buffer is `len * 16` initialised bytes.143        unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(self.blocks.as_ptr().cast::<u8>(), self.blocks.len() * 16) }144    }145 146    #[allow(unsafe_code)]147    fn bytes_mut(&mut self) -> &mut [u8] {148        // SAFETY: as in bytes(); `&mut self` makes the view the only one.149        unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(self.blocks.as_mut_ptr().cast::<u8>(), self.blocks.len() * 16) }150    }151 152    fn zero_row(&mut self, row: usize) {153        let size = self.info.layout.size();154        self.bytes_mut()[row * size..(row + 1) * size].fill(0);155    }156 157    // The first `count` rows as T's. Advanced · lesson 4

Entity handles

src/4.entity_handles/entity_handles.rs

src/4.entity_handles/entity_handles.rs, includes/kayan.rs

The world: tables made on demand, entity handles that survive row moves, despawning with index reuse, and moving an entity between archetypes when a component is added or removed. The code is includes/kayan.rs. The lesson program calls each part and prints what happened.

One file, three programs

Lessons 4, 5 and 6 share the world. Each program brings it in as a module:

#[path = "../../includes/kayan.rs"]
mod kayan;

mod kayan; alone would look for kayan.rs next to the program. #[path] says where it is instead, so every program is still one rustc command, with no crate and no Cargo needed. The module starts with #![allow(dead_code)], because no single program calls everything in it.

A program declares its components with the module's macros, after an enum that gives each one its id:

enum ComponentId {
    Position,
    Velocity,
    Health,
}

pod!(Vec2 { x: f32, y: f32 });
component!(Position { at: Vec2 });
component!(Velocity { per_second: Vec2 });
component!(Health { points: f32 });

component! is the ECS course's macro (2.1, 2.2): a plain-data struct, checked at compile time, with its reflect record and the id of the ComponentId member with the same name. The macro is written in kayan.rs, but ComponentId is resolved where it's used, in the program, so the library never needs to know the program's components.

Handles, slots, rows

pub struct Entity {
    pub index: u32,
    pub generation: NonZeroU32,
}
pub struct Slot {
    pub generation: NonZeroU32,
    pub table: u32,
    pub row: u32,
}

A handle is what the rest of a program keeps. Its index picks a slot, and the slot says where the entity lives now. Rows move all the time: every despawn and every archetype change swap-removes. When one does, the table's entities column says which entity owned the moved row, and that entity's slot gets the new row number. Handles never change.

generation is what makes a handle safe to keep after its entity dies. Despawning bumps the slot's generation and frees the index, and the next spawn reuses the index with the new generation:

spawn d: it reuses a's index with the next generation
    d = 0:2 in table 0 row 2 {Position Velocity} at (4.0, 0.0)
    a = 0:1 is dead

alive is one comparison: the handle's generation against the slot's.

    pub fn alive(&self, e: Entity) -> bool {
        self.slots.get(e.index as usize).is_some_and(|s| s.generation == e.generation)
    }

A free slot already holds its next generation, which no handle carries yet, so no separate "alive" flag is needed. a can't reach d's data, get returns None for it, and despawning it again returns Err(Dead) and changes nothing.

Generations start at 1, and NonZeroU32 makes that a rule of the type. Rust uses the forbidden 0 to store None, so "no entity" is Option<Entity>, at no cost:

    no entity is None, and an Option<Entity> is 8 bytes, an Entity's size

rin-dod used a zeroed handle, 0:0, for "no entity". It works, and nothing stops you from using one as if it were real. None has to be checked before it can be used.

Results

despawn, add, remove and move_to return Result<(), Dead>: Ok(()), or Err(Dead) when the handle no longer names a live entity.

pub struct Dead;

That's the only way a change can fail here, so the error type is a single value with no fields. A Result is must-use: dropping one unread is a warning, and these programs build with warnings as errors. Where the lesson knows the handle is alive, it says so:

    w.add(b, Health { points: 75.0 }).expect("b is alive");

add itself shows ?, Rust's early return for errors. If the move fails, ? returns the Err(Dead) from add at once; if it works, add writes the value:

    pub fn add<T: Component>(&mut self, e: Entity, value: T) -> Result<(), Dead> {
        self.move_to(e, self.signature(e) | mask_of::<T>())?;
        *self.get_mut::<T>(e).expect("its table has a T now") = value;
        Ok(())
    }

Tables on demand

    pub fn table_for(&mut self, signature: u64) -> u32 {
        if let Some(&index) = self.by_signature.get(&signature) {
            return index;
        }
        let index = self.tables.len() as u32;
        self.tables.push(Table::new(&self.infos, signature));
        self.by_signature.insert(signature, index);
        index
    }

The signature is looked up in a HashMap<u64, u32>, and the table is made if it's new. Nobody declares archetypes; they appear when an entity first needs that combination. Tables live in a Vec<Table> and are referred to by index, because adding one can move the whole list.

Tables start with room for 16 rows and double when full. Growing a column resizes its Vec, which copies the rows to a bigger allocation and frees the old one. rin-dod's arena left the old columns in place, unused, until the whole arena went. The last part of the program spawns 40 entities so the first table grows twice, despawns every other one, and checks the result two ways.

Checking the world

Reading back each survivor's position is a weak check. Swap-remove copies rows, so a stale row often still holds the right numbers. verify checks the invariant instead: every row of every table belongs to a live entity whose slot points back at that table and row, and the rows add up to the live count. It prints each problem it finds and returns how many there were. The lesson prints verify: 0 problems and fails if that is not so:

    if right == 20 && problems == 0 { ExitCode::SUCCESS } else { ExitCode::FAILURE }

main returns an ExitCode, so tools/check.py sees the failure.

get reads the row through a slice cut to the rows in use, so a slot that points past the end of its table stops the program at the first lookup, in Release too: Rust checks every index.

Moving between archetypes

give b health: b moves to a new table and keeps its position

add::<Health> computes signature | bit(Health), finds or makes that table, appends a row, copies every component the two tables share, then swap-removes the old row. remove is the same move with the bit cleared.

        let to = self.table_for(signature);
        let [old, new] = self.tables.get_disjoint_mut([from as usize, to as usize]).expect("two different tables");

The move needs two tables of the Vec at once, one to read and one to write. Two &mut self.tables[i] would be two mutable borrows of one Vec, which the compiler refuses whatever the indices are. get_disjoint_mut checks at run time that the two are different, then lends out both. And the order matters: table_for can push a table and move the rest, so no table is borrowed until it returns. In rin that was a comment. Here, borrowing first doesn't compile.

A move costs two row copies, one into the new table and one to fill the hole in the old, so components that come and go every frame are better as a field than as a component. A burning rate in Health, say, instead of a Burning component.

Advanced · lesson 5

The inspector

src/5.inspector/inspector.rs

src/5.inspector/inspector.rs

A soldier and a crate, printed field by field by code that names no component type, then edited by component and field name, then a table layout report. Everything comes from the reflect records the world already holds for sizes.

Where the records come from

rin's compiler writes a reflect record for every struct, T<>. Rust has no reflection built in, so includes/kayan.rs writes them in the macro that declares each component. A record is a type's name, its layout, and what its bytes are:

pub struct Info {
    pub name: &'static str,
    pub layout: Layout,
    pub kind: Kind,
}

pub enum Kind {
    F32,
    U32,
    I32,
    // A [u8; N]: text, padded with zeros.
    Text,
    // An i32 that is one of these named values (pod_enum!).
    Enum(&'static [(&'static str, i32)]),
    // A struct, field by field (pod!).
    Struct(&'static [Field]),
}

A struct's record lists its fields, and each field links to the record of its own type:

pub struct Field {
    pub name: &'static str,
    pub offset: usize,
    pub info: &'static Info,
    pub hidden: bool,
}

pod! fills them in. For each field, the compiler supplies the name (stringify!), the byte offset (offset_of!), and the field type's record:

                    kind: Kind::Struct(&[$(Field {
                        name: stringify!($field),
                        offset: std::mem::offset_of!($name, $field),
                        info: <$ty as Reflect>::INFO,
                        hidden: $crate::kayan::is_hidden!($($attr)?),
                    }),*]),

Every type a component is made of implements Reflect, so the field types' records are there to link to. f32, u32 and i32 have records written by hand, a [u8; N] of any length has one through a generic impl, and every struct made with pod! has one. A record is a constant, built when the program is compiled, and it costs nothing until a tool reads it.

rin-dod's kind and type were strings like "f32", compared with strcmp. Here Kind is an enum, so a match on it has to handle every kind, and the compiler says so if one is missing.

Printing from records

print_fields takes the component's bytes, from get_bytes, and cuts each field's bytes out by offset and size:

fn print_fields(fields: &[Field], base: &[u8], depth: usize) {
    for f in fields.iter().filter(|f| !f.hidden) {
        let at = &base[f.offset..f.offset + f.info.layout.size()];
        print!("{:indent$}{}:", "", f.name, indent = depth * 4);
        print_value(f.info, at, depth);
    }
}

A record that disagreed with the data would stop the program at the slice, not print garbage. print_value is one match on the kind:

fn print_value(info: &Info, at: &[u8], depth: usize) {
    match info.kind {
        Kind::F32 => println!(" {:.2}", f32::from_ne_bytes(number(at))),
        Kind::U32 => println!(" {}", u32::from_ne_bytes(number(at))),
        Kind::I32 => println!(" {}", i32::from_ne_bytes(number(at))),
        Kind::Text => {
            let end = at.iter().position(|&b| b == 0).unwrap_or(at.len());
            println!(" \"{}\"", String::from_utf8_lossy(&at[..end]));
        }
        Kind::Enum(members) => {
            let value = i32::from_ne_bytes(number(at));
            let name = members.iter().find(|m| m.1 == value).map_or("(not a member)", |m| m.0);
            println!(" {name}");
        }
        Kind::Struct(fields) => {
            println!();
            print_fields(fields, at, depth + 1);
        }
    }
}

Numbers are read with from_ne_bytes, which turns an array of bytes into a number. rin-dod cast a pointer into the bytes instead. Rust can do that too, in an unsafe block, but there's no need: the inspector has no unsafe at all. Because components are structs, even a single float like Health.points has a name to print.

Enums in components

pod_enum!(Side { RED = 0, BLUE = 1 });
component!(Team { side: Side });

Why not a Rust enum Side { Red, Blue }? Because a column holds bytes, and a component has to be valid whatever its bytes are (2.2's Pod). A Rust enum isn't: its only valid values are its members, and a Side with the bytes of 7 would be undefined behaviour, not just a wrong answer. So pod_enum! declares what C would: an i32 with named values.

        struct $name(i32);

Side::BLUE is Side(1). The record keeps the names, and a value that isn't one prints as (not a member) instead of breaking anything.

Tags

component!(Health { points: f32, max: f32, #[hidden] regen_timer: f32 });

#[hidden] is only text the macro matches, recorded as the field's hidden flag. The inspector skips hidden fields. The component decides what a tool shows, and the tool doesn't need to know the component.

Names belong in tools

fn set_f32_by_name(w: &mut World, e: Entity, component: &str, field: &str, value: f32) -> Option<()> {
    let id = (0..w.component_count).find(|&id| w.info(id).name == component)?;
    let Kind::Struct(fields) = w.info(id).kind else {
        return None;
    };
    let f = fields.iter().find(|f| f.name == field && matches!(f.info.kind, Kind::F32))?;
    w.get_bytes_mut(e, id)?[f.offset..f.offset + 4].copy_from_slice(&value.to_ne_bytes());
    Some(())
}

It finds the component by name, the field by name, checks the field is an f32, and writes it. Each ? is a way to refuse: no such component, no such f32 field, or the entity doesn't have the component. It refuses Weapon.ammo, a u32, and the crate's Health, which it doesn't have:

the editor writes three fields by name
    soldier Health.points = 55: written
    soldier Weapon.ammo = 1: refused, ammo is a u32, not an f32
    crate Health.points = 1: refused, the crate has no health

That's the flexibility an editor or a console needs. It's also the string comparison kayan did in every query, once per archetype. Here it runs once per edit, and systems keep using ids.

Layout

print_layout lists each table's columns with size and alignment, and each column's bytes in use out of the bytes allocated for the table's capacity:

table 0 {Position Health Team Weapon Label}, rows in use: 1 of 16
    Position 12 bytes, align 4, column 12 of 192 bytes
    Health   12 bytes, align 4, column 12 of 192 bytes
    Team      4 bytes, align 4, column 4 of 64 bytes
    Weapon   12 bytes, align 4, column 12 of 192 bytes
    Label    16 bytes, align 1, column 16 of 256 bytes

It's the kind of report that shows when a component has grown padding (here it can't: pod! refuses padding), when a table has far more room than rows, or when a table carries a column most of its systems never read.

Try

  1. Add a u8-sized flag to Weapon and see pod! refuse it. Then add a u32 armed field instead, and give it its own Kind::Bool that prints yes or no. What has to change in kayan.rs, and what in the inspector?
  2. Give Position a #[readonly] tag and make set_f32_by_name refuse fields that carry it. (is_hidden! shows how a macro turns a word into a flag.)
  3. Write set_by_name for u32 and i32 as well, picking the write from the field's kind.
  4. Write the bytes of 7 into the soldier's Team with get_bytes_mut, and inspect it. Why is that safe here, and why would it not be with a Rust enum?
  5. Print a whole table as rows and columns: one line per entity, one column per field.

Advanced · lesson 6

kayan

src/6.kayan/kayan.rs

src/6.kayan/kayan.rs

A turret at the centre, five wings of three drones, 140 frames. Seven systems run each frame, and every structural change they want goes through a command buffer applied at the end of the frame.

The frame

spawner    wings of drones enter                    records spawns
turret     shoot at the nearest drone               records spawns
movement   position += velocity * dt                writes
lifetime   bullets expire                           writes, records despawns
collision  live bullets against drones              writes health, records despawn and add
burning    burning drones lose health               writes
outcome    destroy dead drones, catch leaks         records despawns
  blast    a destroyed drone hurts its neighbours   writes health, records adds
apply      every recorded change, in order

Writes to components happen in place, during queries. Changes to which table an entity is in are recorded, and applied once nothing is iterating.

    for frame in 1..=frames {
        g.log.frame = frame;
        spawner_system(&mut g);
        turret_system(&mut g, dt);
        movement_system(&mut g.world, dt);
        lifetime_system(&mut g, dt);
        collision_system(&mut g);
        burning_system(&mut g.world, dt);
        outcome_system(&mut g);
        skipped += g.commands.apply(&mut g.world).skipped;
    }

Lifetime runs before collision, and collision skips bullets whose lifetime is used up. Those bullets are only still in their table because nothing structural happens until the end of the frame. Without the skip, a bullet that hit on its last frame would be despawned twice and counted as both a hit and a miss.

The game's state, in four fields

struct Game {
    world: World,
    commands: Commands,
    stats: Stats,
    log: Log,
}

A system takes &mut Game and uses its fields directly: g.world.tables, g.commands, g.stats. The compiler treats different fields as different borrows, so a system can walk the world's tables and record a command in the same loop. If recording a command were a method on Game, it would borrow the whole game, tables included, and the loop couldn't call it. That's why the event log is a field of its own, with its own method:

    fn event(&mut self, what: fmt::Arguments) {
        if self.printed != self.frame {
            println!("frame {}", self.frame);
            self.printed = self.frame;
        }
        println!("    {what}");
    }

g.log.event(format_args!("drone {e} is destroyed")) borrows only the log. format_args! builds the text's pieces without making a String; println! puts them together.

Systems and kernels

movement_system and burning_system are each a query and a kernel:

fn integrate(ps: &mut [Position], vs: &[Velocity], dt: f32) {
    for (p, v) in ps.iter_mut().zip(vs) {
        p.at.x += v.per_second.x * dt;
        p.at.y += v.per_second.y * dt;
    }
}

fn movement_system(w: &mut World, dt: f32) {
    let movers = Query { all: mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>(), none: 0 };
    for t in w.tables.iter_mut().filter(|t| t.matches(movers)) {
        let (ps, vs) = t.pair_mut::<Position, Velocity>();
        integrate(ps, vs, dt);
    }
}

The system walks the tables and calls the kernel once for each table that matches. The kernel sees two slices, so the compiler sees a straight loop over two arrays. rin-dod split the kernels out because noalias is a parameter qualifier, and the loop needed a proc of its own to carry it. Rust needs no qualifier: a &mut slice is always the only way to its memory. The kernels stay split because it reads well, and because a kernel is what you time and read the assembly of.

pair_mut (from the ECS course, 3.1) lends out two columns of one table, the first to write and the second to read, after checking at compile time that they're two different components.

burn is the cleanest loop in the game. Health and Burning are each one f32, so their columns are plain runs of floats. integrate works on Vec2s and spends some of each pass separating x from y; lesson 1 shows what the fully split layout looks like.

integrate and burn are streams: every row of every matching table, in order. collision_system and blast_system are closer to lookups: for each bullet or each blast, they visit drones that could be anywhere. Lesson 7 measures what each layout costs for both kinds of loop, and why the components here stay small structs.

lifetime_system is two passes, where rin-dod's was one loop:

        age(t.column_mut::<Lifetime>(), dt);
        for (&e, l) in t.entities.iter().zip(t.column::<Lifetime>()) {
            if l.seconds <= 0.0 {
                g.commands.despawn(e);
                g.stats.misses += 1;
            }
        }

A column to write and the handles to read are two borrows of one table, and column_mut borrows all of it. So the kernel writes, then a second loop reads. The output is the same, and the kernel, which calls nothing, can be vectorized.

Row numbers, within a frame

Some systems hold no slices at all. They read one row at a time, by number:

        for i in 0..g.world.tables[ti].count() {
            let t = &g.world.tables[ti];
            let (e, at, points) = (t.entities[i], t.column::<Position>()[i].at, t.column::<Health>()[i].points);
            if points <= 0.0 {
                g.commands.despawn(e);
                g.stats.destroyed += 1;
                g.log.event(format_args!("drone {e} is destroyed"));
                blast_system(g, e, at);

outcome_system can't hold its table's columns while it calls blast_system, which writes the health of every drone near the blast, including drones in the very table outcome_system is walking. A slice held across that call would be a second way to the same memory, and the compiler refuses it. So it copies what it needs out of row i (the handle, the position, the health) and lets go before the blast. Each row is read afresh, so a drone that an earlier blast in this loop took below zero is destroyed in turn. That chain is the point of frame 113.

The ECS course spent several chapters on why a row number isn't safe to keep. Here it is, and the reason is the command buffer: until the buffer is applied, no row moves. turret_system does the same, reading a turret, searching every table for the nearest drone, then writing the turret back.

collision_system finds the hit with slices and acts on it with numbers. The search lends out each drone table's health and positions, and returns where it hit:

fn hit_first_drone(w: &mut World, at: Vec2, damage: f32) -> Option<(usize, usize, f32)> {
    let drones = Query { all: drone_mask(), none: 0 };
    for (ti, t) in w.tables.iter_mut().enumerate().filter(|(_, t)| t.matches(drones)) {
        let (hs, ps) = t.pair_mut::<Health, Position>();
        for (row, (h, p)) in hs.iter_mut().zip(ps).enumerate() {
            if distance(at, p.at) <= 1.0 && h.points > 0.0 {
                let before = h.points;
                h.points -= damage;
                return Some((ti, row, before));
            }
        }
    }
    None
}

Then the caller, with the slices gone, looks up the drone's handle in that table and row, and records the commands.

Why not change tables during a query

Each of these would be a real bug with the world from lesson 4:

  • Despawn. The swap-remove moves the last row into the hole, behind the loop, so that entity is not processed this frame.
  • Spawn. A table that is full grows, and its columns move to new memory. In rin, a system holding a slice from before the spawn kept writing to the old copy.
  • Add or remove. The entity moves to another table, which the same query may reach later. That entity is processed twice this frame.

In Rust, the second one can't happen: a system holding a slice can't call spawn, which needs the whole world (lesson 4's Try). The first and third can, in any system that walks rows by number, like outcome_system. The borrow checker sees references, and a row number is not one.

The buffer

enum Command {
    Spawn { signature: u64 },
    SetSpawned { pending: usize, id: u32, start: usize, len: usize },
    Add { entity: Entity, id: u32, start: usize, len: usize },
    Remove { entity: Entity, id: u32 },
    Despawn(Entity),
}

Each variant carries only what it needs. Spawned entities have no handle until the buffer runs, so spawn returns a pending number, how many spawns came before it, and set_spawned::<T> writes a component into "the entity that pending spawn will create". T has to be in the spawn's signature, and applying the buffer stops the program with a message if it is not.

Payloads are copies of the component value, as bytes, in the buffer's byte store:

    fn payload<T: Component>(&mut self, value: &T) -> (usize, usize) {
        let start = self.bytes.len();
        self.bytes.extend_from_slice(bytes_of(value));
        (start, size_of::<T>())
    }

bytes_of is in kayan.rs, the library's one unsafe line outside its columns: a Pod value seen as its bytes.

apply runs everything in order, then clears the Vecs:

        self.list.clear();
        self.bytes.clear();
        self.spawned.clear();
        self.spawns = 0;

rin-dod kept the buffer in a frame arena and freed it with one memops_arena_clear. A cleared Vec keeps its memory the same way, so after the first few frames the buffer allocates nothing: a frame arena made of Vecs.

Skipped commands

Frame 113 is the interesting one. A bullet destroys one drone, and its blast takes two burning neighbours below zero in the same loop. Each of them is destroyed in turn, and each blast reaches back to drones already recorded as destroyed:

frame 113
    bullet 8:9 hits drone 6:1, health -13.2
    drone 6:1 is destroyed
    drone 7:1 is caught in the blast, health -14.4
    drone 4:2 is caught in the blast, health -4.8
    drone 7:1 is destroyed
    drone 6:1 is caught in the blast, health -54.0
...

The blast can't know 6:1 is doomed: its despawn is only recorded, and it is still in its table. So it records an add of Burning against it. When the buffer is applied the despawn comes first, move_to returns Err(Dead) for the add, and the command is skipped. The summary counts three:

after 140 frames
    drones: 15 entered, 6 destroyed, 3 leaked
    bullets: 20 fired, 16 hit, 3 expired
    commands skipped because their entity was already gone: 3

Every line of the output is the same as rin-dod's: the same game, frame for frame.

Try

  1. Call g.world.despawn(e) directly in outcome_system instead of recording it. In rin-dod, frame 56 reported drone 3:1 destroyed while removing 1:1, and the game went on. Here it stops in frame 56: index out of bounds: the len is 1 but the index is 1. Explain both, from the swap-remove and the loop's range.
  2. Make blast_system skip neighbours whose health is already at or below zero. The skip count drops to zero. Is the buffer's check still needed?
  3. Give the turret a Health component and let leaking drones damage it. When it reaches zero, despawn it through the buffer and end the game.
  4. Print the buffer before applying it, as a log of every structural change the frame made.
  5. Write lifetime_system as one loop, the way rin-dod did, by adding a Table method that returns the handles and one column to write at once. Which two fields of the table does it borrow?

A spawned entity has no handle until the buffer is69// applied, so the commands for it name it by `pending`: how many spawns were70// recorded before it. A payload is `len` bytes at `start` in the byte store.71// The buffer is complete, though this game never removes a component.72#[allow(dead_code)]73#[derive(Clone, Copy)]74enum Command {75    Spawn { signature: u64 },76    SetSpawned { pending: usize, id: u32, start: usize, len: usize },77    Add { entity: Entity, id: u32, start: usize, len: usize },78    Remove { entity: Entity, id: u32 },79    Despawn(Entity),80}81 82// The frame's commands, the bytes of their payloads, and, while the buffer is83// applied, the handles its spawns made. All three are cleared after.84#[derive(Default)]85struct Commands {86    list: Vec<Command>,87    bytes: Vec<u8>,88    spawns: usize,89    spawned: Vec<Entity>,90}91 92#[derive(Default)]93struct Applied {94    applied: u32,95    skipped: u32,96}97 98impl Commands {99    // A copy of `value` in the byte store, kept until the buffer is applied,100    // as the bytes the component's column will receive.101    fn payload<T: Component>(&mut self, value: &T) -> (usize, usize) {102        let start = self.bytes.len();103        self.bytes.extend_from_slice(bytes_of(value));104        (start, size_of::<T>())105    }106 107    fn spawn(&mut self, signature: u64) -> usize {108        self.list.push(Command::Spawn { signature });109        self.spawns += 1;110        self.spawns - 1111    }112 113    // T must be in the pending spawn's signature: the spawn decides the table.114    fn set_spawned<T: Component>(&mut self, pending: usize, value: T) {115        let (start, len) = self.payload(&value);116        self.list.push(Command::SetSpawned { pending, id: T::ID, start, len });117    }118 119    fn add<T: Component>(&mut self, entity: Entity, value: T) {120        let (start, len) = self.payload(&value);121        self.list.push(Command::Add { entity, id: T::ID, start, len });122    }123 124    #[allow(dead_code)]125    fn remove<T: Component>(&mut self, entity: Entity) {126        self.list.push(Command::Remove { entity, id: T::ID });127    }128 129    fn despawn(&mut self, entity: Entity) {130        self.list.push(Command::Despawn(entity));131    }132 133    // Every command, in the order it was recorded. Then the Vecs are cleared,134    // which lets go of every command and payload at once.135    fn apply(&mut self, w: &mut World) -> Applied {136        let mut result = Applied::default();137        for &cmd in &self.list {138            let done = match cmd {139                Command::Spawn { signature } => {140                    self.spawned.push(w.spawn(signature));141                    Ok(())142                }143                Command::SetSpawned { pending, id, start, len } => {144                    let e = self.spawned[pending];145                    if write_component(w, e, id, &self.bytes[start..start + len]).is_none() {146                        panic!("set_spawned: spawn {pending} has no {} in its signature", w.info(id).name);147                    }148                    Ok(())149                }150                Command::Add { entity, id, start, len } => {151                    w.move_to(entity, w.signature(entity) | bit(id)).map(|()| {152                        write_component(w, entity, id, &self.bytes[start..start + len]).expect("it was just added");153                    })154                }155                Command::Remove { entity, id } => w.move_to(entity, w.signature(entity) & !bit(id)),156                Command::Despawn(entity) => w.despawn(entity),157            };158            match done {159                Ok(()) => result.applied += 1,160                Err(Dead) => result.skipped += 1,161            }162        }163        self.list.clear();164        self.bytes.clear();165        self.spawned.clear();166        self.spawns = 0;167        result168    }169}170 171// Copy a payload into e's component. None if e is dead or has no such172// component.173fn write_component(w: &mut World, e: Entity, id: u32, payload: &[u8]) -> Option<()> {174    w.get_bytes_mut(e, id)?.copy_from_slice(payload);175    Some(())176}177 178// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------179// The game180// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------181 182#[derive(Default)]183struct Stats {184    waves: u32,185    drones: u32,186    destroyed: u32,187    leaked: u32,188    shots: u32,189    hits: u32,190    misses: u32,191}192 193// Each frame's events are printed under one "frame N" line.194#[derive(Default)]195struct Log {196    frame: i32,197    printed: i32,198}199 200impl Log {201    fn event(&mut self, what: fmt::Arguments) {202        if self.printed != self.frame {203            println!("frame {}", self.frame);204            self.printed = self.frame;205        }206        println!("    {what}");207    }208}209 210// The game's state is four separate fields, so a system can walk the world's211// tables and record commands, count and log at the same time.212struct Game {213    world: World,214    commands: Commands,215    stats: Stats,216    log: Log,217}218 219fn drone_mask() -> u64 {220    mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>() | mask_of::<Health>()221}222 223fn bullet_mask() -> u64 {224    mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>() | mask_of::<Damage>() | mask_of::<Lifetime>()225}226 227fn distance(a: Vec2, b: Vec2) -> f32 {228    let dx = a.x - b.x;229    let dy = a.y - b.y;230    (dx * dx + dy * dy).sqrt()231}232 233fn toward(from: Vec2, to: Vec2, speed: f32) -> Vec2 {234    let d = distance(from, to);235    Vec2 { x: (to.x - from.x) / d * speed, y: (to.y - from.y) / d * speed }236}237 238const ORIGIN: Vec2 = Vec2 { x: 0.0, y: 0.0 };239 240// Drones come in wings of three, side by side, from each side in turn.241const ENTRY_POINTS: [Vec2; 4] = [242    Vec2 { x: 20.0, y: 0.0 },243    Vec2 { x: 0.0, y: -20.0 },244    Vec2 { x: -20.0, y: 0.0 },245    Vec2 { x: 0.0, y: 20.0 },246];247const WAVE_EVERY: i32 = 20;248const WAVES: u32 = 5;249const DRONE_SPEED: f32 = 2.0;250 251fn spawner_system(g: &mut Game) {252    if (g.log.frame - 1) % WAVE_EVERY != 0 || g.stats.waves == WAVES {253        return;254    }255    let centre = ENTRY_POINTS[g.stats.waves as usize % 4];256    let heading = toward(centre, ORIGIN, 1.0);257    for k in -1..=1 {258        // Side by side: 2 units apart, across the direction of flight.259        let side = 2.0 * k as f32;260        let at = Vec2 { x: centre.x - heading.y * side, y: centre.y + heading.x * side };261        let drone = g.commands.spawn(drone_mask());262        g.commands.set_spawned(drone, Position { at });263        g.commands.set_spawned(drone, Velocity { per_second: toward(at, ORIGIN, DRONE_SPEED) });264        g.commands.set_spawned(drone, Health { points: 100.0 });265        g.stats.drones += 1;266    }267    g.stats.waves += 1;268    g.log.event(format_args!("a wing of three drones enters at ({:.1}, {:.1})", centre.x, centre.y));269}270 271// The nearest drone to `from`, by walking every table a drone can be in.272fn nearest_drone(w: &World, from: Vec2) -> Option<Vec2> {273    let drones = Query { all: drone_mask(), none: 0 };274    let mut best = 1000000.0;275    let mut found = None;276    for t in w.tables.iter().filter(|t| t.matches(drones)) {277        for p in t.column::<Position>() {278            let d = distance(from, p.at);279            if d < best {280                best = d;281                found = Some(p.at);282            }283        }284    }285    found286}287 288// Each turret is read, then the drones are searched, then the turret is289// written: one borrow after another, never two at once, because the search290// reads every table and the turret's table is one of them.291fn turret_system(g: &mut Game, dt: f32) {292    let turrets = Query { all: mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Turret>(), none: 0 };293    for ti in 0..g.world.tables.len() {294        if !g.world.tables[ti].matches(turrets) {295            continue;296        }297        for i in 0..g.world.tables[ti].count() {298            let t = &g.world.tables[ti];299            let p = t.column::<Position>()[i];300            let Turret { cooldown, timer } = t.column::<Turret>()[i];301            // The timer stops at zero, so an idle turret is ready to fire but302            // does not save up shots.303            let mut timer = (timer - dt).max(0.0);304            let target = if timer > 0.0 { None } else { nearest_drone(&g.world, p.at) };305            if let Some(target) = target {306                timer += cooldown;307                let bullet = g.commands.spawn(bullet_mask());308                g.commands.set_spawned(bullet, p);309                g.commands.set_spawned(bullet, Velocity { per_second: toward(p.at, target, 12.0) });310                g.commands.set_spawned(bullet, Damage { amount: 30.0 });311                g.commands.set_spawned(bullet, Lifetime { seconds: 2.0 });312                g.stats.shots += 1;313            }314            g.world.tables[ti].column_mut::<Turret>()[i].timer = timer;315        }316    }317}318 319// A system is a query and a kernel. The query finds the tables; the kernel320// runs over one table's columns. Each `&mut` slice is the only way to reach its321// memory, so the compiler can vectorize without checking for overlap.322fn integrate(ps: &mut [Position], vs: &[Velocity], dt: f32) {323    for (p, v) in ps.iter_mut().zip(vs) {324        p.at.x += v.per_second.x * dt;325        p.at.y += v.per_second.y * dt;326    }327}328 329fn movement_system(w: &mut World, dt: f32) {330    let movers = Query { all: mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Velocity>(), none: 0 };331    for t in w.tables.iter_mut().filter(|t| t.matches(movers)) {332        let (ps, vs) = t.pair_mut::<Position, Velocity>();333        integrate(ps, vs, dt);334    }335}336 337fn age(ls: &mut [Lifetime], dt: f32) {338    for l in ls {339        l.seconds -= dt;340    }341}342 343// The kernel writes the lifetimes; the loop after it reads them with the344// handles. Two passes, because a column to write and the handles to read are345// two borrows of one table.346fn lifetime_system(g: &mut Game, dt: f32) {347    let q = Query { all: mask_of::<Lifetime>(), none: 0 };348    for t in g.world.tables.iter_mut().filter(|t| t.matches(q)) {349        age(t.column_mut::<Lifetime>(), dt);350        for (&e, l) in t.entities.iter().zip(t.column::<Lifetime>()) {351            if l.seconds <= 0.0 {352                g.commands.despawn(e);353                g.stats.misses += 1;354            }355        }356    }357}358 359// The first drone within reach of `at` that still has health loses `damage`.360// Returns its table, its row, and its health before the hit.361fn hit_first_drone(w: &mut World, at: Vec2, damage: f32) -> Option<(usize, usize, f32)> {362    let drones = Query { all: drone_mask(), none: 0 };363    for (ti, t) in w.tables.iter_mut().enumerate().filter(|(_, t)| t.matches(drones)) {364        let (hs, ps) = t.pair_mut::<Health, Position>();365        for (row, (h, p)) in hs.iter_mut().zip(ps).enumerate() {366            if distance(at, p.at) <= 1.0 && h.points > 0.0 {367                let before = h.points;368                h.points -= damage;369                return Some((ti, row, before));370            }371        }372    }373    None374}375 376// Every bullet against every drone. A hit lowers health in place, which is not377// a structural change; removing the bullet and setting the drone on fire are.378// A bullet that expired this frame is skipped: lifetime_system has already379// recorded its despawn, and it is only still here because nothing structural380// happens until the end of the frame.381fn collision_system(g: &mut Game) {382    let bullets = Query { all: bullet_mask(), none: 0 };383    for bi in 0..g.world.tables.len() {384        if !g.world.tables[bi].matches(bullets) {385            continue;386        }387        for b in 0..g.world.tables[bi].count() {388            let t = &g.world.tables[bi];389            if t.column::<Lifetime>()[b].seconds <= 0.0 {390                continue;391            }392            let (bullet, at, damage) = (t.entities[b], t.column::<Position>()[b].at, t.column::<Damage>()[b].amount);393            let Some((ti, row, before)) = hit_first_drone(&mut g.world, at, damage) else {394                continue;395            };396            let t = &g.world.tables[ti];397            let (drone, points) = (t.entities[row], t.column::<Health>()[row].points);398            g.stats.hits += 1;399            g.commands.despawn(bullet);400            g.log.event(format_args!("bullet {bullet} hits drone {drone}, health {points:.1}"));401            if before >= 50.0 && points < 50.0 && t.signature & mask_of::<Burning>() == 0 {402                g.commands.add(drone, Burning { per_second: 8.0 });403                g.log.event(format_args!("drone {drone} catches fire"));404            }405        }406    }407}408 409fn burn(hs: &mut [Health], bs: &[Burning], dt: f32) {410    for (h, b) in hs.iter_mut().zip(bs) {411        h.points -= b.per_second * dt;412    }413}414 415fn burning_system(w: &mut World, dt: f32) {416    let q = Query { all: mask_of::<Health>() | mask_of::<Burning>(), none: 0 };417    for t in w.tables.iter_mut().filter(|t| t.matches(q)) {418        let (hs, bs) = t.pair_mut::<Health, Burning>();419        burn(hs, bs, dt);420    }421}422 423// A destroyed drone's blast hurts every drone near it and sets it on fire.424// Lowering health is a plain write, so a blast can finish off a neighbour later425// in the same loop, and that neighbour's blast reaches back to the drone that426// started it. That drone's despawn is only recorded, so it is still in its427// table and gets an add of Burning too. By the time the buffer is applied it428// is gone, and the add is skipped.429fn blast_system(g: &mut Game, from: Entity, at: Vec2) {430    let drones = Query { all: drone_mask(), none: 0 };431    for t in g.world.tables.iter_mut().filter(|t| t.matches(drones)) {432        for i in 0..t.count() {433            let e = t.entities[i];434            if e.index == from.index || distance(t.column::<Position>()[i].at, at) >= 4.0 {435                continue;436            }437            let h = &mut t.column_mut::<Health>()[i];438            h.points -= 40.0;439            let points = h.points;440            g.commands.add(e, Burning { per_second: 8.0 });441            g.log.event(format_args!("drone {e} is caught in the blast, health {points:.1}"));442        }443    }444}445 446// Drones at zero health are destroyed; drones that reach the turret leak. Each447// row is read afresh, by number, because a blast earlier in this loop may have448// lowered its health.449fn outcome_system(g: &mut Game) {450    let drones = Query { all: drone_mask(), none: 0 };451    for ti in 0..g.world.tables.len() {452        if !g.world.tables[ti].matches(drones) {453            continue;454        }455        for i in 0..g.world.tables[ti].count() {456            let t = &g.world.tables[ti];457            let (e, at, points) = (t.entities[i], t.column::<Position>()[i].at, t.column::<Health>()[i].points);458            if points <= 0.0 {459                g.commands.despawn(e);460                g.stats.destroyed += 1;461                g.log.event(format_args!("drone {e} is destroyed"));462                blast_system(g, e, at);463            } else if distance(at, ORIGIN) < 1.5 {464                g.commands.despawn(e);465                g.stats.leaked += 1;466                g.log.event(format_args!("drone {e} reaches the turret with {points:.1} health"));467            }468        }469    }470}471 472fn main() {473    let mut g = Game { world: World::new(), commands: Commands::default(), stats: Stats::default(), log: Log::default() };474    g.world.register::<Position>();475    g.world.register::<Velocity>();476    g.world.register::<Health>();477    g.world.register::<Damage>();478    g.world.register::<Lifetime>();479    g.world.register::<Turret>();480    g.world.register::<Burning>();481 482    let tower = g.world.spawn(mask_of::<Position>() | mask_of::<Turret>());483    *g.world.get_mut::<Turret>(tower).expect("just spawned") = Turret { cooldown: 0.6, timer: 0.6 };484 485    let dt = 0.1;486    let frames = 140;487    let mut skipped = 0;488    for frame in 1..=frames {489        g.log.frame = frame;490        spawner_system(&mut g);491        turret_system(&mut g, dt);492        movement_system(&mut g.world, dt);493        lifetime_system(&mut g, dt);494        collision_system(&mut g);495        burning_system(&mut g.world, dt);496        outcome_system(&mut g);497        skipped += g.commands.apply(&mut g.world).skipped;498    }499 500    let s = &g.stats;501    println!("after {frames} frames");502    println!("    drones: {} entered, {} destroyed, {} leaked", s.drones, s.destroyed, s.leaked);503    println!("    bullets: {} fired, {} hit, {} expired", s.shots, s.hits, s.misses);504    println!("    commands skipped because their entity was already gone: {skipped}");505    println!("    {} entities alive in {} tables", g.world.live, g.world.tables.len());506    for (ti, t) in g.world.tables.iter().enumerate() {507        println!("    table {ti} {}, rows in use: {}", g.world.names(t.signature), t.count());508    }509}

Advanced · lesson 7

Layout follows access

src/7.access_patterns/access_patterns.rs

src/7.access_patterns/access_patterns.rs

Lesson 1 found the layout SIMD wants: one array per float. This lesson asks what that layout costs everywhere else. 1,048,576 bodies are stored four ways, and two kinds of loop run over each, and the program checks that all four end with the same positions.

Two kinds of loop

Stream: every body, in order, the same math. Integration is the example:

    for i in 0..n {
        vy[i] += GRAVITY * dt;
        px[i] += vx[i] * dt;

The next body is always right after the last one, so the hardware prefetcher has it ready, and SIMD can take four or eight at once if they sit side by side.

Lookup: bodies picked by index, two at a time, in no particular order. Contacts are the example, the way collision and constraints reach bodies:

    for c in cs {
        let (a, b) = (c.a as usize, c.b as usize);
        let dx = px[b] - px[a];

Each body is somewhere else in memory. What matters is how many cache lines one body's data sits in, because each one is a separate trip to memory. SIMD does not help: there are no four neighbours to load at once.

Four layouts

aos      [ x y z vx vy vz m r ][ x y z vx vy vz m r ] ...      32 bytes a body
columns  positions  [ x y z ][ x y z ][ x y z ] ...
         velocities [ vx vy vz ][ vx vy vz ] ...                 24 bytes a body
split    px [ x x x x ... ]   py [ y y y y ... ]   pz ...  vx ...  vy ...  vz ...
blocks   [ x0..x7 | y0..y7 | z0..z7 | vx0..vx7 | vy0..vy7 | vz0..vz7 ][ x8..x15 ...
  • aos keeps everything about a body together, two fields neither loop uses included.
  • columns is one array per component, each component a small struct. This is what an ECS table stores, and what lessons 2 to 6 use.
  • split is one array per float, lesson 1's move_split.
  • blocks is eight bodies at a time, each coordinate a run of eight floats. It is split cut into pieces of eight, with the pieces of one body kept near each other. The usual name is AoSoA, an array of structs of arrays.

The program prints how many 64-byte cache lines one body's position sits in:

cache lines one lookup touches: aos 1.000, columns 1.125, split 3.000, blocks 2.000

A 12-byte Vec3 crosses a line boundary 2 times in 16, hence 1.125. In split, x, y and z are in three different arrays. In a block, x and y share a line and z is in the next.

Those counts assume each array starts on a cache line. rin-dod's arena made sure of it. A Vec only promises its element type's alignment, so the two types whose count depends on it say so themselves:

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Default)]
#[repr(C, align(32))]
struct Body {

align(32) on a 32-byte body costs no padding and means no body ever straddles a line. A BodyBlock is align(64): 192 bytes, exactly three lines. For Vec3 and f32 the count comes out the same wherever the array starts.

Measured

Release (-C opt-level=3), best of three runs, on the 2.8 GHz Xeon these lessons were checked on: 4 MB of L2, 33 MB of L3. The body and contact counts were changed in a copy of the file for the first and last columns. At 65,536 bodies each layout fits in L2; at the lesson's 1,048,576 each is about the size of L3; at 8,388,608 each is 192 to 256 MB and comes from RAM.

Stream, ns per body:

layout65,5361,048,5768,388,608
aos1.824.574.64
columns2.442.963.19
split1.091.912.60
blocks1.002.673.09

Lookup, ns per contact:

layout65,5361,048,5768,388,608
aos6.4049.6076.93
columns3.8522.6564.14
split6.8944.92103.67
blocks7.4755.4192.91

These are slower than rin-dod's tables for the same lesson, lookups most. So rin-dod's C, built with clang -O2, ran turn about with this program on the same day, at a million bodies. The two came out the same within noise, about 50 ns a lookup for aos and split, 28 to 36 for columns: the difference is the machine on the day, not the language. The order of the layouts is the same as rin-dod's. Where two numbers are within about 20 percent, the order can change from run to run.

What it says:

  • Split wins the stream and loses the lookup. From RAM it streams a fifth faster than columns, and looks up 1.6 times slower: three lines a body instead of one.
  • Columns win the lookup everywhere and come second or third in the stream. AoS also has one line a body, but its bodies are 32 bytes, so the same lookups spread over more memory. At a million bodies, columns' positions are 12 MB and sit comfortably in L3; AoS spreads them over 32 MB, about all of it.
  • Blocks are the compromise. In L2 they streamed as fast as split, and from L3 they sit between split and columns. From RAM their stream fell back to about columns' speed, as it did for rin-dod. They look up a little worse than split in cache, and better from RAM.
  • Out of cache, a lookup costs fifteen to forty times a streamed body. From RAM, 64 to 104 ns a contact against 2.6 to 4.6 ns a body. Turning lookups into something closer to a stream, by sorting contacts or walking space in order, usually saves more than any layout choice.

What the compiler makes of it

rustc 1.97, -C opt-level=3, x86-64 Linux, read from --emit asm (lesson 1 shows how):

loopbodies a passinstructions a passshuffles
integrate_aos2292
integrate_columns47730
integrate_split4200
integrate_blocks8370
integrate_split, -C target-cpu=native8140
contacts_columns1 contact290
contacts_split1 contact360

Blocks vectorize as cleanly as split: the inner loop over eight lanes is a fixed-size loop over consecutive floats, which compilers turn into whole registers. The contact loops are one contact a pass in every layout. The columns, split and blocks streams are the loops clang made of rin-dod's C, instruction for instruction, since both are LLVM. The contact loops are four instructions longer than clang's, and the next paragraph is why.

Bounds checks. The contact loops index with numbers read from memory, so each index is checked, in Release too: a compare and a branch that's never taken. contacts_columns has two a contact, 4 of its 29 instructions. contacts_split indexes three slices with each of a and b, which was six checks and 44 instructions, until it cut the three to one length first, as lesson 1's move_split does:

    let n = px.len();
    let (py, pz) = (&mut py[..n], &mut pz[..n]);

Now a check of a against px covers py and pz too: two checks, 36 instructions. In a loop that waits on memory for every contact, neither number shows in the timing, at any of the three sizes. Bounds checks cost most where nothing else does, in streams, and that's where zip and cut slices take them out.

**target-cpu=native and blocks.** On this AVX-512 machine, LLVM vectorized integrate_blocks the wrong way round: not the eight lanes of a block, but lane 0 of eight different blocks, then lane 1, gathering and scattering each float with vgatherdps and vscatterdps. 267 instructions a pass, 80 of them gathers and scatters, and about ten times slower than the default build: 9.6 ns a body at 65,536 bodies instead of 1.0. The same thing happened to lesson 1's move_aos. "Vectorized" and "fast" are different claims; read the assembly before believing either.

Two bodies in one slice

A contact reads two bodies and writes both, and both are in the same slice, sometimes the same body. In rin-dod, the loop took two pointers into the array. Rust won't lend two &mut into one slice at once, and the loop doesn't need them. It reads both bodies, then writes one, then the other:

        let (p, q) = (&bodies[a].position, &bodies[b].position);
        let (dx, dy, dz) = (q.x - p.x, q.y - p.y, q.z - p.z);
        let p = &mut bodies[a].position;
        p.x += dx * STIFFNESS;

Two shared borrows to read, then one &mut at a time to write. When a and b are the same body, dx is 0 and both writes leave it as it was, exactly as rin-dod's did, so the checksums match to the bit. The machine code is the same loads and stores as rin-dod's: the borrows only decide what the source may say.

In between

Engines that have both kinds of loop do one of these:

  • Blocks, as above. One layout, decent at both.
  • Gather, work, scatter. Storage stays in columns or AoS, good for lookups. The hot loop copies a batch of bodies into a wide layout, x's in one register and y's in another, does its math, and copies them back. The copy pays off when the same batch is worked on many times, as a constraint solver does over several iterations. Box2D v3 solves contacts this way, four or eight at a time.
  • Two layouts for two jobs. A particle system that only ever streams stores split. The bodies that collision looks up stay in columns.

How an ECS decides

An ECS does not decide where each float goes. The component is the unit it stores together, and the programmer decides what a component is.

  • Tables. kayan, Unity's entities, Bevy and flecs keep one table per archetype, with one column per component. That is this lesson's columns layout: an array per component, and each component's fields side by side inside it. Unity cuts its tables into 16 KB chunks, each holding every component array for as many entities as fit, which is close to blocks at the level of components.
  • Sparse sets. EnTT stores each component in its own dense array with a lookup table from entity to index, and can keep several components in the same order ("groups") so a system over them streams. Bevy lets each component choose: table storage, or a sparse set for components added and removed often.
  • Systems are streams. A system is a query and a kernel, as in lesson 6: the ECS finds the tables that match, and hands the kernel each table's columns as slices. That stream over columns is the fast path every ECS is built for. Systems that say which columns they read (&[T]) and which they write (&mut [T]) are what lets a scheduler run them in parallel, and in Rust the borrow checker can check the split.
  • Lookups go through the handle. Reaching one entity is handle, slot, table and row, then the column: get in lesson 4, and in the course's 2.5. That is this lesson's lookup loop with an extra hop in front. ECS code keeps lookups for the places that need them, such as relationships between entities and collision, and finds the rest by query.

So the decisions that are yours:

  1. Keep components small, to what one stream system reads. A component a system reads half of is AoS's wasted bytes again.
  2. Leave components as small structs, Position { x, y, z }, unless a profiler shows a stream over them is the bottleneck. They are the best layout for lookups and good enough for most streams.
  3. For a hot stream over huge counts, particles above all, store split or blocks, or gather into them for the hot loop.
  4. Make lookups rarer and less random before tuning their layout.

Try

  1. Sort cs by a before the timing loops (cs.sort_by_key(|c| c.a)) and run --time again. Which lookup numbers change, and by how much?
  2. Set BODY_COUNT and CONTACT_COUNT to 8388608 and run --time in Release. Compare with the tables above.
  3. Make the contacts push velocities too, vx, vy and vz of both bodies. How many lines does a lookup touch in each layout now?
  4. Build with -C target-cpu=native and compare the stream column. Then rewrite integrate_blocks so the native build does eight lanes of one block at a time instead of gathering. (One way to start: a function that takes one block, marked #[inline(never)].)
  5. Write contacts_gather: for every eight contacts, copy the sixteen bodies' positions into [f32; 8] arrays, do the arithmetic over the arrays, and copy back. Contacts that share a body in the same eight break it; find the case and decide what to do about it.
  6. Make Body 64 bytes with fields neither loop uses, and watch aos in both tables.
  7. Remove align(32) from Body, print the address of aos[0] with {:p}, and work out whether the line count still holds for it.
